en: The Sixth Chapter.

Having thus stated the two divisions of poetry by way of *dhvani* (suggested meaning) and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion), he further states the two divisions by way of being visible (*dṛśya*) and audible (*śravya*):
"Furthermore, poetry is considered to be of two kinds according to the distinction between the visible and the audible."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) Having spoken of poetry intended for hearing (*śravya-kāvya*), he says "Thus—Dhvani" in order to speak of dramatic poetry (*dṛśya-kāvya*), which is the essence of drama (*nāṭya*).
Locanā:
(Lo, a) He states the connection with the section [of the work]— namely, "thus": the visible object therein is that which is to be represented—
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, kha) *Abhineya* refers to drama (*nāṭya*).
Locanā:
(lo, ā) *Dṛśya* is that which primarily consists of what is visible.
"Śravya" means merely that which is to be heard.
"Abhineya" refers to that which is to be enacted by actors through gestures and so forth; this is the implied meaning. He states the reason for its designation as "rūpaka" (drama):
Metaphor (*rūpaka*) arises from the superimposition of that [other] form.
Locanā:
(lo, i) It is called *rūpaka* because it represents other actors as having the form (*rūpa*) of others, such as Rāma;
that visible poetry is termed *rūpaka* because of the superimposition (*āropa*) of the essential nature of Rāma and others upon the actor.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ga) Since "drama" (*nāṭya*) and "representation" (*rūpaka*) are synonyms, he says [the following] to state the reason for the designation "representation" (*rūpa*): "Of that"—meaning, because of the superimposition (*āropa*) of the essential nature of Rāma and others; the meaning is that this makes known the superimposition of that [nature] through both costume (*veśa*) and acting (*abhinaya*). He asks: what is this acting? He says:
Mimetic representation (abhinaya) is the imitation of states; it is fourfold:
the physical (āṅgika), the vocal (vācika), the extrinsic (āhārya), and likewise the internal (sāttvika).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, gha) Since it is the cause for the superimposition of that [meaning], the mimetic representation (abhinaya) is questioned—"What is this?"—and it is said:
"It is the artificial" (āhārya).
The bodily and vocal [abhinayas] are both artificial (āhārya), as is the involuntary (sāttvika); thus there is a fourfold division.
Among these, because of the lack of intensity of inner being (sattva) in drama (nāṭya), the artificial [expressions] are performed due to the absence of immersion in rasa.
Those produced by the influence of *rasa* through the predominance of *sattva* are *sāttvika*.
Locanā:
(*lo*, *ī*) Those performed by the limbs are *āṅgika*.
The vocal [expression] is that which consists of speech;
the artificial [expression] is the arrangement of crowns, armlets, and so forth;
the sattvic [expression] consists of paralysis, perspiration, and the like.
Abhinaya is the imitation of the conditions of Rāma, Yudhiṣṭhira, and others by actors through means such as the limbs (*aṅga*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi ṅa):
He states the definition of abhinaya, which is common to all four [types], beginning with "by actors through the limbs and so forth."
"Aṅga" means the body;

by the word "ādi" (and so forth), speech is included. "States" refers to its properties (*dharmas*), such as the mind, the words of discourse, paleness, and the maintenance of physical appearance. "Imitation" (*anukaraṇa*) of that [state] is the communication of it through the assumption of that very form.
He states the divisions of drama (rūpaka):

"The drama (nāṭaka), then the play (prakaraṇa), the monologue (bhāṇa), the interlude (vyāyoga), the mixed drama (samavakāra), the farce (ḍima), the hunting-drama (īhāmṛga), the moon-play (aṅka), the street-scene (vīthī), and the farce (prahasana)—these are the ten types of dramas. (VisSd 6.3)
Furthermore:
the *nāṭikā*, *troṭaka*, *goṣṭhī*, *saṭṭaka*, *nāṭyarāsaka*, *prasthāna*, *ullāpya*, *kāvya*, *preṅkhaṇa*, and likewise the *rāsaka*. (VisSd 6.4)
Saṃlāpaka, Śrīgadita, Śilpaka, Vilāsikā, Durmallikā, Prakaraṇī, Hallīśa, and Bhāṇikā. (VisSd 6.5)
The wise have declared there to be eighteen minor dramatic forms (uparūpaka);
it is held that, without distinction, the characteristics of all of them are like those of the *nāṭaka*.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ca) Having proclaimed the tenfold drama (*rūpaka*), he now proclaims the eighteenfold drama,
beginning with "the *kiñcanāṭikā*."
"Consisting of drama" is one [point].
Regarding "without distinction": it has been stated that those very specific [details] are what differentiate [the types];
setting those aside, the definition (lakṣma) or characteristic of all [types] is exactly like that of the *nāṭaka*—this is the meaning.
Locanā:
(lo, u) "Lakṣma" refers to the definition that will be stated hereafter;
it applies to all forms of drama, such as the *prakaraṇa* and others, as well as the minor dramatic forms (*uparūpaka*), such as the *nāṭikā*.
In that regard:
A *nāṭaka* (drama) should have a well-known plot and be endowed with the five junctures (*saṃdhi*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, cha) He states the definition of the *nāṭaka*:
"The *nāṭaka*—[it is] that which possesses well-known plots and so forth;
it is endowed with qualities such as grace (*vilāsa*) and prosperity (*ṛddhi*), and is characterized by various manifestations of splendor. (VisSd 6.7)
The arising of pleasure and pain, continuous with various flavors—
therein, the numbers beginning with five and ending with ten are proclaimed.

A hero (nāyaka) is considered to be one of renowned lineage, a royal sage (rājarṣi), fierce and noble, and possessed of majesty; he may be divine, or both divine and non-divine, and endowed with excellent qualities.
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ja) [text missing in printed edition]
There should be only one hero, either the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) or the heroic (*vīra*).
Vijñapriyā:
"Only" means precisely that.
Even though various intermediate sentiments (rasas) may arise in a drama, they are merely its subordinate members (aṅgas).
The resolution of all sentiments occurs within either the erotic (śṛṅgāra) or the heroic (vīra); the meaning is that one of these alone is the primary principal sentiment (aṅgin).
All other sentiments are subordinate members; the marvelous (adbhuta) should be employed in the conclusion (nirvahaṇa).
Four or five principal men occupied with the task [should perform it];
its binding is said to be like the tip of a cow's tail. VisSd 6.11.
Locanā: (lo,
ū) She states the definition according to the enumeration— namely, "naṭakām" and so forth—
as was spoken by the poet.
"And by means of qualities such as the display of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) joined with various manifestations.

In the *nirvahaṇa*, the final juncture, the mention of "four or five" is merely illustrative; one should not restrict the number of those engaged in the performance of the action, for a large number would cause difficulty in the acting (*abhinaya*).
*Khyāta* refers to a narrative well-known from such works as the *Rāmāyaṇa*,
for example, the life-story of Rāma and so forth.
The junctures (*sandhi*) will be explained [later].
It is called "having great companions" because it is endowed with various manifestations.
The arising of pleasure and pain is well-known from the accounts of Rāma, Yudhiṣṭhira, and others.
The royal sages (rājarṣis) include Duṣyanta and others.
The divine ones are Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others. "Divine" (divya) refers to one who, though divine, possesses the conceit of being a human being.
Just as with Śrī Rāmacandra;
some say that the digits should be made increasingly subtle, like the tip of the end of a cow's tail.
Locanā:
"Subtle" means very small.

Others, however, say: "Just as in a cow's tail some hairs are short and some are long, so here some actions are completed in the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture), some in the *pratimukha* (development juncture), and likewise some in each of the others."
The drama should feature characters whose actions are directly observable, be radiant with aesthetic flavor (rasa) and emotion (bhāva),
have words and meanings that are not obscure, and be composed of short, concise verses.
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) To the question "What is this flaw? he says: "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*).
The two leaders are the hero (*nāyaka*) and the heroine (*nāyikā*).
The sense is that the conduct of one or both of them should be shown there directly.

Regarding the *cūrṇaka* verses, their brevity and the fact that they yield the fruit of awakening instantaneously—due to their consisting of a single interrupted intermediate meaning—are established by logical necessity, with the exception of the final act (*aṅka*).
An interrupted intermediate meaning is one where the dots (*bindu*) are slightly connected.
One should not be occupied with many tasks, nor should one be intent on the mere accumulation of seeds.
It is joined with various types of meters and does not contain an excessive abundance of *padya* verses; [this is because],
as Locanā says (*lo*, *ḷ*), all objects [of worldly concern] are cut off therein.
An abundance of verses is to be avoided because it causes distress during the performance;
however, this rule is established provided that it does not conflict with necessary duties.
It should not be composed as a narrative to be completed over many days;
rather, it should have a nearby hero and be joined by only three or four characters.
Summoning from afar, killing, combat, the ruin of kingdom, country, and so forth, marriage, feasting, the utterance of a curse, death, and likewise sexual union; (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.16).
Biting with the teeth, tearing with the nails, and whatever else causes shame;
drinking from the lips while lying in bed, and the confinement within cities and the like.

"Devoid of bathing and anointing, and free from excessive elaboration. Regarding the statement that "the marvelous (*adbhuta*) task is to be accomplished in the *nirvahaṇa* [concluding juncture]," as it is known from the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other works, the meaning is that in the *nirvahaṇa*, which consists of the gathering together of various scattered matters, the marvelous task is to be performed.
For it will be stated that the *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture) is the unification, in the form of a distinctive excellence, of matters scattered across various locations.
The *sandhis* (junctures) will be explained;
therein, the general definition of a *sandhi* is the connection of sub-plot elements—each of which is linked to a single primary purpose—with a single intermediate objective.
And in that context, "by each one" is the meaning.

Therein, the *mukha-sandhi* (opening juncture) is the emergence of the seed (*bīja*) accompanied by energy (*utsāha*) within the plot (*itivṛtta*). The plot (*itivṛtta*) is the narrative context to be enacted.

The seed (*bīja*) is that very sprout; its manifestation through effort is the *pratimukha* juncture (*sandhi*). The *garbha* juncture is the manifestation of the primary means to the fruit, characterized by fluctuations of decline and emergence, and joined with hope for the attainment of the objective. The *vimarṣa* juncture is the further development of the primary means to the main fruit—which had already begun to emerge from the *garbha* juncture—but which is obstructed by curses and other impediments.

The *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture) is the attainment of a single unified purpose for those elements possessing seeds, which have been scattered throughout and whose meanings were fully stated in the *sandhi*s [of the preceding acts].
This is called the *upasaṃhṛti-sandhi* (concluding juncture). These are the five *sandhi*s.
*Mahāsahāyamati*:
Sugrīva and others were the great companions (*mahāsahāya*) of Rāma and the rest.
The *nāyaka* is the principal character (*pradhānapātra*).
Since it has been stated that "the numbers there are ten plus five more," he describes the essential nature of the number, which consists of measurement, with the words beginning "pratyakṣanetrī.
The connection with the subsequent phrase is: "is proclaimed as a number" (*aṅka*). "Pratyakṣanetrī" means having direct perception as its eye.
The leader is the protagonist;
such is that [drama] in which his deeds are directly witnessed. "Rasa and bhāva," etc.
*Bhāva* refers to the inner intention (*ākūta*) of the hero and the heroine;
it is composed in Sanskrit using short *cūrṇaka* verses and avoiding long compounds; and it is characterized by its structural divisions (*vicchinna*).
The meaning of a pervasive *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is that which is interrupted and then concluded within the form of a single section;
such is what is called a "point" (*bindu*). Even when there is an interruption of an intermediate matter, a "point" is a subject that arouses an expectation for the statement of another *prasaṅga*.

Because it will be stated later that "the cause for the non-interruption of the *bindu* [essential element] during an interruption of intermediate matters," the meaning is "possessing a small portion of that. The meaning of *bīja* (seed) is the sprout of the context of what is intended to be enacted.
Nor does it possess that dissolution or that interruption.
He states the prohibition regarding the elements to be enacted within the *aṅka*—namely, "calling from afar.
This means the calling of a person situated at a distance.
"Bhojana" means eating food;

it signifies a prohibition against consuming even those things that are to be bitten with the teeth or cut with the nails. The meaning is that even such things should not be feigned as being consumed.
The intention is that the performance of these [scenes] would be inauspicious for the members of the assembly (*sadasya*).
Locanā:

By the words "not many" (*na-aneka*) and so forth—[it is implied that] the story itself should be performed in a single day within the act (*aṅka*]; thus, "three or four" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), as before.
The connection is with the phrase "avoided by [the faults] such as 'calling from afar' (*dūrāhvāna*) and so forth.
Furthermore, battles, combats, and the like should be depicted through the mouth of any character whatsoever, or by some other means arising from the poet's creative intuition (*pratibhā*);
this will be stated later in the words "by means of the introduction of a purpose" (*arthopakṣepakaiḥ*).
[One should likewise offer] to the queen, her attendants, and so forth, as well as to ministers and merchants.
"Endowed with direct and varied actions arising from the [dramatic] sentiments and emotions (*bhāva-rasa*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is "endowed with direct and varied actions of the queen, her attendants, and so forth."
Regarding the phrase "arising from the essence of emotional states" (*bhāvarasodbhavaiḥ*): *bhāva* refers to playfulness (*līlā*), and *rasa* refers to wit (*vaidagdhya*).
Therefore, there is no tautology with the expression "resplendent with *rasa* and *bhāva*."
An act (aṅka) is defined as that in which all the characters have exited at the end.
The *bindu* and other [mudrās] will be explained later.
The *saṃdhyāvandana* (evening prayers) is mandatory.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, ṭha) "Kandhyāvandanādi" (the kissing of the cheeks and so forth) should be understood as referring to the hero who is attached to another woman. Following the introduction of the "aṅka" (act), he states the "garbhāṅka" (intermediate act):

That other act which has entered the belly [of the main plot], beginning with the entrance to the stage door and so forth, is the "Act within an Act" (garbhāṅka); it possesses a seed and is also endowed with fruit.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍa) An *antaraṅka* (intermediate act) is another act in the form of an internal division occurring within a principal act (*pradhānāṅka*). He states its definition [as follows]: "In the interior of the act...
First, the entrance of the actors onto the stage by means of dramatic representation is the *raṅgadvāra* (stage-door).
He will state this with the words, "Because [it occurs] prior to the *abhinaya*," and so forth; here, *abhinaya* refers to the presentation of the dramatic subject matter (*nāṭyavastu*).
Since there is no fixed rule that the *garbhāṅka* must occur in the first act alone, he says: "from the *raṅgadvāra*, the *āmukha*, and so on.
*Āmukha* means the prologue (*prastāvanā*), the definition of which will be stated later.
At the opening of the stage door in the first act;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādipadāt*), there is the inclusion of the two types of *viṣkambhaka*—pure and mixed—as well as the *praveśaka*, whose characteristics will be described later.
For it will be stated: "A *viṣkambhaka* is a dramatic performance that indicates portions of the story already occurred or those yet to occur."
That which is performed by people of middle status is pure;
that performed by those of middle and low status is mixed;
and that performed solely by low-status people is a *praveśaka*.
However, their occurrence consists of complete acts (*aṅka*).
Regarding "act within an act" (*aṅkodara*): the meaning is that within the midst of a primary drama, the presentation of another drama by some character is called a "womb-act" (*garbhāṅka*).
He states the purpose of demonstrating that [seed] as follows: "Possessing the seed" (*sabīja*) is used because of that demonstration;
it means possessing both of those two, because of the attainment of the sprout and the fruit of the primary subject matter to be enacted in the drama.
For example, in the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, Kohala says to Rāvaṇa:
“The drama of Sītā’s self-choice marriage has been composed as if for your sake, to be drunk in by many ears and beheld by numerous long eyes.”

Thus, the intermediate act (*garbhāṅka*) named "Sītā’s Svayaṃvara" has been composed with these [verses]. *Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍha): He shows that intermediate act, beginning with "As in the Bālarāmāyaṇa," and so forth; for there, a certain poet has composed the "Sītā-svayaṃvara," which is endowed with qualities such as being "pleasing to the ear," and so on.
The drama named [the *Mahānāṭaka*] was presented by the chamberlain to Rāvaṇa;

because it contains the seeds of the abduction of Sītā, the golden deer, and the anger of Rāma—[all] resulting from hearing that [news]—and because it indicates the form of the abduction of Sītā, it possesses those two [characteristics].
It was composed in such a manner, and so forth.

The meaning is that [the work] has been composed by someone, as indicated by such statements; for there is no composition by him [the author] through the words of the chamberlain (*kañcukin*). — *Locanā* —
(Ro, Ai) Even though Rāvaṇa is a dancer in this inner act (*garbhāṅka*), which is to be performed by other actors, he is the spectator.

In that regard, first comes the *pūrvaraṅga* and the worship of the assembly (*sabhāpūjā*); after that, the narration of the poet’s name and so forth, and then the prologue (*āmukha*) of the drama. (Viśvavidyāsāra 6.21)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṇa) Having concluded the discussion on the *garbhāṅka* as a digression, he states what is to be performed in the drama at hand, beginning with "therein, first": the *pūrvaraṅga* is the entire sequence of ritual actions—from the stage door and so forth, via the actors' preliminary performances, up to the exit of the *sūtradhāra*—of that which is called a *nāṭaka*.
The meaning is "even the mention.
Locanā:
(lo, o) Regarding the phrase "saṃjñā and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), [names such as] *gotra* and others are included.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "the statement of the name, nature, and so forth of the drama as well.
"Therein" means in the drama.
That which [is performed] prior to the dramatic subject matter for the sake of pacifying obstacles on the stage...
Those who are skilled in performance carry out the preliminary rites; that is called the *pūrvaraṅga*.
Although its ancillaries, such as sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and the rest, are numerous,
nevertheless the *nāndī* must necessarily be performed for the sake of pacifying obstacles (*vighna*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) He explains the etymology of the term *pūrvaraṅga* for this [work] with the words "that which is called *nāṭya*.
*Nāṭyavastu* refers to the subject matter to be enacted, that is, the substance in the form of a narrative such as the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
"Kuśīlavas" refers to the *sūtradhāra*, actors (*naṭa*), and so forth.
"Pratyāhārādi" refers to the specific actions of the *sūtradhāra*, actors, and others, beginning with *pratyāhāra*. — Locanā.

The ancillaries such as *pratyāhāra* and so forth, which are to be performed by the actor alone for the sake of pacifying obstacles on the stage, should be understood from the authoritative treatises (*ākaras*).
Since they are not to be performed by the poet, they are not described here. He states its essential nature:
Locanā: (Lo,
a) Because a hymn of praise joined with words of benediction is employed at the beginning of this drama.
Therefore, for gods, brahmins, kings, and others, it is designated by the name *nāndī*.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ā) "Blessing" (*āśis*) means the prayer or aspiration for gods, brahmins, kings, and so forth; it is that which is joined with the speech expressing such [aspiration].
It is invariably and necessarily employed in dramas and the like; its occurrence is not occasional.
It is established as "nāndī" from the verbal root *nand*.
It proclaims auspiciousness through conchs, moons, lotuses, ruddy geese, and white water-lilies,
and is composed of ten or eight words.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) He states the etymological derivation of the term *nāndī*—namely, "the word of benediction" (*āśīrvacana*).
*Nāndī* is prosperity that accords with one's aspirations.

In the etymological derivation of the term *nāndī*, it is said that *nāndī* means "prosperity" (*samṛddhi*). Since the *nāndī*—consisting of words of praise—is set forth and heard among those present in the assembly, therefore the speech itself, by virtue of its connection to that [prosperity], is called *nāndī*.
The grammatical construction is: "it is a benedictory utterance for the gods, the twice-born, kings, and so forth."
Furthermore, such a description of the *nāndī* does not belong to Muni [Bharata]; in his view, the *raṅgadvāra* itself is the *nāndī*.
However, it will become clear later that this description of the *nāndī* belongs only to those authors of *kārikās* who differ from the Sage.
He states what its essential nature is by saying "auspicious" (*maṅgalya*).
The meaning is that one or another of these [two] alone is to be praised. Regarding the phrase "with twelve words" (*padaiḥ dvādaśabhiḥ*):
here, "word" (*pada*) refers both to a quarter-verse of a *śloka* and to a word ending in a case-suffix (*vibhaktyanta*).
It is intended according to what is possible;
the meaning is that it is joined with those [qualities] other than that.
— Locanā:
(Lo, i) By the word "ut" [in the definition], it is indicated that [the *muktaka*] is sometimes joined with eight or twelve words.
An example of one with eight words is found in the *Anargharāghava*: “niṣpratyūham” and so forth.
An example of one with twelve words is found in the *Puṣpamālā* of my venerable father: [text follows].
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) "In the *Anargharāghava*, [the work] consists of eight-pada verses.
Here, the quality of having eight padas is established by the eight padas of the two verses beginning with "niṣpratyūha" and ending with "viramati mahākalpa."

And we worship without hindrance the two eyes of the Blessed One, characterized by the grace of the moon, which possess a brilliant light capable of providing a feast for the cakora birds that are the eyes of lovers;
by means of which the lotus-bud of the navel—possessing a sweet beauty charmingly half-awakened and rendered as if half-asleep—is made the rival of the conch shell.
To this it must be said: although there are twelve words consisting of inflected bases in this passage, how is it that eight words are shown?
Even though both [numbers] exist, the explanation was given because the state of having eight words is not lost and because showing that [number] is appropriate.
In the event that eight-word lines are impossible, he provides an example of a *nāndī* consisting of twelve words in the form of inflected phrases:
"May the daughter of the Lord of Mountains— whose head bears the celestial river, who is as beautiful as the moon-faced consort of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva),
and who is full of gentle smiles when her own beloved bows at her feet— be the cause of your prosperity."
The same applies elsewhere;
this has been stated according to the opinion of some that this is the *nāndī*.
In reality, however, others maintain that "the introductory rite (*pūrvaraṅga*) is a constituent part called the *raṅgadvāra*."
Vijñapriyā: (vi, dha) This is the *nāndī*; the meaning is that the *nāndī* consists of words of benediction.

By the statement "for the pacification of obstacles on the stage" (*raṅgavighnopaśāntaye*), it has been stated that the preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*) has the pacification of stage-obstacles as its fruit; nevertheless, the *nāndī* must certainly be performed for the sake of pacifying obstacles—this was said according to the opinion of a certain author of a commentary on drama other than the Sage (Bharata).
In reality, however, others say that the *raṅgadvāra* alone is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the preliminary rite, and not the *nāndī*. This is the meaning.
As it has been said:
"Since the enactment (abhinaya) is introduced here first of all,
the 'Entrance to the Stage' (raṅgadvāra) should therefore be understood as consisting of vocal and physical enactment."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, because this aforementioned *nāndī* must first be performed by the actors themselves at the stage-door (*raṅgadvāra*), the Great Sage did not provide an instruction for it [in the text].
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, na) He presents the verse that indicates the constituent parts of the stage door: "Because the dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) is indeed here.
The meaning is "because of being first," which refers to its primacy even among the words of benediction (*āśīrvacana*).
[He then mentions] "speech and body" (*vāgaṅga*).
The meaning is that it consists of both vocal expression (vāgabhinaya) and physical expression (aṅgābhinaya).
Here, by the phrase "because of its being first," the status of the *raṅgadvāra* as a constituent part of the *pūrvaraṅga* is shown; the intention is not, however, that this applies to the *nāndī*.
He states that even the Great Sage’s failure to demonstrate its status as a preliminary rite (*pūrvaraṅga*) or a constituent part (*aṅga*) serves as proof for its [status as a *stotra*];
this is expressed by the phrase "in the manner described.
The meaning is: "in the manner consisting of twelve or eight lines (*pada*)."
Since the *maharṣi* has not specified the *nāndī* itself,
nor even its performance, it follows that it is to be performed by the actors alone.

The meaning is that it must necessarily be performed by the actors themselves, who follow the opinion of those other than the *maharṣi*, according to the rule that "in drama, the *nāndī* must be performed."
The meaning is: "not by those who follow the opinion of the Great Sage.

Sūtradhāra: Who is this who, by addressing me as "Noble Lady," even provides me with assistance?
(Looking) Alas! What a most piteous situation has arisen!

“Having resided for a very long time in the palace of the Lord of Laṅkā, this Lakṣmaṇa now drags Sītā— who is heavy with child— away to the forest from the inhabited country, as Rāma is agitated by the fear of public scandal.”

In this context, the stage director (sūtradhāra), desiring to summon his own wife for the purpose of performing a dance, departed after indicating the entrance of Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa with the words, "Here is Lakṣmaṇa leading Sītā away to the forest," and while still surpassing his own performance, he enacted another performance.
Vijñapriyā:
By saying "having descended from here," she gave instructions regarding her departure upon being called by the weaver’s wife.
Regarding the phrase "of the Lord of Laṅkā":
the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that she was exiled—that is, driven out—from the country of Ayodhyā while pregnant with a heavy burden.
To explain the meaning of the expression "surpassing her own practice" (*svaprayogamatiśayāna*), he provides the following commentary: "by means of the application of an excellence."
"Thus the *prayoga* is indicated"—the meaning is that another *prayoga*, consisting of the entrance of Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, has been indicated.
Regarding the word "indicated" (*sūcita*), there is a variant reading in some places as "employed" (*prayojita*).
Locanā:
"Lo, here!"—
here, the meaning of the noble word refers to Sītā, who is intended as the character on stage;
however, the form of the *naṭī* (the actress) is understood by the *sūtradhāra* (director) as surpassing his own performance through the presentation of the subject matter at hand.
When the playwright describes a time that has already begun, the entry of a character based upon that [time] is what sets the action in motion. (VisSd 6.37)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) Regarding the initiator [of action], he says "time" by way of its temporal basis;
that is, the basis for that [action] which is indicated by it.
For example: "Having attained the manifest... and so forth (p. 332);
and "Then enters Rāma as previously described. In these cases, through a single entrance, another purpose is accomplished.
Indeed, that object of knowledge should be understood by the wise as being attached to the name during the stage of application.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) He states the characteristic of *avalagita*: "wherein, in one place" (*yatraikatra*).
Another [commentator] explains: "when there is a single application" (*yatraikatra prayoge sati*).
The meaning is that, because the application of that [element] is indicated as being equal through its integration (*samāveśāt*), another effect is accomplished.
As in the *Śākuntala*, the Director says to the Actress:
"I am yours by the passion of your song... (p. 333).
Then follows the entry of the king.
Here, the other components of the *vīthī* should be applied as available.
In this context, at the outset:
The other components of the *vīthī*, excluding the *uddhātyaka* and the *kāvalagita*, will be described hereafter.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭha) "I am yours.

Here, while there was the employment of praising the song, another task—the king’s entrance—was accomplished. Therefore, it should be understood that the distinction lies in the recourse to time within the instigator.

Having thus described the five varieties of the *udghātaka* (the introductory element) as part of the *prastāvanā* (prologue), he states— "they are to be employed here"— meaning that within that same performance (*prayoga*), the constituent parts (*vīthyaṅgas*) of the minor dramatic form (*uparūpaka*) called *vīthī* should also be used as they may be available.
He will later describe the ten constituent parts of that [minor form], beginning with the *udghātyaka*, the *avalagita*, and so forth.
Since the *udghātyaka* and *avalagita* have also been mentioned by way of their introductory divisions (*āmukhaprabheda*), he says—
"the others [belong] to the *udghātyaka* and *avalagita*"— implying that because they share a portion of those [divisions], their constituent elements (*aṅga*) should also be applied here.
As for the *nakhakuṭṭa*, however:
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ḍa) These five varieties of *āmukha* have been described as being composed of the entry of the characters already present, the entry of other characters indicated [by them], and the combination of both;
however, there is also a sixth variety called *nakhakuṭṭa*, which is composed of the indication of characters who have not yet entered. Thus he says: "But the *nakhakuṭṭa*..."
Where that which is spoken from behind the scenes is heard, as well as speech directed toward the empty space (ākāśa).
Even when relying [on these], one should employ some one of these varieties of the prologue (*āmukha*) in plays (*nāṭaka*) and similar works. (VisSd 6.40)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) He states its definition: "In the costume" (*nepathya*), etc.

The meaning is that the *āmukha* (prologue) should be performed by relying on a character who has been introduced in the dressing room—the place for arranging the costume—or whose speech is directed toward the empty space (*ākāśa*).

Thus, there are six varieties of the *āmukha* (prologue). Therefore, having briefly introduced either the subject matter or the characters, the director should exit at the end of the prologue and then present the main plot (*vastu*). VisSd 6.41.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṇa) "Therefore, having indicated the meaning" means that the holder of the thread (sūtradhṛk), having either indicated or implied the meaning—which is distinct from the vessel (pātra)—should exit at the conclusion of such an introductory scene (prastāvanā). This is the sense.
*Vastu* refers to the plot (*itivṛtta*).
Locanā:
(*lo*, *u*) "Plot" (*itivṛtta*) refers to the subject matter of the present work, which has been heard from the mouth of some person standing before one.
And the elaboration of the characters occurs, by implication, solely through the medium of the prologue (*prastāvanā*).

Although it is stated that no character may enter the stage unless they have been previously indicated, and thus all characters must enter the stage only after having been indicated, nevertheless, following the prologue, the characters who are to enter do so in the manner described.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "indication by means of artistic embellishments (*vicchitti*).

However, in some cases, there is indication through the entrance of characters possessed of agitation and so forth, and not even the dropping of the curtain (*apaṭīkṣepa*); as for example, in the *Candrakalā*: "Entering without the dropping of the curtain, the Śabara is agitated," and so on.
Furthermore, this subject matter (*vastu*) is conceived by the wise as being of two kinds.
Locanā:
(lo, ū) "By the wise authors of treatises, there may be one [type] that is primary and another that is incidental. (VisSd 6.42)
Authority is mastery over the fruit, and the one possessing authority is its lord;
the life-story of such a person is called "authoritative" (ādhikārika) by poets. (Viśvavidyā 6.43)
Regarding the fruit, it refers to the principal fruit;
for example, the *Bālarāmāyaṇa* is a work concerning the life of Rāma.
*Vijñapriyā*:
In the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*, it is stated that "the life of Rāma" (*rāmacarita*) refers to this:
"I am Rāma, the Lord whose fruit is the slaying of Rāvaṇa and others"; the meaning is that his life story constitutes the primary subject matter (*ādhikārika*).

However, that which serves as an accessory to this is considered "incidental" (prāsaṅgika). That conduct which exists for the purpose of providing an accessory to this primary plot (adhikāriketivṛtta) is incidental;
for example, the conduct of Sugrīva and others.
The *patākāsthānaka* (the station of the banner) should be applied here, having thoroughly examined the subject matter.
In this drama:
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) "For the sake of the requisite materials."
"Upakaraṇa" means assistance or aid;
it refers to the internal constituent of the drama, namely the "patākāsthānaka" (the situational motif).
This occurs "here in the drama."

"At the beginning" (āmukhe) means in the drama that possesses a common plot-structure (vṛtta-sādhāraṇa). By this, it will become clear later that its occurrence is possible both at the beginning and within the plot itself.
When one meaning has been conceived and another [word] possessing its characteristic mark is employed—
But that is the *patākāsthānaka* (the station of the banner) by means of an adventitious state.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
da) "Takṣmiṅga" means having a mark identical to the object that was thought of.
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) By means of an adventitious [quality] other than the natural one; he states its varieties: "The sudden attainment of the object through figurative usage is *guṇāvatī*."
This first patākāsthānaka has thus been fully described.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
dha) "Suddenly" means that it is virtuous by way of metaphorical designation and by way of action.
The attainment of the object (*arthasaṃpatti*) is the attainment of the intended goal;
it means "all at once.
For example, in the *Ratnāvalī*, when the King unties the noose around her neck thinking, "This is Vāsavadattā," she recognizes him by saying, "This is Sāgarikā," and [the King asks], "How?"
"Sāgarikā is dear to me? Enough, enough of this excessive rashness of yours! Forgive me, my lady; quickly release this noose of vines!"
O Lord of Life, even though my life is departing, place the noose of your arms around my neck for a moment here.”
In this case, the attainment of the object in the form of the fruit is superior and endowed with excellence due to the greater degree of metaphorical application compared to the previous [state].
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, na): "This is Vāsavadattā."

Vāsavadattā was the king’s wife. Knowing that Sāgarikā would arrive disguised in her (Vāsavadattā’s) attire, the king remained at the rendezvous having made an appointment; however, Vāsavadattā herself, learning of this, arrived before Sāgarikā’s arrival, broke the appointment, and departed after causing the king to feel ashamed.
And the king set out afterwards to appease her;
meanwhile, Sāgarikā, dressed in that same attire, arrived and, finding no way to reach the king, spoke with despondency and prepared to kill herself by binding herself with a noose of creepers.
The king, however, had already departed to appease Vāsavadattā.

On the path, having seen her and thinking, "This is Vāsavadattā dying," he released the noose; then, upon hearing Sāgarikā’s words, realizing, "This is Sāgarikā," he attained the attainment of the intended fruit, which was Guṇavatī.

Here, while another matter—the death of Vāsavadattā—was being contemplated, there occurred the employment of the matter of Sāgarikā, who was about to die marked by the signs of Vāsavadattā’s death through the adventitious vine-noose;
this should be understood as the general definition of the *patākāsthāna* (the episode of the banner).
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) "In comparison with the former"—that is, in comparison with the previous knowledge of Vāsavadattā;
"the speech" is "excellent," "cohesive," and "based upon various compositions."
This second [type] is proclaimed as the Patākāsthānaka.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) He states the second position regarding the banner: "the speech is preeminent.
The various compositions consist of forms such as the revelation of the seed-syllable, the leading [of the plot], auspicious indications, and so forth.
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*:

“May the sons of the Kuru king, together with their servants, have their lands adorned with blood [or: consecrated by affection], may they be free from physical conflict [or: free from bodily injury], and may they be well.

Here, because the seed-meaning (*bīja*) is conveyed through the power of paronomasia (*śleṣa*)—where words such as *rakta* signify both blood and affection, and *vigraha* signifies both body and conflict—the second *patākāsthāna* (subsidiary juncture) occurs upon the realization of the leader’s auspiciousness.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) "Adorned with blood" means that the grounds were smeared with red blood.
The meaning obtained through *śleṣa* (punning) is: "May those whose bodies were wounded come to dwell in heaven.
Thus it is said: "In this case, of blood and so forth...

Here, when the sense of "attached" (*anurakta*) and so on is considered, there exists the presence of the general characteristic of the location of the banner (*patāka*), because another meaning—namely "blood" and so on—is conveyed by a different word possessing that same formal mark (*liṅga*) as the word itself, due to its being employed as an adventitious term (*āgantuka*).

This "place of the banner" (patākāsthāna) should be understood as being included within the *āmukha* (prologue), as well as that which will be described as occurring within the *vṛtta* (the main action).

That which suggests the plot (*arthopakṣepaka*), which is subtle (*līna*) and modest (*savinaya*), and which is endowed with a clever retort (*śliṣṭapratyuttara*), is called the third [type]. (VisSd 6.48)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) He states the third [type]: "that which introduces the matter" (*arthopakṣepakam*).
The meaning is that "introducing the matter" refers to speech that indicates the subject at hand.

He explains the word *śliṣṭā* [as "coherent"]: by the phrase "suitable for connection," the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the stated sentence is indicated. Regarding the term *savinayam*, *vinaya* is a qualifier meaning "guidance" or "certainty"; he explains this with the words "particular... (*viśeṣa*). *Līna* means "of obscure meaning."

That which is accomplished through a reply that is "coherent"—meaning it is suitable for connection with the context yet prompted by a different underlying intention—and which is "accompanied by modesty," meaning it is joined with the attainment of a specific certainty, is the third *patākāsthāna*.
For example, in the second act of the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: "Chamberlain—Your Majesty..."
"Broken! Broken! The King: "By whom? The Chamberlain: "By Bhīma. The King: "Whose? The Chamberlain: "Yours."
The King: Ah! What are you babbling? Chamberlain: (With fear) My Lord, I am indeed speaking.
"It has been broken by Bhīma!
O King, fie upon you, you wretched old man! What is this delusion of yours today?"
Chamberlain: My Lord, it is not a delusion;
it is indeed the truth.
“O Lord, the banner of your chariot has been shattered by Bhīma;
it lies upon the earth like a cry of distress produced by the tinkling of its bells.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, bha) "It is broken"—the banner of your chariot has been shattered by Bhīma as if by the wind;
the cluster of small bells has fallen upon the earth like one uttering cries of lamentation.
When the chamberlain was about to say this, it was spoken in fragments out of agitation.

This [speech] introduces the meaning of the breaking of Duryodhana’s thighs; by the words "by Bhīma," it is meant "by Bhīmasena" in his capacity as one capable of performing his own duty, endowed with an intention beyond the mere breaking of the banner. It is accompanied by Duryodhana’s reply.
Here, the hidden meanings and so forth should be understood clearly.
In this instance, there is an introduction of the subject matter (*arthopakṣepaṇa*) by means of the breaking of Duryodhana’s thighs, which is the topic at hand.
*Vijñapriyā* explains the nature of introducing the subject matter with the words "In this instance" (*atra*).

In this case, while another matter in the form of the breaking of the banner (ketubhaṅga) is being contemplated, there is the employment of a meaning in the form of the breaking of the thighs (ūrubhaṅga) through an adventitious word with a double meaning (śliṣṭaśabda); therefore, the general definition of a *patākāsthānaka* is present.

"A composition of words possessing two meanings, well-knit and employed in poetry, which implies a primary subject as well as another [secondary] subject, is the supreme *patākāsthānaka*. (VisSd 6.49)
Vijñapriyā:
He states the fourth [type]—*vdyartho vacana*—"a word having two meanings. *Suśliṣṭaḥ* means beautifully connected with two meanings.
In poetry, a *śloka* is a "joining" (*yojati*).
This means it is that which indicates another primary meaning—that is, another principal meaning intended to be conveyed—by way of its primary sense.
As, for example, in the *Ratnāvalī*:

“Beholding this garden creeper today— like another woman filled with passion, its buds loosened and pale-hued, already beginning to yawn, and instantly manifesting its own exhaustion through incessant sighs— I shall surely cause the face of the Queen to take on a glow as crimson as anger.”
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ra) "Uddāmā" refers to this speech of the King as he points out to him the *mādhavī* creeper, which has been taken up by the King, is blooming out of season, and portends Vāsavadattā’s defeat—
just as one might point out another woman who is intoxicated and separated from her lover.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Beholding this garden-creeper, I shall make the face of Queen Vāsavadattā crimson with the flush of anger.

The meaning is that her anger will arise not only from seeing another woman—as it would be for me—but also from seeing the flowering *mādhavī* creeper, which serves as the cause for her defeat [in beauty].
He states the epithets for both the garden-creeper and the woman separated from her lover, beginning with "exuberant" (*uddāma*).
*Uktalikā* means a budding longing and yearning; their "excess" (*uddāmatva*) refers to their intensity. It is "pale-white" both by its very nature and due to separation.

Yawning (*jṛmbhā*) is the opening [of the mouth] and a particular kind of sighing. It causes exhaustion (*āyāsa*), agitation (*vyākulatā*), and weariness (*kheda*) by means of the upward movement of the breath, that is, the external air and the exhalation.
— *Locanā* —
*Uddāma* means: a blossoming bud (*kalikā*), a flower-bud (*koraka*), and longing (*utkaṇṭhā*).
*Jṛmbhā* means: blooming (*vikāśaḥ*) and a particular kind of sigh of pleasure (*sukhaniḥśvāsaviśeṣaḥ*).
*Śvasana* means: a sigh (*niḥśvāsaḥ*) and the external wind (*bāhyapavanaḥ*).
Here, the meaning of what is to be explained is indicated.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Here, the meaning of what is to be explained" means:
By indicating that Queen Vāsavadattā’s impending anger due to not seeing Sāgarikā is the primary element, the *pradhāna* (the main plot) is suggested.

Here, while the impending anger resulting from not seeing Kusumalatā has been contemplated, that anger [toward Sāgarikā] is presented through a pun (*śliṣṭa-śabda*) as being adventitious (*āgantuka*).
Therefore, the general definition of a *patākā-sthāna* (a situational episode) is present.
These four points of the banner (patākāsthāna) occur at all junctures (sandhi), sometimes for the sake of auspiciousness and sometimes for the sake of inauspiciousness;
furthermore, they occur repeatedly according to the will of the poet.
As for what has been stated by someone else—that "they occur in sequence across the four junctures beginning from the Mukha-sandhi"—[that is not the case].
Others do not agree with that, because it is logical that all of these, being absolutely worthy of adoption, should exist everywhere and for everyone without restriction.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(Vi, Va) "In some cases, for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).

For instance, in the passage beginning with *uddāmotkalikām*, because it conveys both the knowledge that Vāsavadattā has set out to die at the outset and the attainment of the desired Sāgarikā, it serves the purpose of auspiciousness. Conversely, in passages such as *raktaprasādhitā* and *bhagnaṃ bhīmena*, because they convey the death of the Kurus and the breaking of Duryodhana’s thighs respectively, they serve the purpose of inauspiciousness (*amaṅgala*).
"Again and again" means at each respective stage. "In the four junctions" means: [the four stages of life].
Because there are four positions for the banner (patākāsthāna), the meaning is "in the first four junctures that present themselves.
The word "everywhere" (sarvatra) means "even in all five junctures."
"For all" means for all locations of the banners.
Whatever object may be inappropriate for the protagonist or for the aesthetic flavor (rasa), that which is contradictory should be abandoned or otherwise conceptualized. (VisSd 6.50)
Locanā:
(lo, e) "That which might be" [is the case].
For when Rāma and others, under a pretext, speak of the slaying of Vālin and so forth, for those who are not adept at discerning his most hidden intention—

Through the medium of the "lump of food" that is the tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in dramas, poetry, and the like, there might arise for those of tender intellect— such as princes and others who are to be directed toward engagement in what should be done and desistance from what should not be done— the possibility of engaging in improper narratives after having reflected upon the life-stories of great beings such as Śrī Rāmacandra.
Therefore, even the life-story of a great being may constitute an "improper subject matter" (*anucita-vṛtta*).
The sense is that [such elements] should be avoided in dramas and similar works.
The "inappropriateness of rasa" refers to the direct verbal expression of transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) and so forth, which will be discussed later.
An example of inappropriate plot (*itivṛtta*) is the killing of Vālin by Rāma through deception.
This has indeed been stated repeatedly in the *Udāttarāghava*;
however, in the *Vīracarita*, Vālī—who had come for the purpose of killing Rāma—was killed by Rāma, thus altering the facts.
Furthermore, that which ought not to be seen in the *Aṅkas* is yet considered necessary to be mentioned.
And whatever discourse there may be lasting up to a year, or that which arises over two days and so forth.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
śa) "And that which might last for a year" means that such a discourse should be performed over the course of two days or more.
"And another" means that other [types of speech], being extensive and numerous, cannot be fully represented;

that narrative is to be indicated by the wise through the five [elements] beginning with the *viṣkambhaka*, which are "introduced by thematic indicators" (*arthopakṣepaka*)—that is, permeated by the thematic indicators of the matters to be described.
Regarding the word *sūcyā*, there is a variant reading in some places as *kṣepyā*.
The phrase "not to be seen on the lap" and so forth is connected with the word "another" (*anyā*) in the preceding [verse].
Therefore, the meaning is that she too is indicated by means of the indicators of the plot (*arthopakṣepakaiḥ*).
— *Locanā* —

(La, Ai) Now, if things such as calling from afar are not to be shown in the acts (*aṅka*s), then why are they included in the *nāṭaka*? Furthermore, since a story that lasts for only a single day is to be shown in the acts, how can a story lasting two days or more be incorporated, or how can the expansion of the narrative—which might obstruct the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—be shown in an act? To this, he says: "In the acts... (*aṅkeṣv iti*).

Furthermore, other extensive narratives, such as stories of battles and the like, which are not to be seen in the *aṅkas* and which provide instruction and benefit to the wise, [should be excluded]. However, whatever subject matter occurs after the rainy season (*varṣā*) shall be considered as having originated below the rainy season. (VisSd 6.52)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṣa) An existence occurring after a year—that is, a subsequent existence—is accomplished even by the beginning of the second year.
There is no tautology because there is a distinction: in the former case, the limit is the end of the year, whereas here, it is the period after the year.
"Beyond a year":
all of that must not be performed after a year has passed.
This is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
However, it should not be performed even for as long as a month;
rather, the meaning is that it must be done only upon the breaking of the mark.
— Locanā:
(O, Lo) [Objection: If the story of even a single year must be told by way of introducing the plot, then should the story beyond that be abandoned? To this, he says: "After a year.
For it has been stated by the Sage:
"At the conclusion of an act, one should present what was done in a month, or even what was accumulated over a year."
All that must be performed after one year has passed, and never otherwise.
Locanā:
"Aṅkaccheda" refers to (lo, au).
"Tat" means that which is well-known.
Every task or duty, whether accumulated over a month or even a year, must be performed even at the moment of cutting the [nail] mark;
the meaning is that it should be indicated by those who introduce the matter through its implications (*arthopakṣepakaiḥ*).

And thus, even regarding the fourteen-year exile of Rāma, whatever episodes such as the slaying of Virādha are narrated, they are not to be indicated by any single unit—whether a year, a part of a year, a day, or a pair of days.

Whatever business remains unfinished at the end of the day that cannot be accomplished within that same day should be spoken of by means of characters who introduce the plot, after effecting a break in the act (*aṅkaccheda*). (Viśvavidyāsādhana 6.53)
Vijñapriyā:
"At the end of the day" means that the task to be performed at the end of the day is accomplished during the day itself, because there is an absence of a multitude of activities.
The meaning is that it can be represented in a single day.

To the question of how a matter that requires a whole day to be accomplished can be described, he says: "by means of indicators of the plot" (*arthopakṣepakaiḥ*). He asks: what are these indicators of the plot? He says:
The five elements that introduce the subject matter are the *viṣkambhaka*, the *praveśaka*, the *cūlikā*, the *aṅkāvatāra*, and also the *aṅkamukha*. (VisSd 6.54)
The *viṣkambha*, which provides a summary of the events already occurred and those yet to occur, has been shown at the beginning of the act as a concise statement of its meaning. (VisSd 6.55)
When prepared with the middle [ingredients] or with two middle vessels, it is pure; however, when prepared with inferior and middle [ingredients], it is mixed.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) He states the twofold nature of the *viṣkambha* with the words "in the middle":
the recipient (*pātra*) is divided into the superior, the inferior, and the middling.
"Kapālakuṇḍalā" means "her task";
the same applies to what follows hereafter.
Locanā:
(lo, a) He states the definition according to the enumeration: "vṛtta" (round), etc.
The "middleness" of the vessel [is established] by its being smaller than that of Śrī Rāmacandra and others who are exceedingly large.
Since the use of the Sanskrit language by the characters in the *viṣkambhaka* is observed in the dramatic works, whereas middle-class characters indeed speak in Prakrit;
as it is stated in the *Bhāṣārṇava*: "The language of middle-class characters [is used] especially in dramas and similar works."
The learned have stated that the language is twofold, namely Mahārāṣṭrī and Saurasenī.
Thus it is said.
Among these, the pure [sentiment] is as in *Mālatīmādhava* at the cemetery with Kapālakuṇḍalā;
the mixed [sentiment] is as in *Rāmābhyudaya* with the mendicant and the Kāpālika.
Now, the *praveśaka* (interlude):
A *praveśaka* is to be understood as occurring between two acts (*aṅka*), being enacted by low-ranking characters with speech in the anudātta (low-pitched) tone; the rest is as in the *viṣkambhaka*.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ka) "By two numbers" means that the intention is that the term "two numbers" refers to the second and subsequent numbers.
"The remainder" refers to the form beginning with "vṛtta-vartiṣyamāṇa," and so forth. — *Locanā*
Regarding the phrase "employed by low characters" (*nīcapātraprayojita*), their status as "low" is due precisely to their speaking in unrefined language;
therefore, the *praveśaka* may be employed by female companions (*sakhi*) and others.
The phrase "between two acts" (*aṅkadvayasyāntar*) indicates that its prohibition applies to the first act.
For example: the pair of Rākṣasas in the *Aśvatthāmā* episode of the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*.
Now, as for the *cūlikā*:
"The *cūlikā* is that which indicates the plot by means of those situated behind the curtain (*antarjavanikā*)."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
kha) *Antarjavanikā* is a curtain used for the arrangement of a residence or for surrounding a place.
The grammatical connection is "the indication of the meaning.
For example, at the beginning of the fourth act of the *Vīracarita*: "(Behind the scenes) O you celestial beings!"
"May the auspicious performances of the stage proceed," and so forth.
"Paraśurāma was defeated by Rāma"—this is indicated by the actors offstage.
Now follows the entry into the act (*aṅkāvatāra*).
It is indicated by the actors at the end of the act, due to the lack of division from that act.
Where this act enters [the stage], it is known as an *aṅkāvatāra* (act-introduction).
*Vijñapriyā*:
[It is also called] *aṅkānta* (end of an act).
The meaning is that another act descends from the matter indicated by the characters at the end of the [preceding] act;
thus, "due to the non-division of that act" means that division is its separation.
The meaning is that [the subsequent act] is employed as being non-different from that [preceding one].
Here, the suffix *tas* is used after a word ending in the accusative case.
The meaning is that even when there is a break in the acts (*aṅka*), the subsequent act enters [into the performance] precisely through the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) evoked by that [preceding] act.
Thus he says: "Like a specific limb of that act.
For example, in the fifth act of the *Abhijñānaśākuntala*, the sixth act—which was indicated by the characters—descends as if it were a specific limb of that very act.
Now, the *aṅkamukha* (the prologue to an act):
In this very same [system], all the indications of the numerical figures are contained within the syllables themselves.
They call that "the face of the act" (*aṅkamukha*), and it indicates the purpose of the seed (*bīja*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
That is where there would be an "act" (*aṅka*).

The meaning is that it is the complete indication of the meanings of all the acts (*aṅka*) which are about to be described. The distinction is that in an *aṅkāvatāra* there is the indication of only those specific acts, whereas in an *aṅkamukha* there is the indication of all the acts.
It is called "having the meaning of an elephant" (*gajārtha*) because it makes manifest the meaning that serves as the seed (*bīja*).
The meaning is that it is designated as "indicating the seed" (*bījārthākhyāpaka*).

For example, in the first act of the *Mālatīmādhava*, Kāmandakī and Avalokitā, in the course of their conversation, have indicated the arrangement of Bhūrivasu and others who will appear later, as well as the plot-structure of the entire dramatic composition.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṅa) The arrangement of those things belonging to future stages and those that will follow in the future has been briefly set forth;
one should not represent it in its full detail.
Or, by means of objects from another act, one may indicate the meaning of a broken act through an object belonging to that same act.
"By the characters entering at the end of the act" means by those characters who have entered at the conclusion of the act.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ca):
He states another definition of the *aṅkamukha* as spoken by Dhanika—namely, "by the characters at the end of the act."
The meaning is that the indication of a subsequent act (*aparāṅkasūcana*) occurs through characters who enter at the end of an act that has been cut short or is being concluded.

The distinction from the previous definition is this: in the former case, there is an indication of the entire subject matter of the [current] act by means of characters already present; here, however, there is an indication of the subject matter of the *subsequent* act alone by means of characters who have entered at the end of the act.
For example, at the end of the second act of the *Vīracarita*: "(Entering)..."
Sumantra: The venerable Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, along with Bhārgava, are summoning you both.
The others: Where are the venerable ones?
Sumantra: In the presence of the great king Daśaratha.
The others say, "In that case, let us go right there," at the conclusion of the act.
Then: "(Then enter Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and Paraśurāma seated).

Here, because the character Sumāntra—who entered at the very end of the preceding act—interrupts the conversation between Śatānanda and Janaka and thus indicates the opening of the subsequent act, this is called *aṅkāsyam* (the face of the act).
And this has been stated according to the opinion of Dhānika;
others, however, say: "This matter is already understood through the descent into the limbs (*aṅkāvataraṇa*) alone.
[Thus ends] *Vijñapriyā*.
(Vi, Cha) He states that this characteristic belongs specifically to the *Dhanika* by saying "and this" (*etacca*).
By the phrase "precisely through the introduction of the mark" (*aṅkāvatāreṇaiva*),
he means that because this [text] possesses those characteristics, the mark was shown at the very beginning.
When one should display that which is required, that which is to be abandoned, the insipid, and the extensive— namely, the remainder— then it should be done immediately after the introduction.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ja) It was previously shown that the *viṣkambhaka* (interlude) occurs at the beginning of the *aṅka* (act) and so forth; now, he states that by virtue of specific requirements, it may also be performed at the end of the *āmukha* (prologue), saying: "It is required.
The remainder [of the plot] is [determined] from what is required for the action.
The connection [of the meaning] is that the remainder is "insipid" (*nīrasa*) and "divided" (*bhinna*), referring to the expansion of the subject matter.

The connection is that the "interlude" (*viṣkambhaka*) follows immediately after the "introduction" (*āmukha*). The phrase "employed by Yaugandharāyaṇa"—the word "interlude" (*viṣkambhaka*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
For in that [drama], the story of Vatsarāja and Sāgarikā was expected;
yet, having abandoned it, immediately after the *āmukha*, Yaugandharāyaṇa displayed a fear devoid of essence, saying, "I am truly afraid of my master," acting according to his own whims.
In drama, a *viṣkambhaka* should be employed when characters introduced in the *āmukha* [reappear].
For example, as that which was employed by Yaugandharāyaṇa in the *Ratnāvalī*;
however, when a charming subject matter proceeds from the very beginning—VisSd 6.62.

"At the very beginning, that [plot] should belong to the act (*aṅka*), based on the introduction (*āmukha*) and the *ākṣepa*. Regarding the statement "it has been shown at the beginning of the act," [the author] shows its scope with the words "But when...
(*yadā tu*). Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) He demonstrates the subject matter of what was stated—that it is shown at the beginning of the act—with the words "But when... (*yadā tu*).
"From the very beginning" means precisely from the lack of mixing with insipid matter.
"Resorting to a direct introduction" (āmukhākṣepasaṃśraya) means that it proceeds by relying upon the direct introduction of a character.
Regarding *Śākuntalā*:
for in that case, it is that very aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), initiated from the very beginning by Anasūyā, which constitutes the separation from Śakuntalā—
as, for example, in the *Śākuntala*.
Even by means of the Viṣkambhaka and other such [devices], the killing of the protagonist (adhikārin) must not be mentioned.
One should not cause a mutual subordination between the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the object (*vastu*). [The commentary *Vijñapriyā* states:
"Regarding the qualified persons (*adhikārin*)."
The meaning is "the owners of the primary fruit.
By this, it is meant that the killing of the hero (nāyaka) should never be described.
"Rasa" refers to the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and the others.
As Dhanika has said: "One should not, out of excessive passion, lead the subject matter too far into fragmentation,
nor should one obscure the aesthetic flavor (rasa) with the characteristics of mere plot-matter (vastu) or poetic figures (alaṅkāra)."
Thus [ends the section].
*Vijñapriyā*:
“Of flavor and substance” (rasavastunoḥ).
The subject matter (*vastu*) is the meaning distinct from the poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
It is known by its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), which are the indicators (*jñāpaka*):
the seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), the banner (*patākā*), the minor episode (*prakarī*), and the plot-goal (*kārya*) itself. (Viśvavidyā 6.64)
Having understood the five fundamental elements of affairs, they should be applied according to the rules.
The fundamental elements of affairs are the causes for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Among them, the seed is as follows:
That which is taught as a mere small portion spreads forth in many ways.
The first cause of a fruit is called the seed.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṭha): He states another duty to be performed in drama with the words "only a very small amount."
*Yudhiṣṭhirautsāha* (the enthusiasm of Yudhiṣṭhira) means his enthusiasm for power;
for example, in the *Ratnāvalī*, the activity of Yaugandharāyaṇa—which is cherished by the favor of destiny—is the cause for the Vatsarāja’s acquisition of Ratnāvalī.
Or, for example, in the *Veṇī*, the enthusiasm of Yudhiṣṭhira, augmented by the wrath of Bhīmasena, is the cause for the binding of Draupadī’s hair.
When there is an interruption in the intermediate meaning, the *bindu* is the cause that prevents its severance.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ḍa) He states that the nature of the object consists of the form of the *bindu*— namely, "in the interim," etc.—
and this [term] "without interruption of the *bindu*" is a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*).
The term *bindupada* (the "drop-word") is neuter in gender.

For example, in the *Ratnāvalī*, when the worship of Anaṅga has been completed and there is an interruption in the narrative flow, Sāgarikā hears the words, “He gazes [at her] like the rising moon,” and says, “(With joy) How is this? Is this not that King Udayana? and so forth; such is an intermediate causal element (*avāntarārthahetu*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) "Like the moon of Udayana," and so forth, is the speech of a panegyrist.
How so?
"How is it that he himself is King Udayana? is the Sanskrit rendering. [This means] the King of Vatsa himself is named Udayana.
For, during the intermediate episode of separation from Sāgarikā, because he is recognized as King Udayana, there is an interruption in the progression of the description of his own separation.
However, because it proceeds even without a specific indicator, since the cause—the king’s appearance—is already present, there is a distinction such as the *aṅkāvatāra* (entry into an act).
In the *aṅkāvatāra*, however, the indication is made by characters who have already entered [the stage].
—Locanā:
(Lo, i) How so? How is this King Saudāyana?
It is just as in the second act of the *Ratnāvalī*, where immediately after the Queen’s departure, and without any interruption, the King speaks these words to the Vidūṣaka.
"Fie on you, fool! Enough of this jesting; because of your noble birth, you did not perceive the Queen's hidden anger.
For we must go now to appease the Queen herself."
The pervasive, incidental narrative is called the *patākā* (the banner).
*Vijñapriyā*:
[The author] states the dramatic element (*arthaprakṛti*) in the form of a *patākā*—namely, "pervasive" (*vyāpī*).
The conduct of the hero’s associate is both pervasive— meaning it extends across many acts—
and incidental, occurring in connection with the hero;
as, for example, that of Sugrīva and others in the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
In the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, [the episode] of Bhīma and others;
in the *Śākuntala*, the conduct of the Vidūṣaka; and that of the secondary hero (patākānāyaka) shall not have its own separate final fruit. (VisSd 6.67)
"Whether in the embryo, at the juncture, or in the deliberation, its conclusion comes about.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ta):
He states another variety—namely, "even for the hero of the secondary plot (*patākānāyaka*)."

The term "anāyakasyāpi" (even of one who is not the hero) involves the elision of the letter *a* [from *na*]. Thus, the meaning is that even for those such as Sugrīva who are not the hero, whatever other fruit there may be—such as the attainment of their own kingdom—that too is another *patākā* (subsidiary episode).
From the word "api" (even), it should be understood that for the hero Rāma, other fruits such as the construction of the bridge are also another *patākā*.
"In the womb, in the transition" (*garbhe sandhau*).

The word "in the transition" (*sandhau*) applies to both "in the womb" (*garbhe*) and "in the deliberation" (*vimarśe*). For the five transitions (*pañcasandhi*), which consist of the womb, deliberation, and withdrawal, will be described [later].

In that context, the "carrying forward" (*nirvāha*)—meaning the accomplishment—of that which is termed the *patākā* (the secondary plot), which constitutes an intermediate fruit for the two non-heroic and heroic characters, occurs within the two junctures (*sandhi*) of the *garbha* (embryo) and *vimarśa* (deliberation).
For example, the attainment of a kingdom by Sugrīva and others.
As for what was stated by the Sage: "The *patākā* ceases either at the *garbha* or at the *vimarśa*."
Thus it is said.
In this context, "the banner" (*patākā*): it is called the banner because the activity of the banner is seen to continue even until the conclusion of the *nirvahaṇa*, which is the fruit of the hero.
Thus it was explained by Abhinavaguptapāda.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, tha) "From the womb" (*āgarbhāt*).
Having proclaimed that "the banner" (*patākā*) is mentioned in the words of the Sage, he explains: "the banner of the hero" (*patākānāyaka*).

Here too, there is an elision of the vowel *a* (i.e., *anāyaka*). The meaning is that the banner itself, which takes the form of a fruit that lacks a [primary] hero (*anāyaka*), ceases from the *āgarbha* stage up to the *vimarśa* stage.
In this commentary by Abhinavaguptapāda, he states the reason: "even until the conclusion" (*nirvāhaparyantam api*).
This refers to the *patākā* (the secondary plot), which takes the form of a subsidiary incident.

The meaning is that even for a *patākā* that does not have a [primary] hero and whose fruit is of a different nature, its cessation occurs either at the *garbha* (the "embryo" juncture) or at the *vimarśa* (the "deliberation" juncture).
The *prakarī* is considered to be a conduct that is incidental and situated in a particular region.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) He states the nature of the subject matter in the form of a *prakaraṇa*—namely, "incidental" (*prāsaṅgika*).
The meaning is: that which has arisen from a relevant context (*prasaṅga*), which resides in a particular section, and which is established within a specific portion [of the work].
For example—the conversation between Rāvaṇa and Jaṭāyu on the lap of the Kulapati.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) Regarding the "conversation between Rāvaṇa and Jaṭāyu":
Its status as the *arthaprakṛti* (the causal basis of the plot) arises through the description of and the recovery of Sītā, who was abducted by Rāvaṇa;
it constitutes a *prakarī* (subsidiary episode) for the hero, not some other independent fruit of his own.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(VI, na) The *patākā* is another fruit for the *nāyaka*, whereas the *prakarī* is not another fruit for the *nāyaka*; this is the meaning. Nor should it be argued that because Rāvaṇa is not the *nāyaka*, the fact that [the *prakarī*] has him as its fruit entails that it must be a *patākā*.
Because it is intended to express one who is a companion to the leader precisely by virtue of being "without a leader," since the negative particle (*nañ*) carries the sense of similarity—
as, for example, in the case of Jaṭāyu attaining liberation.
But that which is required is the goal to be accomplished, upon which the undertaking depends.
It is agreed that whatever leads to accomplishment must be performed.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi,
pa) states the nature of the object in the form of what is to be done— namely, "that which is required."
The "commencement" is the beginning of the drama;
the "conclusion" likewise belongs to the drama itself,
namely, the slaying of Rāvaṇa.
For when that [success] is achieved, there is the conclusion of the drama;
as, for example, the slaying of Rāvaṇa in the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
There are five stages of an undertaking initiated by those seeking its fruit: (VisSa 6.70).
"Commencement, exertion, attainment, hope, certainty of attainment, and the arrival of the fruit"—[the author] states "stages" (*avasthā*) to indicate that there are five stages of this task.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, pha):
[He says "stages"] to indicate that there are five stages of this task.
The meaning is that these are states consisting of the producer and the produced.
Among them, it should be understood that there are four states that produce [the result], characterized by undertaking, effort, attainment, and the certainty of attainment;
whereas the state consisting of the arrival of the fruit is that which is produced.
In that regard:
"Initiation (ārambha) is the eagerness for the attainment of the primary fruit. (Viṣṇusamhitā 6.71)

For example, in the *Ratnāvalī*, there is the eagerness (*autsukya*) of Yaugandharāyaṇa for the purpose of settling Ratnāvalī in the inner apartments; in the same way, the eagerness of the hero, the heroine, and others should be understood from the source texts (*ākara*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ba) Regarding that, he states the characteristic of *ārambha* (the commencement): "it would be" (*bhavet*).
"In the source" (*ākare*) means in each respective drama.
*Prayatna* (effort), however, is an activity directed toward the attainment of the fruit, characterized by extreme urgency.
As it says in the *Ratnāvalī*: “Nevertheless, since there is no other means for seeing [him], I shall draw [his likeness] and accomplish whatever I desire.
*Vijñapriyā*:
“*Tahavi* (nevertheless).”
Nevertheless, thinking "there is no other means of seeing [her]," he refined his resolve, saying, "I shall draw her in such and such a way that I may act according to my desire.
Immediately after the movement of his fingers, he spoke thus;
for the means of union is an integral part of the activity itself, as it is described as being the very effort involved.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ī) "Nevertheless" means that even so,
there is no other means for vision.
"Having painted [the likeness] in whatever manner, I shall act according to my intention;
just as King Candrakaḷā obtained his wife through the attainment of the fruit consisting of the granting of a boon by the Yakṣiṇī.
By such statements, the means for the Vatsarāja’s union with Ratnāvalī—such as the painting of a portrait—is established.
And as it is said: "In the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the building of the bridge across the ocean and so forth [are examples].
Through the apprehension of means and obstacles, there arises the hope for attainment and the possibility of attainment. (Viṣṇusiddhānta 6.72)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) He speaks regarding the possibility of attainment: "By means of the method" (*upāya*).
The possibility of attainment arises from both the apprehension of the method and the apprehension of its absence.
The hope for attainment (*prāptyāśā*) is the possibility of achieving the intended object.

For example, in the third act of the *Ratnāvalī*, due to means of union such as changing one's dress and secret meeting, yet because of the apprehension of obstacles characterized by Vāsavadattā, there is the attainment of a result in the form of an indeterminate, certain union; this is the hope for attainment.
Similarly elsewhere:
*Vijñapriyā* explains that the exchange of dress consists of Sāgarikā assuming the guise of Vāsavadattā.
Therefore, her secret meeting was held in the presence of the king;
that is to say, out of fear of the king's discovery of the means of their union— the means of Sāgarikā’s union with him— which would take the form of Vāsavadattā’s arrival.

The attainment of certainty regarding acquisition is determined by the absence of states of woe (*apāya*). Because there is no possibility of falling into states of woe, the attainment of the fruit is resolved as being exclusively certain.
As it says in the *Ratnāvalī*: “The King said: ‘Apart from propitiating the Queen, I see no other means in this matter.’”
Thus, by means of the pacification that wards off the deficiency of the goddess's characteristics, the attainment of the certain fruit is indicated.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"The attainment of the certain fruit is indicated."

In this instance, there is the certain attainment of the fruit consisting of the pacification of the Goddess’s anger. Nor should it be argued that this cannot be considered the "state of effect" (*kāryāvasthā*) because the effect—namely, the union with Sāgarikā—is not yet accomplished by it;
for her anger acts as an obstacle to that [union], and thus its absence serves as the cause of it.
That state in which the fruit arises in its entirety would be the conjunction with the fruit.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) He states the attainment of the fruit: "At Śrāvastī. The attainment of the fruit is the conjunction with the fruit.
"Arising of the complete fruit" means the accomplishment of all intended fruits. "Completeness" (sāmagrya) consists in the accompaniment of other intended fruits by the primary intended fruit;
he will state this later with the words "accompanied by other fruits."
This state is to be accomplished by means of the four previously mentioned states.
For example, as in the *Ratnāvalī*, the attainment of the *Ratnāvalī* is accompanied by the attainment of another fruit characterized by universal sovereignty (*cakravartitva*);
so it is elsewhere as well.
Through their connection with these five states in their respective order,
the divisions of the plot (itivṛtta) become fivefold, consisting of the five junctures (pañcasandhi).
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding the phrase "according to their respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*):
because of the connection with these five states, the divisions of the verse are exactly fivefold.
The meaning is that there are five junctures (*sandhi*).
Locanā:
by means of these states, beginning with the commencement (*ārambha*) and so forth.
He states the definition of *sandhi*: "When there is a single underlying connection, *sandhi* is the relationship between intermediate parts of a narrative that are connected by a single purpose.
That is to say, when portions of a story are linked by one primary objective, the connection between those intermediate sections through a single subordinate purpose constitutes *sandhi*.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, śa) Its characteristic is the general characteristic of the juncture (*sandhi*).
Regarding the phrase "in this [context] of the names of the parts of the narrative," it is an explanation of the clause "when there is a single continuity."
"By one" means by each individual purpose.
"Avāntara" and so forth is explained as "intermediate."
He states its divisions:
"The Opening (mukha), the Counter-opening (pratimukha), the Embryo (garbha), the Deliberation (vimarśa), and the Conclusion (upasaṃhṛti)."
Locanā:
(lo, ū) Upasaṃhṛti is synonymous with Nirvahaṇa;
thus there are five varieties [of the conclusion], and their definitions are stated in order.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṣa) "Their divisions" refers to the divisions of the junctures (*sandhi*).
Regarding "in sequence": this is because it has been stated that the fivefold juncture is established only in conjunction with the five aforementioned states.
The meaning is: "in the sequence beginning with the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture) together with that [plot].
Thus, it is said to be "endowed with the stage of the commencement.
The *mukhasandhi* is the appearance of the *vṛtta* (past events) and so forth.
