The *pratimukha-sandhi* (opening juncture) is characterized by the application of effort;
the *garbha-sandhi* (developmental juncture) is characterized by the intention for attainment;
the *vimarśa-sandhi* (investigative juncture) is characterized by the certainty of attainment.
The conclusion is joined with the attainment of the fruit.
He states the definition according to its respective location:
"Where there is the arising of seeds, which gives rise to various objects and essences. (Viṣṇudharma 6.76)
Locanā:
"Containing manifold meanings" (*nānārthā*) means that in which there is the presence of various kinds of meanings in the form of denotable objects (*vācya*) as well as aesthetic flavors (*rasa*).
That which is joined with an opening is proclaimed as its "mouth" (*tanmukha*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
"Where there is the seed-syllable (*bīja*)."
"Bīja" refers to the plot;
"by means of the beginning" means that they are endowed with the stage of the beginning, which consists of enthusiasm (*utsāha*).
In the first act, the seed (bīja) is established through the meeting of Sāgarikā with the King during the worship of Kandarpa, brought about by destiny;
and that [seed] is accompanied by Sāgarikā’s enthusiasm for union with him,
as in the first act of the *Ratnāvalī*.
Of the primary means for attaining the fruit, which is situated within the *mukhasandhi* (the opening juncture).
And that where the unfolding is both manifest and unmanifest is the *pratimukha* [sandhi].
Regarding the phrase "situated in the *mukhasandhi*": *Vijñapriyā* (vi, ha).
The meaning is: that which was introduced in the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture) as having the form of the arising of a seed (*bīja*).

For example, in the second act of the *Ratnāvalī*, the seed of passion (*anurāgabīja*), which is the cause for the union of Vatsarāja and Sāgarikā and was projected in the first act, is made slightly perceptible through its being known by Susaṃgatā and the Vidūṣaka, by means of the incident concerning the picture-board involving Vāsavadattā.
The "unfolding" (*udbheda*) is the form of a brief indication (*uddeśa*) of something that is being slightly revealed; as [stated] in the *Vijñapriyā*:
"By Vāsavadattā, [it was seen] on a picture-board."

King Udayana received a picture-board joined with his own likeness painted by Sāgarikā. Vāsavadattā, having obtained it after it slipped from Vasantaka’s hand, discerned the seeds of mutual passion depicted therein.
Such was the "separation" form of the *pratimukha-sandhi* (the intermediate juncture), which, upon Vāsavadattā's arrival, took the form of the efforts and activities of Susaṅgatā and Vasantaka.
Of that primary means for attaining the fruit which has previously emerged slightly.
Wherein the embryo is the initial manifestation, characterized by repeated contraction and seeking;
[Vijñapriyā] comments: "of that which has previously manifested."
The meaning is "of that which has burst forth at the point of confrontation.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that "bursting forth" (*samudbheda*) consists in repeatedly seeking out a reduction (*hrāsa*).
Regarding the word *hrāsa*, there is also a reading as *trāsa* in some places.
It is called *garbha* (the embryo) because it contains the fruit within;
as in the second act of the *Ratnāvalī*: “Susaṃgatā:

Friend, you are indeed lacking in courtesy, since even though you have been taken by the hand by your husband, you do not abandon your anger,” and so forth—this constitutes the *samudbheda* (the disclosure).
Furthermore, upon Vāsavadattā’s re-entry, there is a reduction [in the tempo].
In the third act—[the line] “How is it that Vasantaka, who went to search for news of her, is delaying?”—there is the search.
Viḍūṣaka: Oh, oh, sir!
"Even by the acquisition of the kingdom of Kosambī, my dear friend’s satisfaction will not be such as it will be upon hearing pleasant words from me"—in such passages there is *udbheda* (emergence).
Again, there is *hrāsa* (diminution) due to Vāsavadattā’s recognition [of Sāgarikā].
There is *anveṣaṇa* (searching) regarding Sāgarikā’s arrival at the place of assignation.
Furthermore, the manifestation [of the body] consists in making nooses of creepers;
"Vijñapriyā" means "O friend."
"Friend, you are now without merit,
you who, even though thus taken by the hand by your husband, do not relinquish your anger"— this is the Sanskrit [translation].
"Hī hī" [expresses laughter].
"Hī hī" expresses wonder.

"O, o! Even by the acquisition of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, my dear friend will not experience such satisfaction as he shall upon hearing kind words from me"—this is the Sanskrit [text]. "Udbheda" refers to the disclosure of the means for union with Sāgarikā.
"Because of the recognition of Vāsavadattā" means having seen her who had come for the purpose of breaking the secret agreement.
Furthermore, it refers to Sāgarikā as the agent;
"unveiling" (udbheda) refers to the primary means toward the attainment of the fruit.

For, through the creation of the noose from the creeper, there is the sight of Sāgarikā by the King; from that, there is the connection with the stage of "attainment" (*prāpti*), which consists of the hope for the attainment of the *garbhasandhi*.
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) "Friend! [she says].
Friend, you are now without courtesy, you who do not release your anger even though you have been thus addressed by your husband and even while his hand is grasping yours!
Oh, oh, Master Paritoṣa!

Even by the acquisition of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, my dear friend’s satisfaction will not be such as it will be upon hearing pleasant words from me. Now, the deliberation (*vimarśa*): where the means to the primary fruit is disclosed, it is superior to the *garbha* [stage]. (ViSd 6.79)
And that which possesses obstacles such as curses and the like is known as the *vimarśa* (the juncture of deliberation).
*Vijñapriyā*:
[It is so called] because it is greater than the *garbha* (the juncture of the womb).
In the "embryo" stage (*garbhasandhi*), there is a slight manifestation (*udbheda*) accompanied by a search for diminution;
here, however, it is greater than that because of the absence of diminution.
It is "with obstacles" (*sāntarāya*), meaning with impediments (*savighna*).

As in the *Śākuntala*, beginning from Anasūyā’s words in the fourth act— "Priyaṃvadā, although my heart is relieved that my dear friend Śakuntalā has attained auspiciousness through the Gandharva marriage and has become the wife of a worthy husband, nevertheless this much remains to be considered"— up until the recognition of Śakuntalā introduced in the seventh act, the accumulation of the plot is embraced by the obstacle consisting of her forgetfulness.
Now, the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*):
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṅa) [This refers to] Anasūyā.
The mention of the speaker is [the term] "O Priyaṃvadā" and so forth; this is the utterance.

"O Priyaṃvadā, although my heart is at ease because my dear friend Śakuntalā, having completed her auspicious marriage by the Gāndharva rite, has come to be united with a worthy husband"— this is in Sanskrit. This concludes the sixth act.
Prior to that, by the curse of Durvāsas, the means for the king’s primary fruit—the union with Śakuntalā—was obstructed in the form of forgetfulness. [As it was said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, thinking of no one else in your mind, you did not perceive me when I arrived before you."
"Even though he has awakened, being intoxicated, he will not remember you, just as one does not recall a story told long ago.
Thus,
there was a loss of memory due to the curse of Durvāsas.

This is the *vimarśasaṃdhi* (the juncture of deliberation), which consists of the primary means for counteracting the curse; it is accompanied by the state consisting of Śakuntalā’s hope for reunion with the king.
Locanā: (lo, ḷ) "Piaṃvadā! [she says].

Priyaṃvadā: Even though my dear friend Śakuntalā has completed her auspicious marriage according to the Gāndharva rite and has come to be united with a worthy husband, my heart is set at ease. Just as seeds containing potential, when scattered, find their respective purposes in the fields. (Viśuddhimārga 6.80)
"That in which [the elements] are brought to a single purpose is indeed the *nirvahaṇa*. Vijñapriyā comments: "They are brought to a state of having a single purpose (*aikārthyamupanīyante*)."
The state of having a single purpose (*ekārthatā*) arises from the accomplishment of a single objective.
The rest is clear.
For example, in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: “Kañcukī—(approaching, with joy)…”
"O Great King, you are victorious!

Indeed, this Bhīmasena has his entire body made crimson with the blood of Duryodhana, and his form is difficult to discern. By such means, there is the unification toward a single purpose of the seeds—such as the binding of Draupadī’s hair—which were introduced at their respective places during the *mukhasandhi* (opening juncture) and so forth.
Or, for example, in the seventh act of the *Śākuntala*, the subsequent mass of meaning [arises] from the token of recognition belonging to Śakuntalā.
He states their constituent parts:
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) This is the *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* (concluding juncture), which consists of the unification of the various scattered elements into a single whole.
It is accompanied by the attainment of the fruit in the form of the union with Śakuntalā, which is the intended goal.
"Of these" means of the five junctures (*sandhi*). [The elements are:
the introduction (*upakṣepa*), the preparation (*parikara*), the conclusion (*parinyāsa*), and the seduction (*vilobhana*). (VisSd 6.81)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) Regarding that, he states the twelve components of the *mukhasandhi*—beginning with "the introduction" (*upakṣepa*)—as follows:
the application (*yukti*), the attainment (*prāpti*), the resolution (*samādhāna*), the arrangement (*vidhāna*), and the cultivation (*paribhāvanā*).
Udbheda, karaṇa, and bheda—these indeed are the limbs at the beginning.
He states the definition according to the enumeration:
"The initial emergence of the poetic subject matter is known as the *upakṣepa* (the introductory hint). — Locanā.
(Lo, e) *Samutpattiḥ* is merely the origin.
The meaning of the poem (*kāvyārtha*) is the subject matter under discussion, characterized by the historical narrative (*itivṛtta*).
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: “Bhīma—”
Having struck at our lives and our accumulated wealth through the seizure of gains, fire, poison, food, and entry into assemblies,
and having dragged away the hair and garments of the Pāṇḍava wives, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remain at ease while I am still alive!
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, jha) Regarding the phrase "lākṣāgṛhānalena" and so forth—this is the speech of Bhīma upon entering [the hall] after hearing the stage-manager's words: "May the sons of the Kuru king, along with their servants, be at ease.
By the words beginning with "lākṣā," he asks: "While I am alive, how can those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra be at ease, having struck us down in our lives and our accumulated wealth?"
In this context, the meaning is that they will not remain at ease due to the sound of the crow.
By the words "lac" (*lākṣā*) and so forth, it is indicated that there is a blow both upon the vital breaths through the entry of the strike and upon the accumulations of wealth.
In the phrase "the lower garment and the hair" (*paridhānakeśān*), a *dvandva* compound is used.

In this context, the "embellishment" (*parikara*) is to be understood as the emergence of the subject matter of the poem—the narration of the destruction of the Kuru lineage—and the subsequent abundance of details concerning that subject once it has emerged. (VisSd 6.83)
As it is said in that very same place:
"The enmity that has grown between me and the Kurus is indeed due to my child; neither the noble Arjuna nor you two are the cause therein.
Yet Bhīma will once again shatter the peace treaty out of anger, like tearing apart the chest of Jarāsandha; you must bring about a reconciliation."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) He states the definition of the *parikara* ornament: "samutpanna...
etc. "The enmity that has grown intense"—this is Bhīma’s speech directed toward Sahadeva, as he is disinclined to make peace.
"Of the child alone"— even my youth was not taken into account by them, since they administered poison while I was still in my childhood.
"The noble one" refers to Yudhiṣṭhira.
Arjuna is the one with the diadem;
you two are Nakula and Sahadeva. You have grown up through the mission of Kṛṣṇa.
The connection is with the word *sandhi*.
Here, there is a multiplicity of meanings consisting of the description of the house of lac that has already arisen and so forth;
the completion of that is the *parinyāsa*.
As it is said in that very same work:

"O Queen, Bhima shall plait your hair with his hands stained crimson by the thick, congealed blood of Suyodhana, whose pair of thighs have been crushed by the blows of his fierce mace whirled by his trembling arms."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) He states the definition of *parinyāsa*: "the accomplishment thereof" (*tanniṣpatti*).
This means the accomplishment of the plot (*itivṛtta*) which constitutes the subject matter of the poem—the description of the fulfillment of the dramatic states (*bhāva*).
"Cañcat" etc.— this is a statement by Bhīma addressed to Draupadī:
"O Queen Draupadī, making your hair— your locks bound in braids— disheveled, Bhīma will adorn them [with flowers]."
The meaning is that he will distinguish [himself] by adorning Duryodhana’s thighs with ornaments.
Of what nature is Bhīma?
His hands are red with the thick, congealed, and profuse blood of Suyodhana.
Of Suyodhana of what sort? Of him whose pair of thighs was crushed by the blow of a mace whirled with a swinging, moving arm;
here, there is a description of the future accomplishment of the breaking of his thighs.
Locanā:

(lo, ai) "Styāna" means being congealed (*styānaḥ*), that is, bound together or solidified. Here, "introduction" (*upakṣepa*) refers merely to the brief presentation of the characteristics of the subject matter of the poem, such as [the word] "iti."
*Parikara* is the repeated cultivation of that very [mental image]; *parinyāsa* is the placing [of it] all around within the heart by way of attaining certainty even beyond that—
such is the distinction between these.
These factors occur in the sequence already stated,
whereas other factors may occur otherwise.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭha) Having reflected upon the distinction between these three, he shows it with the word "atra" (here).

Furthermore, because it consists of the attainment of certainty (*niścaya*), "attainment" (*āpatti*) means the reaching of, or the bringing about of, certainty—that is, the bringing about of certainty regarding what is to be done in reality;
[it occurs] in the heart of the knower, within the heart of the one who understands.
The description of virtues is seduction;
as in that very same work: “Draupadī:
My lord, what is difficult for you when you are incensed?”
Or, for example, as in my *Candrakalā*, in the description of Candrakalā: "She is the very grace of youth... and so forth (p. 139).

However, that description of the qualities of deer and other animals in works such as the *Śakuntalā*—beginning with "charming with the bending of the neck"—is not a constituent of the juncture (*sandhyaṅga*), because it lacks a connection to the purpose of the seed-plot (*bīja*).
In this manner, the other constituent parts are also to be inferred.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍa) states the definition of allurement (*vilobhana*) as "the proclamation of virtues."
"What is it? translates as *kiṃ duṣkaraṃ tvayā kupitena* in Sanskrit.
This is a statement describing Bhīma’s superior strength and physical excellence.
Regarding the phrase "of youth":
here, the words *vilāsa* (grace) and *hāsa* (laughter) are employed through *sāropā-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication where the superimposition is present), referring to that which produces them.
Herein lies the description of the beauty of the digit of the moon.
Regarding the phrase "the description of qualities such as those of a deer":
*guṇa* (quality) refers to a desirable attribute;
in this context, it takes the form of an action.

The meaning of "seed" (bījārtha) refers to the matter in the form of the seed for obtaining Śakuntalā; for the description of the deer's actions lacks connection to that [seed]. "Yukti" is the deliberation upon matters.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) He states the definition of reasoning (*yukti*): "deliberation" (*sampradhāraṇā*).
It is the demonstration of reasoning that establishes the meaning of what has been proposed.
For example, in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, Sahadeva says to Bhīma: "Noble brother, has this command of the Great King been understood by you in its unrefined sense? From that point until Bhīma’s speech:
"The destruction of the enemy clan in this world brings shame upon you because of your anger."
He does not feel shame for the dragging by the hair in the assembly."
Thus:
attainment is the arrival of happiness. (VisSd 6.84)
As it is said in that very same place: "I shall crush a hundred Kauravas in battle, not out of anger," and so forth (p. 284).
Draupadī—(having heard this, with joy)—My Lord, this is indeed a speech never heard before!
"Tell me that again and again. Vijñapriyā says:
He states the definition of acquisition (*prāpti*) as follows: "Acquisition... [and so on].
"Nādheti" means "nātha. It is indeed a statement such as this that has never been heard before;
therefore, "bhaṇa punaḥ punaḥ" is the Sanskrit [equivalent].
That which is the arrival of the seed is called its "settling" (*samādhāna*). *Vijñapriyā* (vi, ta) states the definition of settling: "of the seed," and so forth.

The statement of the previously mentioned seed-syllable (*bīja*) as being intended for the principal hero is [the *prastāvanā*]. As it says in that very same work: "(After a clamor behind the scenes) O Drupada, Virāṭa, Vṛṣṇi, Andhaka, Sahadeva, and the rest!"
"Listen, O lords of our Akṣauhiṇīs and foremost warriors of the Kaurava army:

that fire of Yudhiṣṭhira’s wrath— which was suppressed with effort by my mind fearing the breach of a vow of truth, and which the peaceful one desired to forget out of a wish for the peace of the lineage— that great flame of anger, fanned by the friction-sticks of the dice-game and kindled by the dragging of the princess’s hair and garments, now blazes forth in the forest of the Kurus."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
tha) "That which is real" means that "the fire of Yudhiṣṭhira’s anger" is the qualifier applied everywhere.

"From the gambling-fire": in the gambling-forest—that is, in the fire-drill wood (araṇi) consisting of the game of dice—the fire of his accumulated wrath was kindled by the dragging of Draupadī, the daughter of Drupada and the princess, by her hair and clothing.
For indeed, other fire as well is produced from the friction of the fire-drill.

In this context, the phrase “May they be well while I live,” and so forth, constitutes *samādhāna* (resolution), because the seed (*bīja*) has been properly established as being desired by the principal hero.
*Vijñapriyā* explains the etymological meaning of the term *samādhāna* here: “in this context.”
In this regard, Bhīma’s statement concerning the horse sacrifice is recounted as being approved by the primary protagonist Yudhiṣṭhira:
"The purpose brought about by pleasure and pain is known as 'arrangement' (vidhāna). (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.85)
As it is said in the *Bālacarita*:
"O child, look at your extraordinary energy and your youth!"
"My mind is simultaneously overcome by both joy and despair. Or as in my *Prabhāvatī*: "A source of delight for the pair of eyes," and so forth (p. 236).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, dha) He states the definition of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) in the form of the injunction: "The meaning is that which is produced by pleasure and pain.
Regarding "enthusiasm" (*utsāha*):
this is a statement by Janaka addressed to Rāma.
In this case, there is happiness through enthusiasm and suffering through childishness;
and in the phrase "pair of eyes," there is happiness according to the meaning as previously stated.
Suffering arises from separation from that [object].

*Paribhāvanā* (contemplation) is said to be speech characterized by curiosity, as for example, when Draupadī in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, doubting whether the battle will take place or not, cries out immediately after the sound of the trumpets: "O Noble One! (*ṇādha*)... [text fragment ends]
"Why now is this drum of battle being beaten moment by moment, like a thundercloud rumbling at the end of the rainy season?
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, na) She states the characteristic of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—namely, "with curiosity," etc.
"Nādheti.
[The King asks: "Nātha, why is this drum of battle—deep as the thundering of the clouds at the dissolution of the world—being struck moment by moment? Thus in Sanskrit.
In this context, Draupadī’s desire for battle is expressed through these words, which are characterized by curiosity.
Locanā: "Because of [her] sight...
(lo, a). ṇādha iti.
"O Lord, why now is this cloud of universal dissolution, so thick with thunder, having the drum of battle struck at every moment?
For there may be the sprouting of the seed's purpose—the manifestation—as it is said in that very same place: 'Draupadī: And furthermore, O Lord...'"
"Furthermore, you must come from the battlefield and comfort her.
Bhīma: "But, O daughter of the King of Pañcāla!
Why this false display of distress now?"
Furthermore, do you not see Vṛkodara, his face distressed by humiliation, exhaustion, and shame, yet having left no Kauravas remaining?
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) He states the characteristic of "breaking forth" (*udbheda*) with the words "of the meaning of the seed" (*bījārthasya*).
"Sprouting" (*praroha*) is the certainty regarding that which is to be produced.
"Ṇadha" means "O Lord, I must be comforted once again"— this is the Sanskrit.
"I" (aham) is Draupadī’s designation of herself.
Regarding the word *bhūyaḥ*:
the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is "you do not see again that which was bound, bent, and lowered.
Here, the present tense is used in the sense of immediate futurity (*bhaviṣyatsāmīpye*), indicating Bhīma’s certainty regarding the impending slaughter of the Kauravas.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ā) "Nātheti. O Lord, I must be comforted by you once again.
Furthermore, the performance [of this] is as follows: // VisSd_6.86 //
The commencement of the subject matter at hand—*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, pha) He states the definition of the instrument (*karaṇa*) as follows: "the instrument" (*karaṇam*).
This is clear;
as it says in that very same place: "O Queen, let us now go for the destruction of the Kuru lineage."
Separation (*bheda*) is the causing of division among those who are united.
As it says in that very same [text]: “Therefore, from this day forward, I am separated from you.
However, some say: “Separation is instigation (*protsāhanā*).”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) He states the definition of difference with the words "difference" (*bheda*).
The phrase "from today onwards" (*adya prabhṛti*) is Bhīma’s address to Sahadeva.
Now, the constituent parts of *pratimukha* (the second juncture):
*vilāsa* (playfulness), *parisarpa* (approach), *vidhuta* (shaking off), and likewise *tāpana* (tormenting).

In the *pratimukha* (opening) [sandhi], there should be play (*narma*), the brilliance of play (*narmadyuti*), as well as further advancement (*pragamana*), conflict (*virodha*), and likewise attendance (*paryupāsana*).

"Flower," "thunderbolt," "introduction," and "withdrawal of colors"—these, as well as "playfulness" (*vilāsa*), are said to be the thirteen components of the *pratimukhasandhi* (the introductory juncture).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, bha) [The author] states the thirteen components of the *pratimukhasandhi*, beginning with "playfulness."
In that regard—striving for the sake of pleasure and enjoyment is called *vilāsa* (amorous play). (Viṣṇu-saṃhitā 6.89)
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ma) "For the sake of the enjoyment of delight" means that delight (*rati*) is passion (*anurāga*).
The enjoyment of that consists of its objects, such as the heroine and so forth;
"endeavor" (samīhā) therein means desire.
If *rati* is indeed the act of sexual union (*nidhuvana*), then the meaning "desire for the enjoyment of that" is appropriate according to the illustrative examples.
Nevertheless, this has been explained in accordance with the author's own commentary:
*vilāsa* (coquetry) is the effort directed toward that object of enjoyment—whether a woman or a man—which serves as the cause for the emotion characterized by *rati* (erotic love).
As in the *Śākuntala*:
Granted that a beloved is not easily obtained, yet the mind is intent upon beholding her;
even when the god of love has not achieved his purpose, the mutual longing creates delight.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ya) "kāmaṃ prayeti" means she sends her desire.
This is the speech of Duṣmanta, who longs for Śakuntalā: "even though [my purpose] has not yet been accomplished," and so forth.

For a lover, the very accomplishment of his desired object is the fulfillment of the Mind-born (Kāma); thus, the meaning is that even when the Mind-born is absent [in one], [the other] fulfills him. "The longing for both" means that it produces in both an excess of passion and affection.
And in the present context, because Śakuntalā’s feelings have been observed, the meaning is that Duṣmanta, who was previously unasked for her hand, now feels passion for her.
Locanā:
(lo, i) "Kāmam" means...

The meaning is that even when the desire born of the mind (*manasija*) has not been fulfilled, the mutual longing—the mutual yearning—of the couple produces *rati*, which is pleasure, even in the absence of physical union.

If the longing of the heroine for the hero, or of the hero for the heroine, is observed, then even in the absence of enjoyment, affection arises between them; thus, by perceiving her state of being, [the lover thinks], "Her longing is manifested toward me," and his mind finds consolation.
The pursuit of what has been seen and lost is called *parisarpa*.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ra) states the definition of *parisarpa*: "the pursuit of what has been seen and lost," and so forth.

Regarding the word *naṣṭā* (lost), according to the meaning of the verbal root *ṇaś* in the sense of "disappearance," it refers to the disappearance of what was previously seen. Thus, the meaning is the pursuit of an object that was seen before but is no longer seen afterward.
As in the *Śākuntala*: "The King: She must have been there."
For instance:
"A fresh line of footprints is seen at his gate in the pale sand— high in the front and sinking deep behind due to the weight of the hips."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) "She must be here"—this is the King's statement;
it means that Śakuntalā must be present there.
He states the reason for this: "Because it is elevated," and so forth.
For on the white sand at the entrance of this bower of creepers, a fresh line of footprints is seen.
Of what kind is it? It is elevated in the front, that is, in the forepart of the footprint.
At the rear, she sinks down due to the weight of her hips;
here follows the pursuit of Śakuntalā as previously seen, and at the beginning of the conciliation, there is a rejection. (Viśvavidyā 6.90)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, va) He states the characteristic of being free from attachment (*vidhūtalakṣaṇa*) with the words "of what has been done" (*kṛtasya*).
The meaning is that there is a subsequent non-acceptance of the affection (*anunaya*) or joy (*prīti*) produced at the outset; it is something to be brought forth (*āhārya*).
As it says in that very same work: “Enough of your longing for the separation from the inner apartments and being obstructed by the royal sage.
However, some say: “It may be *vidhṛta*, which is *arati* (discontent).
*Vijñapriyā*:
"In that very place" means "in the *Śākuntala* itself.

Regarding "enough" (*alam*): the Sanskrit is *alaṃ vā antaḥ-purika-viraha-paryutsukena rāja-ṛṣiṇā uparuddhena*. This means: "Enough with this royal sage who is obstructed [by his duties] and distressed by separation from the women of the inner apartments."

In this case, due to the pressure of her friend, Śakuntalā initially experiences affection; however, because of the prohibition of that pressure, her lack of acceptance [of the proposal] is something brought about by external artifice (*āhārya*). Some say that because such a prohibition leads to the understanding of a lack of passion (*aratī*), there is a lack of aesthetic relish (*asvarasa*) here.
That which consists in the failure to perceive the means is what is called "torment" (*tāpana*).
Vijñapriyā (VI, 6) states the definition of torment: "The means," etc.
The means for attaining the intended object;
as in the *Ratnāvalī*: "Sāgarikā—Love for a rare person, heavy modesty, and a sense of shame."
"Friends, uneven love has death as its only refuge."
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
sa) “O dear friend, love for a person who is difficult to find, shame, and a self dependent on others— [these are the obstacles].”
"Unrequited love has death as its only refuge."
Thus is the Sanskrit. "Durlabhajana" means a king;
"ṇavarī" is purely a regional (deśī) term.
Thus, the syntactical connection is that "the Pradhāna is the refuge. Jocular speech (*narma*) is as follows—for example, in the *Ratnāvalī*: "Susamgatā—Friend! [and so forth].
He for whose sake you have come stands right here before you.
Sāgarikā— (with indignation) For whose sake have I come?
Susaṃgatā: "Enough with this suspicion of another;
it is indeed on a picture-board.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) He states the definition of *narma* (jest): "parihāsa...
and "sahī...".
The Sanskrit is: "O Śikhin! He for whose sake you have come stands right here before you."
*Kasseti* means "for whose sake have I come? in Sanskrit.
*Ayīti* [is used as an address].
"O, do not suspect another; surely it is [the reflection] of the picture-board!"—this is in Sanskrit.
Persistence born of jesting is [the nature of this state]. (VisSd 6.91)
Narmadyuti—likewise in that same [text]: “Susamgatā:
Friend, you are now ungracious, since even when supported by the hand of your husband, you do not relinquish your anger.”
Sāgarikā—(smiling slightly with a knitting of the brows) Susaṅgadā!
Even now you do not cease from playing?
Some, however, say: "The covering up of a fault is laughter, the luster of sport."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) He states the characteristic of playful brilliance (*narmadyuti*)—namely, "fortitude" (*dhṛti*).
The meaning is the capacity to endure jesting.
"Friend! You have now become one who offers no hospitality, you who do not relinquish your anger even though your husband has thus taken hold of your hand."
"Susaṅgatā! Even now you do not desist.
Herein lies Sāgarikā’s endurance of the jest made by Susaṅgatā;
the distinction is that her lack of endurance is shown through her display of resentment toward the jest.
Regarding the phrase "some say": here, there is a lack of natural elegance (*asvarasa*) due to the failure to perceive the concealment of the fault. ...
A statement that proceeds further and further would be a *pragamana*.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) He states the definition of the constituent element consisting of praise: "praise" (*praśaṃsanam*).
That by which something is praised is "praise."
The meaning is that praising such speech in a progressively ascending manner is the limb known as *praśaṃsānāma*.
For example, in the *Vikramorvaśī*: Urvaśī—Victory, victory to the Great King!
The King—
"By whom victory has been won, for you proclaim that victory"— and so forth.
Contradiction (*virodha*) is the attainment of misfortune (*vyasanaprāpti*).
And as in the *Caṇḍakauśika*: “The King: Surely, like a blind man, I—acting without due reflection—have trampled with my feet upon a fire with its flickering mass of flames.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ga): He states the definition of contradiction (*virodha*)—“contradiction” (*virodha*).
King Hariścandra;
Viśvāmitra, blazing with a mass of flickering flames;—and again, the conciliation of one who is angry. VisSd 6.92.
There may be "attendance" (*paryupāsana*), as in the *Ratnāvalī*: “Vidūṣaka—O sir, do not be angry!
For she has gone into the interior of the plantain grove,” and so forth.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, gha) He states the definition of the limb of attending upon [the teacher] with the words "of what has been done.
The meaning is: "of that which has been done as a cause for anger."
Furthermore, conciliation is for the purpose of demonstrating the reasons for not becoming angry.
"O!"— that is,
"O friend, do not be angry."
"For she has gone into the interior of the plantain grove" is the Sanskrit.
"She"—this indicates her entry into the interior of the plantain grove.
"Flower" is considered a term used in a specific sense.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṅa) He states the auspicious characteristics of the name "flower" with the words "flower.
The meaning is that this statement has the sense that "this particular [thing] is a distinct category of object."
As it says in that very same place: "(The King takes her by the hand and acts out the sensation of touch).
The Vidūṣakas: Oh, friend!
This unprecedented splendor has been attained by you."
The King: Friend, it is true—this is Śrī herself, and even her hand is a sprout of the Pārijāta tree;
otherwise, how could this flow of nectar, disguised as perspiration, stream forth?
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ca) "O friend, this unprecedented fortune has been attained by you"— thus [is the meaning] in Sanskrit.
"Śrī eṣā" means "This is Śrī.
The pretext of perspiration is a disguise for sweat;
[it arises] from the flowing of nectar-liquid from the sprouts of the Pārijāta tree.
A thunderbolt of direct harshness—as in that very same place: “The King: How was I, staying right here, known by you? Susaṅgatā: Not only by means of the picture-board.”
"Therefore, I shall go and inform the Queen.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) He describes the characteristics of the limbs having the form of a vajra: "directly perceived," etc.
"Not only that," he said;
"not only will you be equal to the picture-board,
but I shall go and report this to the Queen."
Thus [ends] the Sanskrit. These words of Susaṅgata were harsh to the king in his very presence. ---The presentation [of this] was for the purpose of appeasement. (VisSd 6.93)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ja) He states the definition of the introductory statement (*upanyāsa*)—namely, "the introductory statement. *Prasādana* means the request for favor.
As it is said in that very same place: “Susamgatā—My lord!
Enough with this suspicion!
By the favor of my lady, I too have indeed played with these.”
So why this ornament for my ears? Even more than that, this is a great favor to me:
that my dear friend Sāgarikā was angry because you have depicted me here.
"Let this very [point] be made clear.
However, some say: "For that which is produced by reasoning is called an *upanyāsa* (a formal presentation)."
And they cite this very point: “That slave-girl is indeed the first hour [of the day].
—Vijñapriyā:
(Husband: My lord, enough with this suspicion! By my mistress's grace, I too have already played with these very things.
So, what is the use of an ear-ornament?
"For this reason too, this favor of yours is even weightier to me—that you have depicted me here while my dear friend Sāgarikā was angry; she herself must be propitiated. This is in Sanskrit.
"What use are those ear-ornaments to you? and so forth, is a repetition of Sāgarikā's speech.
The meaning here is that the request for Sāgarikā’s favor is stated because it is supported by reason, being established through logic (*yuktyupapādasatvāt*).
Regarding the word *adī*:
the Sanskrit is *adimukharā*, meaning "this slave-girl from birth is indeed talkative."

The phrase "nārbhadāsī antaḥpuradāsī" (neither a slave-girl from the inner apartments nor a servant of the harem), along with the preceding harsh words spoken by Susaṅgatā such as "equal to a painted board," serves to justify the speech of the Vidūṣaka. The mingling of the four castes is intended here as the "fusion of colors" (varṇasaṃhāra).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) He states the definition of the limb consisting of the synthesis of castes with the words "cāturvarṇya" and so forth;
the meaning is that it is a statement concerning the confluence of the various castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
As it is said in the third act of the *Mahāvīracarita*:
"This assembly of sages, this hero Yudhājit, King Lomapāda along with his ministers and elders,
this ancient master of the Janakas who performs unceasing sacrifices and is a proclaimer of the Veda— O friend, they are all your supplicants!"
Vijñapriyā:
"(vi, ṭa) 'This assembly' refers to this demonstration of a gathering consisting of many castes, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, who have assembled."
This is the assembly of sages;
Yudhājit is the representative of the Kekaya country; and here is the aged King Lomapāda together with the sages and ministers.
This Sīradhvaja, the lord of the Janakas and of the Janaka lineage, is one who performs sacrifices without ceasing and is a proponent of the Veda;
these [people] are renowned as "adrohas," meaning they are devoid of malice—this is the sense of the word "these" (ete) referring to the officiating priests (*yājaka*).
In this context, there is a confluence of the various classes (*varṇas*), such as the Ṛṣikas and others.
Abhinavaguptapāda, however, explains: "By the word *varṇa*, the characters (*pātra*) are indicated; *saṃhāra* means a gathering.
And he cites as an example from the second act of the *Ratnāvalī*: beginning with "Therefore, this great favor of mine... up to "...take him by the hand and grant him [this] favor."
The King—"Where is he? Where is he? and so forth.
Now, the components of the womb (gārbhāṅgas):
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) "Pātrāṇi" means theatrical roles;
"adovī" means... [the rest of the sentence is missing from the source].
The meaning is: starting from the passage "Therefore, this favor of mine is even weightier," and so forth.
In the phrase "starting from" (*ityādeḥ*), the ablative case is used in the sense of a limit (*avadhi*).
The meaning is that the rule beginning with "Whatever I have drawn here... and so forth constitutes the initial injunction.
"ṇaṃ hatthe" means "surely by the hand"; the sense is: "take her by the hand and appease her. "kvāsau kvāsau" is an intensive repetition (vīpsā) used to express joy.

In this [act], the King, Susaṅgatā, and Sāgarikā are the characters; their meeting is the *abhūtāharaṇa* (the bringing together of what was not); the *mārga* (path) consists of the illustration of form (*rūpa*). (Viśvavidyā 6.94)
Gathering, inference, entreaty, and indeed dismissal;
[the states] of being struck, the force of authority, agitation, and likewise flight occur within the womb.
In that regard, a statement based on a pretext is considered *abhūtāharaṇa* (the taking away of what was not).

For example, in the case of Aśvatthāman: "Having clearly stated, 'Aśvatthāman is slain,' by the son of Pṛthā, the speaker of truth then uttered at his own will the remainder, 'an elephant,' in the end."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) He states the twelve factors of the *garbhasandhi* with the words "abhūta... (*Viṣṇupurāṇa* 3.18.1).
He states the definition of "unreal narration" (*abhūtāharaṇa*) with the words "tatra vyāja... (*Viṣṇupurāṇa* 3.18.2).
"Aśvatthāman is slain"—this was Yudhiṣṭhira’s statement, relying on a pretext.
Hearing it, that king, whose son was dear to him, believed it and released both his weapons and his tears in battle with equal measure.
The path consists in the exposition of the true meaning—as in the *Caṇḍakauśika*: “King: Blessed One, please accept this acquired wealth resulting from the sale of my wife and son.”
I shall even sell myself to a Caṇḍāla for the sake of the remainder.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ḍha) He states the definition of the limb of the path that consists of form— namely, "the true meaning"— which means speaking without guile.
"Let it be accepted"—this is King Hariścandra’s address to Viśvāmitra.
The grammatical construction is: "Let this wealth acquired by the sale of my wife and son be accepted.
You shall perform the sale of yourself for the sake of even the remaining wealth.
In that regard, even in times of adversity, the king’s speech is free from guile;
his appearance and his words are full of discernment.
As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*: “The King:
‘The mind is by its very nature fickle and difficult to perceive;
nevertheless, how is it that Kāma has pierced this [mind] of mine with all his arrows simultaneously?’”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) He states the limb consisting of form—namely, "form. Vitarka is the investigation of possible and impossible causes.
"By its very nature"—this is the reflection of the King, who is separated from Sāgarikā.
"Difficult to perceive" means impossible to see or discern.
An "example" (udāharaṇa) is said to be a statement endowed with excellence.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) He states the definition of the constituent member in the form of an example—namely, "the example" (*udāharaṇa*).
It is that which is endowed with excellence and endowed with one's own self-conceit (*svāhaṅkāra*).
As it was said in the presence of Aśvatthāman:

"Whosoever among the armies of the Pāṇḍavas bears arms with pride in the strength of his own arms; whosoever belongs to the lineage of the Pañcālas, whether he be a child, advanced in years, or even lying in the womb;
whosoever is a witness to those deeds—"
Whoever acts as an enemy toward me, whoever is hostile, blinded by anger—I myself am the end-maker of that very person, even here in this world where I am the end-maker of all worlds.
Vijñapriyā: "(vi, tha) 'Whosoever [takes] the weapon'—
this is the speech of the enraged Aśvatthāman."

While I was moving about in battle amidst the armies of the Pāṇḍavas, filled with pride in the strength of my own arms— whosoever wielded a weapon, whosoever belonged to the Pāñcāla clan, and so forth;
likewise, whosoever performed that deed, and so forth—
that deed being the act of severing the head of my deceased father.

Thus, whosoever regards me as one blinded by anger, the meaning is that I am the end-maker of each and every such person. By their very act of inflaming my anger—which is the end-maker of the world—I become the end-maker of the world; this is the meaning.
However, the realization of the true nature of reality would be a gradual process.
As it is said in the *Śākuntalā*: "The King: It is indeed fitting that I gaze upon my beloved with eyes whose blinking has been forgotten.
For instance—her face, with one creeper-like eyebrow raised as she places her footsteps..."
With her cheek bristling with horripilation, she proclaims her passion for me.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) He states the characteristics of the limbs of the sequential form—beginning with "bhāva":

the meaning is that there is the perception of the reality of *bhāva*, which is passion. Regarding "unnamita": as she was composing the words that constitute the verses, her face—the agent—[was directed] toward me with a cheek bristling with horripilation.
The meaning is that she expresses her passion.
Of what nature is the salutation?
It is one in which a single creeper-like eyebrow is raised.
Furthermore, the summary [is as follows]: VisSd 6.97.
Endowed with conciliation, gifts, and purpose—as in the *Ratnāvalī*: “The King: Well done, friend!
Here is a reward for you.”
(Thus she gives him the bracelet.
Vijñapriyā:
(with a smile) "By conciliation and bribery."
The meaning is that the wealth consisting of lamps and honor belongs to the donor through conciliation, affection, and giving.
Regarding the word "well" (*sādhu*)—here it refers to the excellence of the wealth in the form of bracelets being given to the suitor. *Liṅga* (mark/sign) means inference (*anumāna*).
As it is said in the *Jānakīrāghava* drama: “Rāma:

Even when he merely moves about playfully, he causes the earth to tremble with his glances; even as he bows the heads of the worlds with his looks, his body—fair with a golden luster—makes one infer both his descent from the Sun and his invincibility.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, na) He states the definition of the constituent parts of inference by saying "from the mark" (*liṅgāt*). What is this nature of inference? What is its means of cognition (*māna*)?
"Līlā" means this is a description of Paraśurāma; his "līlā" refers to his resolve or undertaking.

Being the son of the Sun (Sūryatanaya) implies, by virtue of possessing splendor equal to the Sun, both his status as the Sun’s son and his invincibility. Of what sort was he? Even by his movements (gataiḥ), that is, his journeys, he caused the earth to tremble;
and by his glances (ālokanaḥ), he caused the heads of the worlds to bow, for all were prostrated before him merely upon seeing him.
For one whose body is as white as the luster of gold,
the longing for the festivals of delight and joy would indeed be a mere longing.
As it says in the *Ratnāvalī*: "My dear Sāgarikā!
Your face is the moon, your eyes are blue lotuses, and your hands resemble lotuses."
Your pair of thighs resembles the trunk of a plantain tree,
and your arms are like lotus stalks;
thus, O lady whose every limb brings delight!
Come, come! Embrace me impetuously and without hesitation, and quench with your limbs those parts of mine that are distressed by the fever of love.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) He states the definition of the limbs of prayer and the limbs of form as "joy" (*rati*) and so forth.
The meaning is: the request for such festivities on the part of the hero, which is the heroine's joy for the sake of pleasure (*rati*).
"O you whose every limb brings delight by virtue of your form as the cool-rayed moon!
Come, come; embrace my limbs impetuously and forcibly, without hesitation, and extinguish them which are distressed by the fever of the bodiless god of love."
The meaning is: "Make them free from distress.
Here, there is a prayer for a festival dependent upon the breaking [of the ice];
and this is the dramatic element (aṅga) called "prayer" (prārthanā).
This was stated according to the view that there is no constituent named *praśasti* because it occurs within the occasion of the *nirvahaṇa*;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the number [of constituents] being sixty-five.
*Vijñapriyā*:

(vi, pha) Here, there is an optional status for this portion of the *praśasti* element belonging to the *nirvahaṇa-sandhi*. However, if these two were to exist simultaneously, the number of *saṃdhy-aṅgas* mentioned as sixty-four would not be maintained;
for that would result in there being sixty-five.
For in this *garbhasandhi* (embryo-junction), when these components are present, there are thirteen of these members;
twelve members of the *mukhasandhi* (opening-junction) have been stated,
and there are thirteen members each for the other two junctions.
Since there are fourteen constituent elements (sandhyaṅgas) of the *nirvahaṇa* juncture, it would follow that [the total number] reaches sixty-five.

Therefore, he says "And this" (*idañca*), meaning that this element exists only according to those views in which the final element named *praśasti* does not exist within the *nirvahaṇa* juncture; otherwise, however, it does not.
Regarding that, he states the reason for the existence of the member named *praśasti*: "because of the absence of the occasion for living beings (*bhūta*).

Living beings (*bhūta*) are sentient creatures who serve as the actors in the drama; their "occasion" (*avasara*) refers to the presence of such beings. Thus, the limbs [of the drama] are said to have living beings as their occasion.
The meaning is that because the benediction of the members [of the assembly] for the praised character lacks that quality [of secrecy],
it would constitute a disclosure of the secret matter— a "kṣipti" (defect)—
as in the *Aśvatthāmāṅka*.
This is the terrible ripening of that very act which now manifests upon the earth; for if there were a second seizing by the hair, surely all living beings would have been utterly destroyed.

Vijñapriyā: (vi, ba) He states the limb consisting of the form of throwing [aside]—namely, "of the secret matter. Secret matter is the matter to be indicated, which takes the form of the plot (*itivṛtta*); its disclosure is the indication of its origin.
Regarding the word "of one":

it refers to the single instance of Draupadī’s hair being seized. In this second instance—the seizing of the hair of the deceased Droṇa by Dhṛṣṭadyumna—there is an indication of the origin of the secret whose nature is the total destruction of all.
Then again,
the *ṭakaṃ* [is used] for speech that is agitated—
as in the *Caṇḍakauśika*: “Kauśika— Ah!”
"Furthermore, why have the golden dakṣiṇās not yet been produced?
Vijñapriyā says: [She] states the characteristic of the *troṭaka* form: "As for the *troṭaka*, moreover..."
"Saṃrabdhavāk" means angry speech; "Āḥ, you sinner!
refers to Viśvāmitra’s angry words directed toward King Hariścandra for the purpose of demanding the gift of the earth as a sacrificial fee.
He who, under the pretext of superior strength and great joy...
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) He states the characteristic of superior strength (*adhibala*)—namely, "superior strength" (*adhibalam*).
"Intention" (*abhisandhi*) refers to a connection made by means of a pretext for the purpose of explaining the six headings (*uddesa*).
As in the *Ratnāvalī*: “Kāñcanamālā: ‘My lady, this is Cittasālikā; I shall prepare the perfumes for Vasantaka,’ and so forth.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ya) "My lady," [she says]. O mistress, this is the picture-gallery.
Thinking, "I shall give Vasantaka the signal," she prepared herself.
When a rendezvous had been arranged with Vasantaka in the picture-gallery near the King in order to bring Sāgarikā there under the guise of Vāsavadattā,
Kāñcanamālā, having discovered this, brought Vāsavadattā herself and Sāgarikā arrived in the place intended for Vasantaka.
Thus, this speech of hers regarding Vāsavadattā was made by means of a gesture with her finger;
the agitation born of fear caused by the king and others is thus described. As it says in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*:
Having arrived and mounted upon a single chariot, they will question you here and there—
both that enemy of Karṇa and that cruel Vṛkodara, whose deeds are like those of a wolf.
Vijñapriyā:
"Produced by the king and others" means that fear has been produced in the king and so forth by someone.
"Prāptāvekaratha" means this:
that Arjuna, the enemy of Karṇa, and that Vṛkodara Bhīma of cruel deeds—these two brothers, mounted upon a single chariot, have arrived; that is to say, they have been encountered.
The production of fear in Duryodhana by means of Karṇa being his enemy and his cruel deeds is [the cause];
the agitation produced by suspicion, fear, and terror is considered to be *vidrava* (flight). 6.100.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) He describes the limb consisting of flight (*vidrava*) with the words "fear caused by apprehension" (*śaṅkābhaya*).
The meaning is that flight is considered to be the agitation or confusion produced by fear and terror—that is, by the apprehension of something undesirable.
Fear (*bhaya*) is aversion toward a future undesirable object;
whereas terror (*trāsa*) is the state of being bewildered as to what should be done due to the sudden occurrence of an undesirable event.
For example:
Upon beholding the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who had arisen in fury with a mouth as terrifying as the Destroyer at the end of time, a certain agitation arose within the monkey host.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, va) "Kālāntaka" means that upon seeing the ten-faced one agitated by wrath—that is, trembling with anger—a certain agitation arose among the monkey army; such is the meaning.
Now, the constituent elements of *vimarśa* (reflection):

Apavāda (denial), saṃpheṭa (collision), vyavasāya (resolution), drava (flowing), dyuti (splendor), śakti (power), prasaṅga (consequence), śeda (cutting off), pratiṣedha (prohibition), and virodhana (opposition). (Viśvavidyā 6.101)
In the *vimarśa* [juncture], there should be *prarocanā*, *ādāna*, and likewise *chādana*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, śa) He states the thirteen components of the *vimarśa-sandhi*, beginning with "apavāda" and so forth.
There may be the disclosure of faults and censure—as, for example, in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: “Yudhiṣṭhira: Pañcālaka!
Has the track of that wicked wretch, that lowest of the Kauravas, been discovered anywhere?”
Pāñcālaka: Not only his tracks, but that very villain himself— the primary cause of the sin of touching the Queen’s tresses—
has been discovered.
The manifestation of faults is the making known of faults. The path of the lowest of the Kauravas, the vilest of the Kauravas, refers to his footprints;
that evil-souled one is Duryodhana.
In this context, the manifestation of faults occurs through mere speech;
*saṃpheṭa* is speech uttered in anger. (VisSd 6.102)
As it is said in that very same place: “The King: Ho there, son of Marutta!
Before an aged king, you boast even of your own blameworthy deed. Listen, you—”
By my command as the lord of the world, the wife of that king—whether it was yours, or yours, or his beast’s, or both—was dragged by her hair at the dice-game and became a slave;

tell me, what harm did those slain kings do in that persistent enmity, that you have such pride in not having conquered me, who am heavy with the intoxication of the wealth of the excessive strength of my arms?
Bhīma—(with anger): Ah, you villain!
The King—Ah, you villain! And so forth.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, sa) He states the limb consisting of the form of *sampheṭa* (conflict): "Are! Re! and so forth.
This is a speech addressed by [Bhīma] to Duryodhana, calling him out.
"Of the aged King Dhṛtarāṣṭra—[she who was] dragged!

By you, Bhīma; by you, Arjuna; or by that King Yudhiṣṭhira, as if she were a sacrificial animal; or by those two animals, Nakula and Sahadeva—the wife of the Lord of the World, by my command, was dragged by the hair in the presence of the kings as a slave won at dice."

Tell me, what harm was done by those kings who were slain by you in such a continuous succession of enmity? By the specific sound of his throat, it is understood that the pride he felt after conquering them is the very same pride he feels after conquering me. Of what sort am I?

"Ah, you sinner!"— this is the mutual address between Bhīma and Duryodhana, [the former] regarding the wealth in the form of the excessive strength in their arms as "wealth" (*draviṇa*) that causes heavy pride.
King Duryodhana;
here, there is the expression of anger by both of them,
and their resolve should be understood as arising from the cause of their vow.
As it is said in that very same place: “Bhīma—
having slain the entire host of Kauravas, intoxicated by the blood of Duḥśāsana,
and having broken the thighs of Duryodhana, here is Bhīma bowing his head.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) He states the limb consisting of resolve (*vyavasāya*)—namely, "and resolve"—as follows:
the possibility or accomplishment of the object of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) from the reason (*hetu*).
The meaning is "the narration of that. Regarding the word *nihatā*:
*kṣība* means intoxicated (*matta*).
*Asṛjā* means with blood. *Bhaṅktā* means one who causes breaking.
*Drava* is a transgression against a guru arising from the force of grief and so forth. (VisSd 6.103)
As it is said in that very same place: “Yudhiṣṭhira: O Blessed One! O elder brother of Kṛṣṇa!
O brother of Subhadrā!”
Affection for kinsmen was not kept in your mind, nor was the duty of Kṣatriyas firmly rooted; even that friendship was not reckoned upon by Arjuna toward his younger brother.
Granted, let there be a bond of affection between your two disciples as you wish; but what kind of path is this, that you have turned your face away from me, unfortunate as I am?
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) He states the limb that has the nature of fluidity—namely, "fluidity.
"Transgression against the guru" means reviling him.
"Bhagavan," and so forth.
This is Yudhiṣṭhira’s rebuke of Balabhadra, who was enraged by his affection for Duryodhana.

The two terms "Kṛṣṇagraja" (Elder Brother of Kṛṣṇa) and "Subhadrābhrātṛ" (Brother of Subhadrā) are used to demonstrate their relationship in order to show the propriety of their affection for their own side.
Regarding the phrase "affection for kinsmen":
it means that we are [mere] kinsmen;
even the duty of the Kṣatriyas has not been kept in mind.
For it is the duty of Kṣatriyas to avoid turning away from the slaughter of those who do not fight; yet we, though not fighting,
have failed to take into account even that friendship which has grown between you and your younger brother Śrī Kṛṣṇa with Arjuna.
The bond of affection between the two disciples, Bhīma and Duryodhana, is equal.
Let it be as you wish;
let it be better so.
"Since you have turned away from me, who am so unfortunate—what kind of person are you? This is the meaning.
Herein lies the rebuke of the elder Balabhadra by Yudhiṣṭhira.
Radiance (*dyuti*) is said to consist of threatening and terrifying;
as was said by Prince Vṛkodara to Duryodhana in that very same place:
"You claim descent from a lineage as pure as the moon even now, yet you carry a mace; you consider me an enemy intoxicated by the honeyed blood of Duḥśāsana's warm gore."
O beast among men! Blinded by pride, you act with such insolence even toward Hari, the enemy of Madhu and Kaiṭabha; now, out of fear of me, you have fled the battlefield and are hiding in the mud.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
kha) He states the characteristics of the limbs in the form of radiance, beginning with "the threatening gesture" and "by the youth."
The meaning is "by Bhīma.
In some places, the reading is simply "by Kumāra Vṛkodara. Regarding the word "janma" (birth):
You claim birth in the lineage of the stainless moon;
yet even now you wield a mace.
You speak to me, your enemy, who am intoxicated by the slightly warm blood of Duḥśāsana.
The meaning is: you do not speak of the giver of life in accordance with his actual deeds.
O beast among men! Blinded by pride even toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the enemy of Mura, Kaiṭabha, and Dhenuka—you act haughtily and arrogantly.
Why is it that now, out of fear of me, you have abandoned the battle and are hiding in the mud? Such is the sense.
In this context, the word "how" is to be understood through intonation (*kāku*). Furthermore, there would be a power [of the statement] consisting in the pacification of contradiction.
As it is said in that very same work:
"Let the trusted ones reduce the bodily burdens of those slain at the head of the battle to ashes; let these kinsmen somehow offer water mixed with tears to their kinsmen.
Let them search for the bodies of their kin, mangled by vultures and herons in the thicket of slaughtered men; the sun has set along with the enemies—let the armies be withdrawn!"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) He states the limb consisting of power—namely, "power.
The meaning is that the "pacification of contradiction" refers to the statement of the conclusion.
"Let the kinsmen perform [the rites]" means that the kinsmen,
the relatives, should consign the physical remains of those killed on the front line of battle to the fire.
Likewise, let these kinsmen somehow offer water mixed with weapons to their kin;
likewise, let them search for the bodies of their relatives, mangled by vultures and crows in the thicket of slain men;
and let the sun, its companion, go to its setting along with the enemies.
The meaning is that the powers (*balas*) should be withdrawn. ...
The mention of the Guru follows as a necessary consequence. (VisSd 6.104)

As in the *Mṛcchakaṭikā*: “The Cāṇḍāla: This is indeed Cārudatta, the son-in-law of Āryaka Viśvadatta and the grandson of Sāgaradatta, who is being led to the place of execution to be put to death; it is said that he was to have been killed by this courtesan Vasantasenā out of greed for gold.
Cārudatta: (With despondency, to himself)”
“That lineage which was illuminated before me by the dense sounds of Vedic recitation in the assembly, purified by hundreds of sacrifices—
that very lineage is now being proclaimed in public by sinful men who are unworthy of it, at the time when I am facing my death.”
By this [statement], "the glorification of the Guru occurs through an incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*) that is favorable to the success of Cārudatta’s execution," the *prasaṅga* is [defined].
*Vijñapriyā*:
He states the subsidiary element (*aṅga*) in the form of an incidental discussion with the words "incidental discussion" (*prasaṅga*).
"Cāṇḍālaka" means that,
having seen Cārudatta being led away to be executed, the executioner said;
"eṣa" (this one) refers to him.
"This is Cārudatta, the son of Sagara-datta and the grandson of the noble Viśva-datta, who is being led to the place of execution to be put to death.
It is said that he killed the courtesan Vasantasenā out of greed for gold.
Upon hearing this, Cārudatta, feeling ashamed because of the mention of his own illustrious lineage, says: "O you who have performed a hundred sacrifices... and so forth.
That lineage of mine which was previously purified in former times, and which was proclaimed loudly in the assembly by Brahmins with resonant voices amidst dense and magnificent shrines—

meaning it was praised— now, while I am in the state of death, that same lineage is being proclaimed for the purpose of announcing my execution by sinful, unworthy men such as Cāṇḍālas; such is the meaning.
By this [phrase] "iti":
the meaning is that it is favorable toward the prosperity of the executioners, which consists of the execution of Cārudatta.
The mention of the teacher (the victim) is made because the executioners desire precisely the destruction of his family.
The recitation of the names of the father, grandfather, and ancestors of one who is to be executed [is prescribed].
Fatigue produced from mental activity is known as *kheda*.
An example of that which arises from the mind is found in the *Mālatīmādhava*:
My heart breaks with intense anguish, yet it does not split in two; my distressed body suffers delusion, yet it does not lose consciousness;
an internal burning consumes my frame, yet it does not reduce me to ashes; Fate strikes me, cutting through my vital organs.
It does not cut off life.
Thus, even that which arises from physical movement is included.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṅa):
He states the limb consisting of weariness as "mental activity" (*manaśceṣṭā*).
"Dalati" means it bursts open;
this is Mādhava’s speech arising from his grief for Mālatī, who was carried off by Kapālakuṇḍalā.
"It does not burst open" means that it does not split into two pieces.
The logical connection is that a defective body carries delusion;
it does not cut, nor does it sever—
such is its activity.
Her two arms, their palms excessively red from lifting heavy loads, still cause her breasts to tremble with her deep breaths;
a lattice of sweat-drops clings to her face like *śirīṣa* flowers stuck to her ears, and as her hair-knot loosens, her disheveled locks fall only partially restrained by one hand.
Thus, the exhaustion of Śakuntalā resulting from the effort of lifting the jar is considered a "prohibition" (pratiṣedha),
which is defined as the obstruction of a desired object.
As Pradyumna says to Vidūṣaka in the *Prabhāvatī*: "Friend!
How is it that you remain here all alone?
Where indeed is my beloved Prabhāvatī, who is followed by her dear circle of friends?"
Vidūṣaka: By the Asuras, having been brought here, she has been led away somewhere.
Pradyumna: (Sighing deeply) Alas, O you with the face of the full moon!
“O you with eyes like those of a intoxicated cakora bird, O lady with slightly stooping limbs, having abandoned me, where have you gone?”
Go now, O life!
Depart quickly; let fate, intent on torment, have its desire fulfilled.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ca) He states the limb consisting of a negation—namely, "īpsitena" (by the desired one).
Regarding "asuravaiṇa": the Sanskrit is "asurapatinā ākṛṣya kutrāpi nītā," meaning "drawn away by the lord of the Asuras and led somewhere."

Having addressed his beloved in the first half-verse with "O Full Moon" and lamented, he addresses his own life in the second half-verse, saying: "Go, you too, this very day! The meaning is: "Let fate, which is intent on tormenting me, have its desire fulfilled. Herein lies the frustration of the desired reunion with Prabhāvatī.
The departure after the completion of the task is known as *vihodhana*.
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, Yudhiṣṭhira says:
"When the great ocean that was Bhīṣma has somehow been crossed, when the fire of Droṇa has been extinguished, when the serpent Karna has been quelled, and when Śalya has departed for heaven..."
When victory had been reduced to a mere remnant by the impetuous Bhīma, who delights in rash deeds, we were all brought to a state where our very lives were in peril by his word alone.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) He states the limb consisting of the form of cessation (*nirodharūpa*)—namely, "the passing away of the task" (*kāryyatyaya*).
The meaning is that existence (*bhavana*) is the arrival at the passing away of the task intended as the objective.
Regarding the word "tīrṇe" (when [the other] has crossed):
this was said by Bhīma to Duryodhana during their mace-duel,
that upon his own defeat, there would be the defeat of all his brothers.

Having heard this, the implication is that Yudhiṣṭhira perceived the failure of his task, which was his own victory, as imminent; for while victory remained with only a small portion left, we were all brought to the brink of death by Bhīma, who is fond of rash acts.
He demonstrates that victory has only a small portion remaining by saying, "He has crossed."
"O peaceful one, extinguished!
O you who have an asp in your ear!"— an *āśī* is a snake, and its poison is within it.
"In such a serpent-like ear" means in a snake that is like an ear;
however, the "enticement" (prarocanā) should be understood as that which demonstrates the purpose of the withdrawal (saṃhāra). VisSd 6.106.
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: Pāñcālaka begins, “I am accompanied by His Majesty Cakrapāṇi,” and concludes, “Enough with doubt!

Let the jeweled jars be filled with water for your royal consecration; let [Kṛṣṇa] for a moment loosen your braid, which Draupadī has long abandoned. While Rāma, with his hand radiant with the sharp axe, cuts down the trees of the Kṣatriyas, and while Vṛkodara, blind with rage, falls upon the battlefield—whence can there be any uncertainty?”
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ja) He states the constituent element in the form of an inducement— namely, "the inducement," which is defined as that which demonstrates the purpose of the summary.
The meaning is that this speech demonstrates the conclusion of the task.
"Let them be filled"—
this is what was said by the Pāñcāla, who had been sent by Kṛṣṇa to Yudhiṣṭhira during the mace-duel in order to ascertain Bhīma’s victory.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "May these [ornaments] be fulfilled for your royal consecration.
The connection is: "Let Draupadī, the dark-complexioned one, celebrate the festival for a moment, even though her braided hair has been untied for an exceedingly long time.
He asks: "How could this be possible when there is doubt regarding Bhīma’s victory? and then says: [the following].

"Rāma" refers to Paraśurāma, whose hand shines with a sharp axe and who cuts down the trees that are the Kṣatriyas; and to Vṛkodara (Bhīma). When he, blinded by rage, falls upon [the enemy] in battle, what doubt can there be of victory?
"The undertaking of the task" (kāryasaṃgraha) means its commencement.
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: "Ho there, you who roam the Samantapañcaka!
I am no demon, nor a spirit; my limbs are drenched in the blood of my enemies. Having fully crossed the deep ocean of my vast vow, I am a wrathful Kṣatriya. Ho there, O warrior-kings!"
Only those who remain as remnants after being consumed by the flames of battle's fire have acted rightly;
for you, who were hidden away within slain elephants and horses, dwell here out of fear.

In this context, because the task of slaying all enemies is summarized, there is "acquisition" (*ādāna*). *Vijñapriyā* (vi, jha) states the definition of the limb in the form of acquisition: "the summary of the task."
The meaning of "attainment" (prāpti) is the gathering together of the intended effects.
"I am not a being" (nāhaṃ bhūtaḥ) means that I am not a particular living being belonging to the divine class of beings (devayoni).
For this very reason, it has the masculine gender, according to the lexicon (kośa) which states: "The word *bhūta* refers to these [spirits] born from the gods.
To the question "Who are you then?", he replies: "With the blood of my enemies," and so forth.

Being wrathful, with my limbs moistened by the water of the enemies' blood, and my body fully gratified, I have crossed over the ocean that was my great vow; for you, O warriors of the royal line, who remain as the remnants after being consumed by the flame of the fire of battle—enough with this seat of yours! O sirs, both the nature of the ocean and the nature of the forest have been manifested.
Enough of this meal for you!
This "āsa" (sword) is meaningless;
the sense is that you must not be killed by me.
To the question, "How is it known that it is 'āsa'?", he says: "hatā" (killed).
"Wherever you sit or stay, hidden by slain elephants and horses"—
the meaning is that because the task consisting of the destruction of all enemies has been gathered together and accomplished.
Regarding this, they say that "covering" (chādana) is indeed the endurance of insults and the like for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose. (VisSd 6.107)
As it says in that very same place: Arjuna said—“Noble sir, be gracious! Why this anger here?
He may do unpleasant things through speech, but he is not capable of doing so through action.”
For one who has lost a hundred brothers and is already suffering, what pain can there be from his lamentations?
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) By the phrase "from insult and so forth," the inclusion of harsh speech is intended;
[this refers to] "unpleasant words."
This is Duryodhana.
Now, the components of the conclusion (nirvahaṇāṅga):
reconciliation (sandhi), awakening (vibodha), tying together (grathana), decision (nirṇaya), and conversation (paribhāṣaṇa).
The act [of union], the bliss arising from his grace, the commitment, and also the embrace.
Speech, the introductory statement, and the conclusion of the poem—these are to be known by name as the components of the *saṃhāra* (conclusion), namely the *praśasti* (eulogy). VisSd 6.109.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) He states the fourteen components of the *nirvahaṇa-sandhi* [concluding juncture], beginning with "the juncture (*saṃdhi*), the awakening (*vibodha*)," and so forth.
Among these—
The "approach to the seed" (*bījopagamana*) is the *sandhi* (union).
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding that, he states the constituent element (*aṅga*) which is the form of *sandhi* as "the approach to the seed."
The meaning is that there is a recollection of that [seed] through the accomplishment of the seed in the form of the matter previously promised.
As it says in that very same work (*Veṇīsaṃhāra*):
"Bhīma: Your Majesty..."
O you who are born from the sacrificial altar,
your ladyship remembers what was said by me— beginning with “*cañcadbhuja*,” and so forth.
By this, there is the *sandhi* (reunion) of the seed cast into the mouth [of the womb] returning once again.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍa) "Having slain a hundred Kauravas, it becomes a sacrifice"—this and so forth is the speech of Bhīma.
"With his trembling arms," and so forth, has been explained previously.
"By this" means:

the seed that was first cast into the mouth [of the discourse], introduced, awakened by the proposition (*pratijñā*), and having returned in the form of the meaning of the proposition, has been made known; such is the meaning.
"Awakening" (*vibodha*) refers to the investigation of the task (*kārya*).
As it is said in that very same place: “Bhīma: ‘May my noble brother release me for a moment.
Yudhiṣṭhira: ‘What else remains?
Bhīma: ‘A great deal remains.’”
"I shall first restrain with this hand, stained by the blood of Suyodhana, the mass of hair of the princess of Pañcāla that was seized by Duḥśāsana.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "May you depart;
let the ascetic woman experience the binding of her braid."
From this, because of the search for the purpose of arranging the hair, there is *vibodha* (awakening). *Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍha): He states the limb whose nature is awakening—namely, "awakening."
“Seeking the task” means the investigation of what must be done.
Regarding the term *keśahasta*: it refers to a mass of hair; for *pāśa*, *pakṣa*, and *hasta* are all synonymous with “mass” (*kalāpa*).
"Following *kaca*," so says the lexicon (*koṣa*).
As for "introduction" (*upanyāsa*), it is the stringing together of matters to be done.
As it is said in that very same place: Bhīma says—“O Princess of Pañcāla!
While I am alive, you must certainly not gather with your own hands this braid disheveled by Duḥśāsana.
Stay still; I myself shall gather it.”
By this, because of the introduction of the matter to be accomplished, there is the "opening" (*āgrathana*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṇa):
He states the constituent element (*aṅga*) in the form of an "introduction" (*upanyāsa*), saying: "the introduction."
*Grathana* is the statement of the action that is about to be performed.
*Vilulita* means shattered or broken apart.
*Upakṣepāt* means from the introduction by way of presenting what is about to be done.
Furthermore, the definitive conclusion is as follows: VisSd 6.110.
The narration of an experienced object—
as in that very same [text],
Bhīma says: "O Lord Ajātaśatru!"
Even now that wretched Duryodhana lives!

For by me, the body of that evil-souled one was cast upon the earth; this blood, resembling sandalwood paste, has been smeared upon my own limbs, along with the Earth bounded by the waters of the four oceans, upon whom Fortune (Lakṣmī) has been firmly fixed.

Servants, friends, warriors, and the descendants of the Kuru clan—all have been consumed by the fire of battle; O King, that which you now call by a single name, "the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra," is the only remnant remaining.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) He states the constituent element consisting of the decision—namely, "the decision" (*nirṇaya*).
"O Ajātaśatru" is another name for Yudhiṣṭhira.
"Cast upon the ground":
the body of that evil-souled Duryodhana was cast—that is, thrown down—upon the ground by me;
this blood of his, though belonging to his own limb, has been laid down like sandalwood, possessing the appearance of sandalwood.
O Noble Lady, Fortune has been assigned to you along with the earth bounded by the waters of the four oceans;
yet this [fortune] was consumed in the fire of battle.
To the question "What is that?", he says: "The servants," and so forth.
The grammatical connection is: "the descendants of Kuru's lineage, beginning with the servants.
O King! the meaning is that now only that which you call the name of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son remains.
They speak of "reproach" (paribhāṣaṇa), which is speech consisting of censure—as, for example, in the *Śākuntala*: "Noble Lady! O King! [the King says].
"Now, of what royal sage is that lady the wife? The female ascetic: "Who would mention the name of one who has taken a lawful wife?"
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, tha) He states the limb consisting of reproach with the words "they say. "Parivāda" means a sentence composed for the purpose of reproach; that is to say, a sentence whose meaning is one of censure.

Noble lady! Now, regarding the inquiry beginning with "Is she here?": after Duṣmanta had abandoned Śakuntalā due to forgetting her under the influence of Durvāsas’s curse, he returned from heaven as one tormented by separation; having failed to find her and having heard the account of her from the mouth of an ascetic woman, [he asks this].
Who will restrain him? Who indeed will take the name of one who has abandoned his lawful wife? — This is the work that brings peace once the goal has been attained. VisSd 6.111.
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: “Kṛṣṇa: Here stand the venerable Vyāsa, Vālmīki, and others, performing the consecration.
By this, the stabilization of one who has attained the kingdom through the auspicious rites of consecration is established as *kṛti*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, da) He states the limb consisting of the form of action: "having attained the following" (*labdhānugamanam*).
"Following" (*anugamana*) means making firm.
"Bearing the consecration" (*abhiṣekaṃ dhārayantaḥ*) means causing it to reach [its goal].
In some recensions, the reading is "dhārayanti" (they maintain).
Favor (prasāda) consists of service and so forth—
as, for example, in that very same context, Bhīma’s binding of Draupadī’s hair.
Joy is the arrival of what is desired.
As it says in that very same work: “Draupadī: I have forgotten this task; by the grace of the Lord, I shall learn it once again.”—Vijñapriyā.
(vi, dha) He states the limb consisting of bliss (*ānanda*): "Bliss" (*ānanda*).
"This has been forgotten" (*visumaridaṃ*) means in Sanskrit: "Having forgotten this activity, I shall learn it once again through the grace of the Lord (*nātha*)."
The activity consists of the act of binding her hair;
the occasion for the departure from suffering—as in the *Ratnāvalī*: “Vāsavadattā—(embracing Ratnāvalī)...”
"Take heart, sister; take heart.
Vijñapriyā:
[She] states the limb consisting of the convention (*samaya*)—namely, "the convention" (*samaya*).
"Samassasa" means "Take heart, sister;
take heart," which in Sanskrit is *samāśvasihi*.
This is the speech of Vāsavadattā upon recognizing that this [woman] is Sāgarikā’s maternal cousin:
"That would be an embrace. (VisSd 6.112)
As for the occurrence of a marvel—
such as when Pradyumna, in my *Prabhāvatī*, upon seeing Nārada, looked upward:
"Carrying a flower garland like a streak of lightning, accompanied here and there by the humming of swarms of bees wandering in the breeze," [he gazed].
Whitening the horizons with its rays as white as the moon, is this Mount Kailāsa falling from the sky? Or what else could this be?
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pa) He states the limb consisting of embracing with the words "that would be":
the attainment of the marvelous is the vision of the marvelous.
Regarding the passage beginning with "dadhat" and so forth:
in the phrase "from Mount Kailāsa," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of departure (*apāya*).
Thus, the ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "some object falls from Mount Kailāsa, having departed from it, with the sky serving as the limit (*avadhi*)."
The reading "kailāsādri" (the Kailāsa mountain) found in some places is an error,
because that [mountain] lacks the wearing of flower garlands.
What kind of object is it?
He wears a garland of flowers like a streak of lightning.
Of what sort is the garland? It is accompanied by the songs of swarms of bees wandering here and there due to its fragrance.
And what is the nature of the object?
It is that which mottles the ends of the quarters with rays as white as the moon;
for there is a mottling resulting from the mixture of white rays with the darkness of the very horizon.
Therefore, the meaning of "what then is this? is as follows:
it refers to speech such as conciliation (*sāma*), bribery (*dāna*), and so forth.
As in the *Caṇḍakauśika*: "O Dharma—come, preside over the world of Dharma."
Vijñapriyā:
(pi, pha) He states the limb consisting of speech—namely, *sāmadāna*—as follows:
