*Tālavṛnta* means a fan. The grammatical connection is that [the wind] is moistened by *śīkara* (sprays). *Saṃvāhayāmi* means I press or rub [it].
In this case, there is the presentation of various means, such as fanning with a palm-leaf fan, for the sake of one's desired object, namely union with Śakuntalā.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) occurs when another meaning is understood from the statement of a different fact. (Viśvavidyā 6.189)
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: Karṇa tells Droṇa that Aśvatthāman desires to be consecrated in the kingdom, to which Droṇa replies: "O King! Well said, O King of Aṅga!
Well said! Otherwise, how could it be that he—the Atiratha—having given away his armor, was slain by Kirīṭin?"
Otherwise, how could he have disregarded the King of Sindhu? Otherwise, it would not be so.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṇa) "Having granted safety" refers to Arjuna, the wearer of the diadem, [granting it] to the King of Sindhu.
"If it were not so" means that there was no desire to consecrate his own son to the kingdom.
Here, by virtue of the statement made for another purpose— namely, the indifference toward the King of Sindhu— the certainty of Droṇa's such desire is indicated.

But in the context of censuring and proclaiming faults, *bhartsanā* (threatening) is indeed *garhaṇa* (reproach). As it says in that very same work regarding Karṇa: "Aśvatthāman—[I am] rendered powerless by the utterance of my preceptor’s curse; why do you treat me as if I were you? Having abandoned the battle just now out of fear, I have arrived here; what of it?"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) He states the characteristic called "reproach" (garhaṇā): "dūṣaṇa... etc.
The meaning is that when there is a proclamation of a fault (*dūṣaṇoddhoṣaṇā*), the threatening of the one being faulted by that very proclamation is what is meant.
"Rendered powerless" means:
Paraśurāma was the preceptor of Karṇa;
because of his curse, which took the form of a spoken word, your weapon is indeed rendered powerless—meaning, "What will it do to me? is the sense.
And here, the particle *eva* (only/just) should be applied according to the sequence shown.
In this context, through the proclamation of the weapon’s defect in the form of its lack of power, there is the perception of a rebuke directed at Karṇa, who is being censured:
"I was born into a lineage of charioteers skilled in proclaiming praises; why should I counteract the unpleasantness caused by a base enemy with a weapon, and not with a non-weapon?"
The seeking of the meaning of a question is considered to consist of words accompanied by entreaties. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.190)
As it says in that very same place: “Sundaraka: Noble ladies, have you perhaps seen the great king Duryodhana by the light of the autumn moon?
[Vijñapriyā:]
(vi, tha) He states the definition of what is called *pṛcchā* (inquiry): "By means of entreaties," etc.
The meaning is that *pṛcchā* is the investigation of a matter being considered through other words consisting of entreaties.
Sundaraka is a follower of Duryodhana.
"Noble sir! Noble sir! Have you perhaps seen the Great King Duryodhana accompanied by his charioteer?
(Thus in Sanskrit.)
Establishment [of the plot] is the accomplishment of the purpose through means that are well-known and superior in worldly convention, as in the *Vikramorvaśī*: "The King:
He whose maternal grandfather and paternal grandfather are the Sun and the Moon..."
He who was made his own husband by both Urvaśī and Bhū.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) He states the definition known as "the well-known" (*prasiddhākhya*)—namely, "the well-known" (*prasiddhi*).

The meaning is that it is the establishment of one's own intended object (*svābhīṣṭārtha*) by means of objects that are already established in the world (*lokasiddha*), which are superior and serve as the means of proof.
Regarding the phrase "the sun and the moon":
the grammatical connection is with the two [names], Urvaśī and Bhuvā; the ellipsis is "I, being such, ask."

In this context, the proof of one’s own desired object—consisting of stating what was asked—is established by mentioning such things as being born from a family of the sun and so forth, which are well-known in the world.
Through similarity, the arousal [of passion] is increased by means of resemblance to that which is appropriate. (VisSd 6.191)
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: [addressing Bhīma] under the delusion that he is Duryodhana—"Yudhiṣṭhira: O evil-souled one! Wretched Duryodhana! and so forth. *Vijñapriyā* [comments]:

(vi, dha) He states the characteristic called *sārūpya* (resemblance): "sārūpyam" [means] the increase of agitation in the self due to the similarity with an experienced object, even when that object is distinct from the specific experience itself.
"O evil-souled one," and so forth.
In this case, because of the resemblance to Duryodhana experienced [previously], there is an intensification of agitation upon seeing Bhīma.
As for *saṃkṣepa* (abridgment): when the self is employed for another purpose through abridgment, as in my *Candrakalā*: "The King: My dear..."
"Why do you pointlessly weary your limbs, which are as delicate as *śirīṣa* flowers?
(Pointing to himself: Here is your servant who shall provide for you the flowers you desire."
Vijñapriyā:
He states the definition known as "concise" (*saṃkṣepa*)—namely, "concise," etc.
The meaning is that for the sake of another person, that is, on account of a purpose, one's own self (*ātman*) is employed, which is to say, it is directed toward action.
"You weary your limbs"—the ellipsis is "for the sake of gathering flowers.
Here, the king has employed himself for the purpose of his beloved's flower-gathering.
As for the praising of virtues, that indeed is the "proclamation of virtues" (guṇākīrtanam). (Viśvavidyā 6.192)
As it is said in that very same work: “The eyes are like the *khañjana* bird, a rival to the lotus,” and so forth (*Vijñapriyā*, vi, pa).
He states the defining characteristic called "the praise of qualities" with the words: "of the qualities," etc.
"His eyes are like those of a wagtail," and so forth, as previously stated. That is called *leśa* (a slight hint), a statement preceded by a comparison, as in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: "The King—"
When the son of Gaṅgā is slain while Śikhaṇḍin is placed in front,
whatever glory belongs to the sons of Pāṇḍu shall likewise belong to us.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) He states the definition known as "with a trace" (*saleśa*):
"preceded by similarity," meaning preceded by an expression of similarity.

"She hates because of old age"—the remainder of the sentence is "because of the slaughter of Abhimanyu. A wish, however, is the expression of an intention by means of a different turn of phrase. (VisSd 6.193)
For example: "Look, O fair-browed one! This kadamba bird, languid with passion and skilled in the arts of love-play, kisses his beloved after her ritual adornment."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) He states the definition known as *manoratha*: "But *manoratha* [is]...
A *bhaṅgī* is the presentation of another person's narrative that corresponds to a narrative residing within one's own intention.
Regarding "ratikelī":
for the sake of the play of love (*rati-keli*), there is a slight sound (*kala*)—a sweet, indistinct, and low-toned noise;

Elsewhere,

And these two, Tiṣya and Punarvasu, both wise and named Kalyāṇa, [are directed] toward Cārucandramas.

Regarding the phrase "it arises":
the attribution of "before you" is due to the rapid arising of the excellences produced by your grace.
In this context, these words of joy are spoken by the sage for the purpose of demonstrating his excellence.
Now, the ornaments of drama (nāṭyālaṅkāra):
Benediction (āśis), lamentation (ākranda), deception (kapaṭa), command (ājñā), pride (māna), arrogance (garva), exertion (udyama), and refuge (āśraya).
Derision, longing, agitation, regret, and attainment.
Aspiration and determination are designated as spreading and scratching;
incitement, disparagement, policy, and the specification of purpose [are the others]. (VisSd 6.196)
Encouragement, assistance, honor, compliance, as well as praise, solicitation, avoidance, and reporting; (Viṣṇu-samhitā 6.197).
Commencement, narration, reasoning, and exhilaration—
these are the ornaments of drama, serving as the causes for its adornment.
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding what was stated [in the previous section], namely that "the thirty-three dramatic ornaments" (*nāṭyālaṅkāra*) [beginning with] "vi" and "ya," he says "atha" in order to explain them.
He enumerates those ornaments starting with "āśīḥ."
Blessing (*āśīḥ*) is the expression of a wish for the welfare of another;
as in the *Śākuntala*:
"May you be highly esteemed by your husband, like Śarmiṣṭhā was by Yayāti."
You too, serve as a sovereign and obtain Pūru as your son.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ra) He states the ornament called *āśis* (benediction)—"āśīriṣṭajane" etc. The meaning is: a benediction directed toward a beloved person.
The syntactical connection is: "Just as Śarmiṣṭhā obtained a son, Purū, so may you likewise obtain a son.
--- *Ākanda* is a lamentation uttered in grief;
as in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: "Chamberlain—Alas, Queen!"
"O Kuntī! O banner of the royal palace! and so forth. [Thus ends] the *Vijñapriyā*.
(vi, la) He states the poetic figure called *ākranda*: "In *ākranda*...
This is clear.
*Kapaṭa* (deceit) is where another form is manifested through illusion (*māyā*). (VisSd 6.199)
Just as in the lap of the family head— having cast off his deer form and assumed a deceptive body,

Intolerance is such that even a slight insult is not endured, as in the *Śākuntala*: "King—O speaker of truth!
We have already accepted it."

But what is obtained by intending this? Śārṅgarava: "A downfall... and so forth. *Vijñapriyā*: [This refers to the following: "What, however, is obtained by intending this? Śārṅgarava: "A downfall... and so on. *Vijñapriyā*: [Commentary.]

"O, O," and so forth.

Ho! [referring to her as] "this wife.

Pride (*garva*) is speech born of arrogance—as in that same [text]: “The King: ‘Even my own house is being overrun by common creatures!

(vi, ṣa) He states the ornament called *garva* (pride): "Pride (*garva*) is haughtiness (*avalepa*), that is, self-conceit (*ahaṅkāra*).

As in the *Kumbhāṅka*: “Rāvaṇa—overwhelmed by grief, I see only Death himself.

In the play named *Kumbha*, the statement “I see him” by Rāvaṇa—who is afflicted with grief for Indrajit—is this declaration that he himself will be his own end at the commencement of the battle.
Taking refuge (*grahaṇa*) is said to be the resorting to someone who possesses virtues for the sake of accomplishing a task;
as in the act concerning the rebuke of Vibhīṣaṇa: “Vibhīṣaṇa—‘I take refuge in Rāma alone.’”

ha) He states the ornament called "the basis" with the words "the grasping," etc.,
[and] "Rāma alone," etc.

As in the *Śākuntala*: “Śārṅgarava: O King, if you have indeed forgotten the previous events due to preoccupation with other matters, then how can there be such an abandonment of one’s wife by one who fears unrighteousness? and so forth.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ka) He states the ornament called *utprāsa* (ironical praise) with the words "utprāsanam" [and so forth].
O you who take pride in your own excellence!
"In one who considers himself virtuous" refers to the mockery expressed by "O King," and so forth;

Desire (*ākāṅkṣā*) is that longing for an object because of its loveliness; as in that very same [work]: "The King:
This [hand] is unscarred and tender, yet it throbs with a beautiful glow."
"The beloved's lower lip seems to grant me permission as I thirst."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) He states the ornament called *spṛhā* (longing): "desire," etc.
Regarding the word "charmingly": this is a statement by the King, who, upon seeing Śakuntalā’s quivering lower lip, desires to drink from it.
The meaning is that this lower lip, tender and unscarred, seems by its quivering to grant me permission to drink from it.
That very agitation which utters words of insult is what is called *kṣobha*. (Viśvāmitra-saṃhitā 6.202)

When Rāma, having falsely uttered a curse upon Sītā due to a slip of the tongue regarding her lineage and so forth, had consoled the proud Sītā and then gone outside on some other business, there arose at that time a remorse in him for having performed the act of kissing her.

This is a compassionate utterance by a lover toward someone who, having been brought to the execution stone (*vadhyaśilā*)—a place where one dies—is lamenting his beloved who is about to die with him.
If you desire your beloved, described in the first half [of the verse], to remain alive, then protect yourself by means of your own life-breaths.
"I shall die for your sake.

Here, the speaker's intention is the protection of one who is to be executed; to accomplish that, the reason is presented in the form of a desire such as "the beloved of the one to be executed" and so forth.

and that [result] has already begun.
Regarding the word "of one":

"This is the ripening of that single act of Duḥśāsana seizing Draupadī by the hair: a battle that brings about the destruction of all the Kṣatriyas."
In the second [act], there was the seizing of my father by the hair;
here, the commencement of the seizing of the hair is joined with an undesirable result, as in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: “This is the ripening of this very one alone,” and so forth (page 376).
The mention of "the effect" refers to the figure of speech called *ullekha*.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, jha) states: he describes the ornament named *ullekha* with the words "the perception of the effect."

The meaning is that this is a demonstration of the king's purpose for awakening [the sages]. "The two ascetics" means they spoke thus after dissuading the king from killing the deer, in order to fetch sacrificial fuel;
here, there is a demonstration of the king's purpose, which consists of his entry into the hermitage distinguished by Śakuntalā.
As in the *Śākuntala*, regarding the king: "The two ascetics—We have set out to gather sacrificial fuel.
And here, as if presided over by a deity, the hermitage of our preceptor Kaṇva, the head of the clan, is seen along the bank of the Mālinī together with Śakuntalā. Unless otherwise..."
"The neglect of duties; enter and accept the hospitality due to a guest"—
this is considered "incitement."

"Just as you are Indrajit and Caṇḍavīrya, you are powerful by name alone;

that which would be assistance in times of distress and favor toward another—as in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra* regarding Kṛpa: "Aśvatthāman—do you also remain by the side of the king."
Kūpa: "I desire to repay [your kindness] today," and so forth.

which is the narration of deeds performed in the past;
as, for example, in the *Bālārāmāyaṇa*:

*Vijñapriyā*: [This is the commentary].

In that [previous type], there is the narration of a previously established matter in its own form, such as "all the Kauravas have been slain," whereas here, it concerns a past event performed by both oneself and others; this is the distinction between them.
Here, the word "āsīt" (there was) occurs in these words of Rāma, who has arrived by means of the Puṣpaka chariot and is showing Sītā the battlefield:
"When your brother-in-law Lakṣmaṇa was deeply struck in the chest by Rāvaṇa with a *śakti* weapon, Mount Droṇa—that is, Mount Gandhamādana—was brought here by Hanumān."
The description of Devarāta is for the purpose of generating affection.

By the divine arrows of Lakṣmaṇa, Indrajit was sent to the other world. O fawn-eyed one! The forest of the neck of Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, has been cut down here by someone—that is to say, by me.

na) He states the ornament consisting of a rebuttal with the words "the rebuttal" and "the departure of life."

"Out of great respect for the God who is the joy of Devakī, let the appropriate preparations be undertaken there for the victory and auspiciousness of our dear Bhīmasena.
Narrative (ākhyāna) is the recounting of past events—as in that same work: "This is that very place where lakes were filled with the blood of enemies," and so forth.

(vi, pha) He states the ornament called *pravartanā* [incitement]: "But incitement (*pravartana*)...
The meaning is that it is the incitement toward a virtuous auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) by means of a connection with the task to be accomplished.

He states the ornament consisting of narration (*ākhyānarūpālaṅkāra*): "In this context, the narration of a past event is to be qualified by its being rooted in anger. Reasoning is the ascertainment of the meaning. VisSd 6.211.
As it is said in that very same work:

ba) He states the ornament consisting of reasoning— “reasoning” means the determination of the meaning of a matter for others by means of demonstrating the logical grounds.
"If [you say] 'battle'":
this is Aśvatthāman's speech directed at the heroes who were fleeing due to the death of Droṇa;
here, by demonstrating the stated reason, there is the determination that battle must be undertaken.
*Praharṣa* (exultation) is an excess of joy—as in the *Śākuntala*: “King: Why then do I not now rejoice in myself, my desires fulfilled?
(*Vijñapriyā*):
(vi, bha) He states the ornament called *praharṣa* (exultation): *praharṣa* is clear. *Śikṣā* is instruction.
As in that very same [work]: "Friend,..."
"It is not fitting for a person dwelling in a hermitage to depart according to their own will, having abandoned the performance of hospitality and special rites of welcome.

Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ya) And "of these" refers to the thirty-six characteristics that have been stated.
"Thirty-three dramatic ornaments have been mentioned;
even though they are of a single nature.

This means that even though there is the possibility of a single nature—since there is no differentiating factor (*vinigamaka*) between being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and being an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), such that the defining characteristics could themselves be ornaments and the ornaments could themselves be defining characteristics—the number remains thirty-three.
"By way of distinction" means by distinguishing them as follows: "these are the characteristics" and "these are the ornaments."
The "stream of the ewe" (*gaḍḍalikāpravāha*) is a beginningless, established, and stainless conventional usage.
Locanā:
Regarding "by the stream of the ewe"—just as one ewe follows after another in its wake.

The meaning is that, just as there is a distinction among those [types of women] based merely on following one after another, so too is there a distinction between *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) and *nāṭyālaṅkāra* (dramatic ornaments). Furthermore, although some of these may be included within specific categories such as *guṇas*, *alaṅkāras*, *bhāvas*, *saṃdhis*, or *aṅgas*, they are mentioned specifically because they must be employed with deliberate effort in a drama (*nāṭaka*). Regarding the phrase "and among these":

the meaning is that even though some of these poetic elements may be included within others— either because they take the form of poetic figures such as *upamā* (simile) or *vyatireka* (contrast) which will be discussed later, or because they function as qualities (*guṇa*) or as suggestors (*vyañjaka*) related to those qualities— it is still possible for them to be subsumed under those other poetic elements.

"Because it must be performed with effort"—and it should be noted that this necessity of performance is according to what is appropriate for each specific context, following its propriety; it does not apply to everyone in every situation.
And these [works] are:
"possessing five junctures, four modes, and endowed with sixty-four limbs."
Endowed with twenty-six characteristics, adorned with ornaments, possessing great aesthetic flavor and great enjoyment, and accompanied by noble composition— Locanā.
"Great flavor" (mahārasa) means that which is uninterrupted by the cultivation of aesthetic sentiment (rasabhāva);
it is the honoring of the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa), characterized by virtuous conduct and beloved by the people.
A poet should compose a drama with well-knit joints and connections, characterized by excellent execution, providing a source of pleasure, and expressed through soft-sounding words.

Since it has been stated by the Sage [Bharata] that "the components of the *vīthī* must necessarily be employed in a drama," they will now be described. Regarding this, the *Vijñapriyā* commentary states: "However, because the Sage has declared that a drama must be composed by a skilled poet as something distinguished in all its parts, he says—'possessing five junctures (*sandhi*) and four manners (*vṛtti*)', and so forth—in order to show that all of this must be performed by him."
One should compose a *nāṭaka* ending with these [elements].
The five junctures (*sandhi*), beginning with the introductory juncture (*mukha-sandhi*), have been mentioned previously;
likewise, the sixty-four constituent parts (*aṅga*) of those junctures have also been mentioned previously.
The thirty-six characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of dramas were stated previously;
the thirty-three ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) have just been mentioned;
and "the thirty-three [elements] to be employed and the thirteen limbs of the *vīthī*."
Since it has been stated thus, and because the thirty-three ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) have already been discussed, the occasion for describing the components of the *vīthī* has now arisen;

however, since the *vīthī*—as a specific type of dramatic form (*rūpaka*) distinct from the *nāṭaka*—has already been specifically shown, he says "the components of the *vīthī*" (*vīthyaṅgāni*), meaning that those components will be explained at the appropriate time when they are about to be presented.
He now states the components of the *lāsya*: [The text continues with the list of lāsyāṅgas.]
The *geyapada* consists of verses recited while standing, sitting, or [in other postures], as well as the *puṣpagaṇḍikā*.
The *pracchedaka*, the triple-secret (*trigūḍha*), that called *saindhava* which is double-secret (*dvigūḍhaka*), the *uttamottamaka*, and another, the *uktapratyukta*. (Viśvavidyā-saṃhitā 6.213)
"Indeed, this tenfold division of the limbs of *lāsya* has been declared by the wise. [The author] says "the limbs of *lāsya*" in order to state the ten limbs of *lāsya*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, va) He says "the limbs of *lāsya*" in order to state the ten limbs of *lāsya*.
There—
having placed the stringed instrument before him, he sits upon his seat with it in front.
Pure song is the verse to be sung—
Locanā: (lo,
u) it is dry and must be imitated.
For example: While playing the lute in the house of Gaurī, Malayavatī says:
"O Gaurī, whose radiance is as fair as the pollen of blossoming *kesara* flowers, for me indeed..."
O Blessed One, may my desire be fulfilled through your grace.

Vijñapriyā: (vi, śa) Regarding that, he describes the *lāsyāṅga* known as *geyapada*: "tantrībhāṇḍa... etc. *Tantrībhāṇḍa* refers to the lute (*vīṇā*) which is the support for the strings; having placed this in front, meaning having made it the primary element, there is *śuṣka-gāna*, which is singing devoid of dance.
"Utphulleti"—the grammatical connection is "my desired [object].
That is called *sthitapāṭhya* (recitation while standing).
It is where one, tormented by love, recites Prakrit while remaining standing. (VisSd 6.215)
But Abhinavaguptapāda says: “This is merely an illustration;
even for one agitated by anger, the recitation of ordinary [verses] is *sthitapāṭhya*.
A woman possessed by grief and anxiety [should perform it] devoid of all musical instruments.
When the body is not adorned with ornaments, it remains exactly as it was while sitting.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ṣa) He describes the seated posture as "free from all musical instruments" (*nikhilātodya*), meaning it is devoid of drums and other such instruments.
The meaning is that she stands with her body covered by a garment while overwhelmed by grief;
[he sees] singing accompanied by musical instruments, various meters,
the inverted behavior of men and women, and clusters of flowers.

Vijñapriyā: (vi, sa) He states the dramatic element known as *puṣpagaṇḍikā*: "ātodya... etc. *Chandāṃsi* refers to prose, verse, and melodies; *viparyāsa* is their inversion, that is, their transposition.
Locanā: (Lo, Ū) The behavior of a woman is the inverted behavior of a man, and the behavior of a man is the inverted behavior of a woman.
Perceiving her husband to be attached to another woman, a woman's singing accompanied by the lute out of the resentment of broken love is considered *pracchedaka*.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ha) He states the dramatic element (*aṅga*) called *pracchedaka*—namely, "another [man] is attached" (*anyāsakta*).
The meaning is that, out of resentment, she sang preceded by the lute while disregarding her husband.
The dance of men wearing women's attire is smooth and characterized by three secrets.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ka): He states the limb called "three secrets" [as follows]: "wearing women's attire," etc.
"Gentle and charming" refers to the term *makaranda*.
This is because, in order to deceive Mālatī, he assumed the guise of Lavaṅgikā, and in order to deceive Nandana, he assumed the guise of Mālatī.
As in the *Mālatīmādhava*: “Makaranda: Here I am, transformed into Mālatī.
This is one who has missed the rendezvous and is clearly possessed of the [appropriate] physical gestures (*karaṇa*). (VisSd 6.219)
Where one speaks in the vernacular (prākṛta) language, that is considered Saindhava;
the instrumental means (karaṇa) consists of the playing of the lute and other instruments;
and the song (gīta) possesses four square sections (caturastrapada) accompanied by the introductory (mukha) and transitional (pratimukha) sections.
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) It consists of four-line verses well-known from Bharata and others;
it is doubly hidden and rich with aesthetic flavors (rasa) and emotions (bhāva).
Furthermore, the most excellent of the excellent [songs] arises from anger or favor, is joined with reproach, and possesses the highest aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) He states the limb known as *dvigūḍhaka*: "consisting of four square feet.
This means a song endowed with four quarters (*pāda*).
And that song is to be sung during the *mukha* and *pratimukha* junctures (*sandhi*); this is the meaning.
He states the limb known as *uttamottamaka*: "Furthermore, the *uttamottamaka*... [is characterized by] "anger," and so forth.
The *lāsya* dance is sometimes characterized by reproach because it arises from anger;
at other times, it is overflowing with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) because it arises from serenity.
This refers to the *hāva* and *helā* gestures.
In this context, *hāva* is distinguished from *helā*; it is for the purpose of intensifying *helā*, following the analogy of a bull.

[The *vilāsa*] is charming due to its composition of variegated verses endowed with both *hāva* and *helā*, joined with dialogue and counter-dialogue, and characterized by reproach as if it were false. (VisSd 6.222)
That which consists of questions and answers containing the meaning of songs accompanied by graceful gestures is called *uktapratyukta*.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ga) states: he describes the *aṅga* [named] *uktapratyukta* with the words "questions and answers" (*uktipratyuktī*).
Reproach is derision; and that occurs by adducing a false matter, as he says: "as if it were false.
The examples are clear.
When this very [work] is endowed with all the dramatic markers (patākāsthānaka), [it is called a *prakarana*]. // VisSd 6.223 //
The ten [verses] with their numerical markers indicate the *Mahānāṭaka*.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, gha) states: "It refers to the specific type of drama called *Mahānāṭaka*—namely, this very one."
The meaning is "the drama itself.
Regarding the phrase "by all the *patākāsthānas*":
it is the sudden attainment of a meaningful purpose, endowed with excellence, through figurative expression (*upacāra*).
This first *patākāsthānaka* has thus been fully described.
The meaning is: by these four *patāka-sthānas* (subsidiary episodes) mentioned [in the preceding verses], beginning with "ityādi.
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) Thus, according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), the definition of the *naṭaka* (drama) is distinct from the definition of the *mahānāṭaka* (great drama).
This very [type of drama] is the *nāṭaka*;
for example, the *Bālarāmāyaṇa*.
Now, the *prakaraṇa*—
The subject matter may be either a historical event or a worldly tale imagined by the poet.

In the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), the hero (*nāyaka*)—whether a brahmin, a minister, or a merchant—is resolute and tranquil, yet devoted to dharma, pleasure, and wealth, which are subject to danger. (Viśvavidyā 6.225)
Locanā:
(lo, ḷ) Now, in accordance with the intended subject matter, he defines the types of drama and so forth, beginning with "bhava" etc.;
[this refers to] the worldly (*laukika*), and not the divine (*divya*) or the mixed (*miśra*).
For example, *Mṛcchakaṭika* has a Brahmin as its protagonist;
*Mālatīmādhava* has a minister as its protagonist;
and *Puṣpabhūṣita* has a merchant as its protagonist.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṅa) Regarding the various divisions of *rūpaka* and *uparūpaka* such as the *nāṭaka*, *prakaraṇa*, and *bhāṇa* which have been proclaimed—since it has been stated that "the definition of all [these] is considered to be like that of the *nāṭaka*, except for their specific distinctions"—having thus explained the definition of the *nāṭaka* along with its limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), he states the second type of *rūpaka*, called the *prakaraṇa*, with the words: "Now, the *prakaraṇa*."
That *vṛtta* is a subject matter to be described in drama;
and because it is purely invented by the poet and is not found in the *purāṇas*, it is worldly (*laukika*).
It is "accompanied by calamity" (*sāpāya*).

The meaning is that, due to being adorned with passion (*śṛṅgāra*), sometimes it belongs to Dharma because of the heroine’s pride, sometimes to Kāma because of the pursuit of sensual desire, and sometimes to Artha because of the undertaking of wealth; thus it is "endowed with decline.
Regarding the term *dhīrapraśānta*:
"One who abounds in general virtues, such as being twice-born and so forth, is *dhīrapraśānta*."
The characteristics of the hero have been described previously.
*Puṣpabhūṣita* is a specific variety of dramatic composition (*prakaraṇa*).
The heroine may be of noble birth, or a courtesan, or in some cases both.
Therefore, there are three divisions of that; among them, the third division is [as follows].
It is crowded with gamblers, players at dice, and other parasites such as jesters and servants.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ca) Therefore, it has three divisions.

In this context, the courtesan of noble birth constitutes three distinct types due to the differentiation between the two kinds of heroines. Regarding the case of the heroine being both [a noble wife and a courtesan], he states the characters for the third type as "the gambler" and so forth;
the noble wife is adorned with flowers.

The courtesan, however, belongs to the *raṅgavṛtta* (stage-action). Both [the *mṛcchakaṭika* and the *prahasanana*] are also [included here]. Because they are the prototypes (*prakṛti*) for the *āsya* and *nāṭaka*, the remainder is like the *nāṭaka*.
Now, as for the *bhāṇa*:
the *bhāṇa* is a performance characterized by the conduct of rogues, consisting of various changing situations. (Viśvavidyā 6.227)
In this [performance], there is only one actor, a clever and learned *viṭa*, who shall manifest on the stage what has been experienced by himself or by another. (Viśvavidyā 6.228)
One should respond to addresses and replies with words spoken from the sky;
one should indicate the heroic and erotic sentiments through descriptions of valor and charm.

In that regard, the plot consists of the already occurred and the invented; the style is generally Bhāratī; and there are the Junctures (sandhi), namely the Opening (mukha) and the Conclusion (nirvahana), as well as all ten members of Lāsya.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) He speaks of the dramatic form called *bhāṇa* with the words "Now," etc.
[He explains] "various situations," etc.
The hero is the inner soul of the drama; he is to be understood as a learned rogue who exists in various states. The grammatical construction is: "the object experienced by himself or by another."
"One should indicate" means:
the heroic sentiment by means of valor, and the erotic sentiment by means of charm.
The meaning is that it should indicate [this].
It must be produced by the poet himself.
Here, even while repeating for oneself a statement from another in the form of an "utterance from the air" (ākāśabhāṣita), one should perform the reply and counter-reply.
One should indicate the sentiments of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and the heroic (*vīra*) through descriptions of beauty and valor;
generally, the *bhāratī* style is employed, though occasionally the *kauśikī* style may also occur.
The components of *lāsya* consist of the lyrics (*geyapada*) and so forth;
an example is the *Līlāmadhukara*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(Vi, Ja) He explains [the term] with "herein":
*līlāmadhukara* is a specific type of dramatic composition (*rūpaka*) called *bhāṇa*.
Now, the *vyāyoga*—
The *vyāyoga* is based on a well-known historical event, involves a small number of female characters, lacks the *garbha* and *vimarśa* junctures, and is populated by many men. (Viśvadatta 6.231)
Locanā:
(Lo, E) Due to the context, there is a distinction [from other types of drama] by the absence of the *garbha* and *vimarśa* junctures;
it should consist of a single act (*ekāṅka*), and its emergence of conflict (*samarodaya*) should not be caused by women.
In that [drama], the hero is renowned as being devoid of the Kaiśikī style.
Whether he be a royal sage or a celestial being, he is both steadfast and haughty;
in this [drama], the dominant sentiments (rasas) other than the comic, the erotic, and the peaceful are present.
Just as in the *Saugandhikāharaṇa*,
so too is the *samavakāra*:
its subject matter is well-known and based on the deeds of gods and asuras.
The junctures (sandhis) are devoid of deliberation (nirvimarśa), and there are three acts (aṅkas) therein, with the first being among them.
Likewise, there are two joints at the end; furthermore, there should be one [joint] each.
The twelve principal characters are renowned as gods and humans, and they are noble.
The fruit of each of these is distinct; the entire essence is the foremost hero.
The dramatic modes (vṛtti) are those of slow skill; there are no *bindu* or *praveśaka* interludes here.
And there should be thirteen components of the ritual path (vīthyaṅga), as they may be obtained;
and here there are various meters (chandas) beginning with Gāyatrī and Uṣṇih.
Locanā:

(Lo, Ai) The characteristics of the meters, such as Gāyatrī and others, are to be understood from the [corresponding] forms. This [deity] should be depicted with three amorous gestures (*śṛṅgāra*), three disguises (*kapaṭa*), and three states of agitation (*vidrava*).
The *vastu* is to be accomplished with twelve *nālīs* and is situated in the first digit.
In the second act with four [verses], and in the third act with two, [the author] speaks of the dramatic form called *vyāyoga*: "Now," says Vijñapriyā. (vi, jha)
The *Saugandhikāharaṇa* is a specific type of drama called a *vyāyoga*.
He now describes the type of drama called *samavakāra*: "Now," etc.
This means that there is a single juncture (*sandhi*) between the first act and the last two acts.
The *mandakauśikya* meters are specific varieties of the *kauśikī* meter itself.

He will explain the *triśṛṅgāra* and others himself—namely, the "subject matter" (*vastu*). This refers to the subject matter pertaining to the first act, that which is to be understood from the first act.
The meaning is that the ritual action is to be accomplished by forty-eight *daṇḍas*, which consist of twelve *nāḍīs* (each *nāḍī* being composed of two *ghaṭikās*).
A *nālikā* is said to be two *ghaṭikās*.
Furthermore, the two "entrances of the *bindu*" mentioned in the *Nāṭaka* are not to be performed here.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) He explains: "And the nāḍikā" refers to a ghaṭikā, which consists of two daṇḍas.
In that regard—
The erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) is threefold— pertaining to dharma, artha, and kāma—
and furthermore, there is the deceptive (kapaṭa).
Furthermore, flight may be natural, artificial, or caused by fate;
it may be produced by inanimate things, by sentient beings, or by both sentient and inanimate things.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭa) Therein, he states the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth by means of a verse, beginning with "dharma-artha...
To explain the state of being threefold in its deceit, he states the threefold nature of deceit: "deceit, moreover..."
In order to explain the nature of *vidrava* (flight/disorder), he says: "Furthermore, *vidrava*...
*Vidrava* is a specific type of flight characterized by curiosity, deception, and so forth.

He will later describe how this occurs through inanimate objects such as wooden puppets, through animate beings who provide comic entertainment, and through beings that are both animate and inanimate—such as animals—who, despite being conscious, lack superior consciousness (*prakṛṣṭacetanā*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of elephants, etc.," he there demonstrates *dharma-śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment of dharma) and the others according to his preference, even in a reversed order.
Among these, *dharma-śṛṅgāra* is that which is performed without contradicting the scriptures;
*artha-śṛṅgāra* is that which is devised for the sake of acquiring wealth.

The erotic sentiment of laughter (*prahasana-śṛṅgāra*) is the erotic sentiment of love (*kāma-śṛṅgāra*). Among these, they say that the erotic sentiment of love belongs specifically to the first act, whereas for the other two, there is no such restriction.
Sentient and insentient beings, such as elephants and so forth, are "thoroughly scattered" (*samavakīryante*) within it; thus it is called a *samavakāra*. For example—the Churning of the Ocean.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) In that regard, for courtesans, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is for the sake of gaining wealth;
for a man, it is the erotic sentiment that is not in conflict with dharma, directed toward his own wife.
He states the etymological derivation of the term *samavakāra*: "they are mixed together" (*samavakīryante*).
Locanā:

(lo, o) Although *prahasana* (the comic) is associated with laughter and was mentioned first, *dharma-śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment of dharma) is explained later because it is that which is to be enjoined.
"Because there is no fixed rule": in some cases the hero is divine, in others human; the "elements of the plot" (*arthaprakṛti*) consist of the "undertaking," "effort," and so forth.
Now, as for the *ḍima*:
it is characterized by activities such as illusions, sorcery, battle, and the agitation caused by anger.
The *ḍima* is mostly characterized by many *uparāga* [sentiments] and has a well-known plot.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ḍa) He speaks of the dramatic form known as *ḍima*— beginning with "atha" and "māyā."
Because its nature is illusory, it is invisible. It is the display of various unreal objects like a magician’s trick;
it is the agitation of movements such as those of one bewildered by battle or anger, a scattering here and there.
The *uparāga* is a calamity (*upadrava*).

The *raudra-rasa* (furious sentiment) is the primary element therein, while all other sentiments (*rasas*) serve as its subordinate members (*aṅgas*). Furthermore, it is considered to have four acts (*aṅkas*), and neither the *viṣkambhaka* nor the *praveśaka* are employed here.
The leaders— the gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and mahoragas,
as well as the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others— numbering sixteen, were exceedingly haughty.

The dramatic styles (vṛttis) should be devoid of the Kauśikī style, and the junctures (sandhis) should be free from deliberation; the sentiments (rasas) should be the six [flavors], excluding the peaceful (śānta), the comic (hāsya), and the erotic (śṛṅgāra).
And regarding this, the Great Sage [Bharata] gives the example: "The Burning of Tripura.
Now, as for the *īhāmṛga*: the *īhāmṛga* is proclaimed to have a mixed plot and four acts.
The junctures are the Mukha (Opening) and Prati-mukha (Development), and therein likewise is the Nirvahaṇa (Conclusion).
The hero and the antagonist are Nara and Divyāvaniyama;
they are renowned as "steadfast and haughty" (dhīroddhata), while the other is one whose intentions are hidden and who performs improper acts.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ḍha) He speaks of the dramatic form called *īhāmṛga*—namely, "atha iha" and so forth.
The meaning is that it consists of mixed events, contains both well-known and unknown narratives, and includes success (*siddhi*) in the form of a conclusion within the *nirvahaṇa* [sandhi].
Regarding the phrase "human and divine":
"human and divine" (naradivyau) means either humans or gods, or both humans and gods; that is to say, the protagonist and the antagonist.
Of these two, the former is the steadfast one.
The last type is the arrogant one;
and due to his state of delusion, he acts improperly,
such as by abducting a celestial woman against her will.
One should display even some semblance of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) for him here and there.
The ten types of leaders of the banners—whether divine or human—are exalted;
having brought about a fierce battle, they turn back from it through a supreme pretext.
"Even those who have reached the point of execution would not be executed by us here, O greatly puffed-up one.
Vijñapriyā:
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that even for one desiring a celestial woman against her will, there is merely a semblance of erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārābhāsa*).

The heroines who set in motion the pervasive, incidental, and secondary plots are twelve in number—divine and human—in accordance with the statement: "That which is pervasive and incidental is called the *patākā* (secondary plot).
Thus, there are two: the hero (*nāyaka*) and the rival hero (*pratināyaka*).
"The ten leaders of the banners" refers to the twelve [heroes].
"Battle" means that having brought the enemy force to a state of combat—characterized by fury and prowess—he should cause them to turn back under a pretext; this is the meaning.
He states the reason for this: "because of their greatness."
The meaning is that they are not fit to be slain.
Thus, the rule regarding the hero and the antagonist—such as their being celestial, mortal, and so forth—has been stated.
However, others say that in this [play], the god alone is the hero in a single act. *Viśvavidyā-sāra* 6.249.
The battle is caused by a celestial woman; there are six principal heroes (nāyakas) and others.
It is a mixed type, involving both famous and unknown characters.
Another is the antagonist (pratināyaka).

The *patākānāyakas* (subsidiary heroes), however, are ten, comprising the heroes and counter-heroes combined. An *īhāmṛga* (desiring-deer) is one who, like a deer, strives for or desires a heroine who is difficult to attain;
as, for example, Kusumaśekhara, Vijaya, and others.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ta) Others, however, state that there is a restriction to a single divine hero;
others, moreover, say there are six heroes—thus he says, "A single act is divine," and so forth.

He explains the passage beginning with "the hero of the *patākā*": "The *patākāsthā*s" means that ten heroes belonging to both the hero (*nāyaka*) and the counter-hero (*pratināyaka*), who stand as *patākās*, have come together and assembled; this is the meaning. He states the etymological derivation of *īhāmṛga*: "the hero is like a deer.
Now, the act (*aṅka*).
The *utsṛṣṭikāṅka* consists of a single act; its leading characters are common men.
In this [drama], the sentiment is the pathetic (karuṇa), with lamentation by many women as the stable emotion;
the poet should mentally elaborate upon the well-known plot.

In this [game], the modes of speech, the sandhi, the meters, and the constituent parts are employed; victory and defeat, as well as the battle itself, must be conducted through words, with much speech of reproach.
Regarding this, some call it *utsṛṣṭikāṅka*, meaning a section or division within a play such as an act that has been omitted;
others, however, say it is an *utsṛṣṭikāṅka* because its creation (*sṛṣṭi*) is "transgressed" (*utkrāntā*), that is,
in reverse order— as in the case of Śarmiṣṭhā and Yayāti.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) He describes the dramatic form known as *utsṛṣṭikāṅka* with the words "atha" [etc.].
The meaning is that the lamentation of many women—sorrow—is the stable emotional state (*sthāyibhāva*).

He explains the meaning of the term *utsṛṣṭikāṅka* with the words "And this... (*imaṃ ca*). Because it falls within the interior of a *nāṭaka* (drama) and so forth—meaning that there are two, three, or more acts (*aṅkas*) within a *nāṭaka*—and because this [work] consists of a single act (*ekāṅka*), some call it by the name *utsṛṣṭikāṅka* due to its exclusion from other acts; such is the meaning.

Others, however, [raise an objection]: since there is also a single act (*ekāṅka*) in the *vīthī* that will be described hereafter, it would follow that this too must be classified as an *utsṛṣṭikāṅka*.
To avoid this, they explain the meaning of the term differently; thus he says, "Others, however...
The word "contrary" (*viloma*) refers to its contrariness by virtue of having a commoner (*prākṛta*) as its hero.
Now, regarding the *vīthī*:

in a *vīthī*, there should be a single act (*aṅka*); herein, a certain [character] is introduced, relying on a variety of dialogues consisting of speeches addressed to empty space and spoken responses.

One should indicate the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) slightly toward other [characters], as well as the *mukha* (opening), *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion), the *sandhi*s (junctures), and all the *arthaprakṛti*s (plot elements). (Viśvavidyā 6.254)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, da) He speaks of the dramatic form called *vīthī*—beginning with "atha" [and so on].
In the phrase "some one person," the word "hero" (*nāyaka*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

The meaning of "the primary elements of the plot" (*arthaprakṛti*) is as follows: all five primary elements previously mentioned—namely, the seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), the banner (*patākā*), the sub-banner (*prakarī*), and the objective (*kārya*)—are included here.
Furthermore, because this [drama] abounds in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), it contains an abundance of the Kauśikī style (*vṛtti*).
*Vijñapriyā*: [This is the commentary].
He explains [the verse] with the words "a certain [hero]" (*kaścit*).
The meaning is that it refers to either the *uttama* (superior) or another type of hero.

Although the *kauśikī* style (*vṛtti*) is not explicitly mentioned here, he states—by saying "because of its abundance of erotic sentiment" (*śṛṅgārabahulatvāt*)—that it is understood because of the presence of abundant *śṛṅgāra*.
The wise point out that this [science] has thirteen components: the *uddhātaka*, the *avalagita*, the *prapañca*, the *trigata*, and the *chala*. (VisSd 6.255)
In the *vāk-keli* and *adhibala* [positions], there are the *gaṇḍa*, *avaśyandita*, and *nālīka*; furthermore, those are the *asat-pralāpa*, *vyāhāra*, and *mṛdu* (or *mārda*). VisSd_6.256.
In this regard, the *uddhātyaka* and *kāvalagita* have been defined with examples during the introductory section of the *Prastāvanā*. [Thus ends] the *Vijñapriyā*.
(vi, na) Regarding the introduction (*prastāvanā*):
"When people,
having already understood the meaning of the [initial] words, employ other words in order to grasp that same meaning, it is called *udghātyaka*."

“Thus, regarding the definition of *uddhātaka*: ‘When, through the inclusion [of one thing] in another, a different effect is accomplished while the [original] application remains, that should be known by the wise as *avalagita* by name.’”
This is because the definition of *avalagita* was stated in the introduction to the section [on dramatic elements].
"Mutual speech that is untrue is considered *prapañca*, which produces laughter."—
*Vijñapriyā*.
(vi, pa) He states the limb called *prapañca* (prolixity): "mutually" (*mithaḥ*)—meaning a statement that is unreal (*asadbhūta*), having a false object, and for that very reason, causing laughter.
Locanā:
(lo, au) The connection is: "a mutually unreal statement."

As in the *Vikramorvaśīya*, where there is mutual speech between the Vidūṣaka and the servant using wrinkles (*valī*): "Trigata" occurs when multiple meanings are joined through similarity of sound. (VisSd 6.257)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) He states the *aṅga* called *trigata*: "It is *trigata*" (*trigatam iti*).

Due to similarity of sound—that is, due to the similarity between two words being heard—there is a joining or communication [of meaning] even though those two [words] are in fact identical in meaning, yet possess multiple meanings or have different meanings. This is the sense.
As it is said in that very same place: "O Lord of all kings,
she who is beautiful in every limb has been seen."
"O Rāma, in this delightful forest, she is separated from me by you."
(An echo from behind the scenes at that very spot:
"The King—how was she seen? he says.
Here, the very question is employed as the answer.
Some maintain that this [verse] refers only to the triad beginning with the actor (*naṭa*).
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ba):
"O you who [rule] all the earth"—this is an address to Himālaya.
The question is: "Have you seen Urvaśī, beautiful in every limb, who was separated from me, in this lovely forest?

To the question "How was she seen?", he replies: "Separated from you, she was seen by me. By applying the meaning of the echo-word (*pratiśabda*), although the words "seeing" (*darśana*) and "crossing over" (*uttaraṇa*) have the same referent, he explains that relationship as one of question and answer according to the method shown—hence the phrase "here the question."
Some explain that this [treatise] is "threefold" (trigata) because it is employed by the triad of the actor, the actress, and the stage-manager;
thus he says: "the actor and so forth."—Locanā.
I saw the mountains— both the peaks and the kings— bereft of me;
alternatively, I saw them bereft of you.

In this context, after the king has spoken these words in the form of a question with the first meaning in mind, he hears an echo on the mountain; thus, the second meaning is understood as the mountain’s response. Due to his madness of separation, he is deceived by the dear and yet unpleasant words of his beloved, which constitutes *chala* (deception).
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, Bhīma and Arjuna say:
The master of gambling deceptions, the incendiary of the lacquer palace, that arrogant king— the preceptor of Duḥśāsana and his hundred younger brothers, the friend of the King of Aṅga,
and skilled in stripping Draupadī of her hair and upper garment— he whose sons are slaves: tell me, where does that Duryodhana dwell?
We have not come out of anger;
we have come here to see you.

Vijñapriyā: (vi, bha) He states the limb called *chala* (deception): "by means of dear things" (*priyābhaiḥ*). Having enticed and deceived, it is so called because of the act of deceiving through mockery.
"Karttā"—this is the speech of Bhīma and Arjuna as they pursue Duryodhana in order to flee.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "We have come to see him who is characterized by being the perpetrator of the deceit at dice and other such acts, and not out of anger.
*Śaraṇa* means a house.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that he is the preceptor of the hundred younger brothers, beginning with Duḥśāsana;
[and] of Karṇa, the King of Aṅga.
Here, having deceived him with the words "I will not look at you out of anger"—spoken under the guise of affection—there is mockery.
Locanā:
(Lo, Ā) "Śaraṇa" means a house. Others, however, say it is a pretext made with reference to some task for someone. (VisSd 6.258)
That speech which is uttered to cause deception, laughter, or anger is called *vākkelī*;
it consists of humorous discourse arising from two or three successive retorts. (VisSd 6.259)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) "Others" means that something is directed toward someone for the sake of some purpose; such is the grammatical connection.
He states the limb consisting of word-play (*vākkelī*): "word-play" (*vākkelī*).
The phrase "two or three" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
For example:
"O monk, you indulge in meat;

why do you do so without wine? And wine is dear to you—oh, how dear!—along with beautiful women. But where does a courtesan find interest in wealth for you? Is your money from gambling or theft? For you even possess the habit of both theft and gambling."
What other recourse is there for one who has perished?
Vijñapriyā: "O monk" (*bhikṣo*)—
this is a question addressed by a householder to a monk who is eating meat for the sake of amusement, beginning with the words "O monk."
"What is the use of that? is the monk's reply;
"And even liquor," and so forth, is that of the householder;
"O, how pleasant with courtesans," and so forth, is that of the monk.
Here, although there is even more improper conduct (*akārya*), the word "aho" is uttered because of the inquiry regarding a minor act.
The passage from "even a courtesan" up to "wealth" refers to the householder;
the passage beginning with "by gambling" refers to the mendicant.
"By theft," and so forth, is the statement of the householder;
"Of what was lost," and so forth, is the reply of the monk.
Some say: "Vākkelī (verbal play) is the cessation of a sentence that has been commenced while still remaining expectant [of further completion]."
Others say: "A single answer to multiple questions.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ra):
"Some" refers to the employment of a sentence that resolves a previously introduced statement which has given rise to an expectation, when that [expectation] has not yet been satisfied.
The exchange of mutually superior statements out of rivalry is considered *adhibala*.
As in my *Prabhāvatī*, Vajranābha says:
"Having crushed his chest in an instant with this mace..."
Today, with ease, I shall uproot both of your worlds.
Pradyumna: Ho there, you lowest of Asuras!
Enough of this excessive prattle;
for indeed, my—
Today, by the falling showers of arrows discharged from the great bows wielded by my fierce, staff-like arms,
let this earth— already drenched with the blood of all the Daityas— be made in an instant a desirable object for the flesh-eaters.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) He states the limb called *adhibala* with the words "mutually" (*anyonya*), etc.
The phrase beginning with "of this [vajra]" (*asya vajrasya*) has been explained previously.

"Today, O Pracaṇḍā!"— the construction of the sentence is as follows: "May this earth, having been sprinkled in an instant by the falling showers (or, according to a variant reading, the thousands) of arrows discharged from that great bow which has been entrusted to my formidable staff-like arms, become a source of temptation for the flesh-eaters through the blood of all the Daityas."
Gaṇḍa is speech that is relevant to the subject at hand but conveys a different meaning, spoken with haste.
As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: The King—
O lady with thighs like an elephant’s trunk, my thigh-jewel has at last become sufficient to rest upon the expanse of your hips.
Immediately after, the chamberlain enters—“Your Majesty!
It is broken, it is broken! and so forth.

In this context, the statement intended for the purpose of breaking the banner of the chariot is connected to the purpose of breaking the thighs; it is thus connected within the relationship [of the plot].
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, va) states the element called *gaṇḍa*: "The *gaṇḍa*... and so forth.
The meaning is that because it was spoken quickly, the speech—which has a different sense from what was intended—is understood as being connected to the description of the subject matter at hand.
"Rājā" refers to Duryodhana.
"Karabhoru" is an address to Bhānumatī.

"To occupy" (*adhyāsitum*) means for the purpose of sitting upon (*adhyāsanāya*). The genitive case is used because the suffix *tumun* is employed in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). "Adequate" (*paryāptam*) means suitable (*yogyam*).
Regarding this, he says "here" [in the commentary] because there is a perception of the breaking of the thigh that was previously introduced.
An explanation would be a deviation from what was stated according to its natural sense, as in the *Chalitarama*: "Sītā—Child! [etc.]
"It is indeed time for the Lord of Oudha to depart;
there, that king must be saluted with humility.
Lava: "What then? Must we become dependents upon a king?"
Sītā: Child, he is indeed your father.
Lava: Is Lord Raghu our father?
Sītā: (With apprehension)
Do not be suspicious otherwise;
it is certainly not as if [the entire earth] belongs to you alone.
(Vijñapriyā:)
(vi, śa) He states the dramatic element called *avasyandita*: "the explanation" (*vyākhyānam*).
The meaning is that when something spoken with natural spontaneity by the speaker is explained otherwise by the listener because it does not accord with his own inclination, that is *avasyandita*.
The passage beginning with "jāda" and so forth is Sītā’s speech addressed to Lava and Kuśa.

"Jāta! You two must indeed go to Ayodhyā at daybreak; there, that king is to be saluted with due decorum. (In Sanskrit: *jāta / kalyaṃ khalu yuvābhyāmayodhyāyāṃ gantavyam / tatra sa rājā vinayena praṇamitavyaḥ* / "Jāta!")
"He was indeed born as the father of you two" (in Sanskrit).
"With apprehension":
the apprehension arises from Vālmīki’s prohibition.
"Do not think otherwise"—do not suspect it to be anything else;
for it is certainly not just for the two of you, but indeed for the entire earth. (Sanskrit)
In the phrase "of the earth" (*pṛthivyāḥ*), the meaning is "of the world situated upon the earth.

Here, because the word "father" (*pitā*)—which Sītā had naturally uttered as referring to her progenitor—has found its opportunity for expansion, she has provided an interpretation of it as meaning "protector.
A riddle (*prahelikā*) becomes endowed with humor (*hāsya*) only when it is not [merely] a hollow tube (*nālikā*).

A riddle (*prahelikā*) follows after a matter of concealment (*saṃvaraṇakārya*), as in the *Ratnāvalī*: Susaṅgatā says, "Friend, he for whose sake you have come is right here. Sāgarikā asks, "For whose sake have I come? Susaṅgatā replies, "Indeed, for the sake of the painted panel."
In this context, the meaning "you have come for the sake of the king" is concealed.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ṣa) states the limb called *nālikā*: "it is *praholikā*."

Regarding the phrase "one who acts with concealment" (*saṃvaraṇakārī*): although this is a member of the explanatory form (*vyākhyānarūpa*) and possesses the nature of concealment, its specific distinction here is that it is accompanied by humor.
*Sahi jasseti*—the Sanskrit is: "O friend, he for whose sake you have come stands right here. *Kasseti* [is the vocative].
"For whose sake have I come? (in Sanskrit: *kasya kṛte aham āgatā*).
"Indeed, for the sake of the painting-board" (in Sanskrit: *nanu citraphalakasya*).
Idle chatter is speech that is incoherent, as is a reply that is likewise disconnected; and so too is beneficial advice spoken before a fool who does not comprehend it. (VisSd 6.262)
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, sa) He states the third limb, called frivolous speech (*asatpralāpa*), with the word "unreal" (*asad*). The meaning is that it is a statement whose subject matter is incoherent, false, or fabricated, and the subsequent [speech] is of the same nature.

He states the third limb, called *asatpralāpa* (incoherent speech), with the words "even though he does not accept. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "even of a fool who does not accept beneficial words.
Regarding that, the first example is as follows from my *Prabhāvatī*: Pradyumna—
(Seeing a mango creeper, with joy) Oh, how is it that right here—
she who has locks as lovely as a swarm of bees, who is thick with fragrance, full of nectar, and slender?
My beloved has hands as delicate as young shoots and a voice as sweet as the cuckoo's call.

The same applies to an irrelevant reply (*asaṃbaddhottara*). An example of the third [type] is the speech of Gāndhārī to Duryodhana in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*. *Vijñapriyā*: [This is as follows: "O King, you have indeed performed a great deed; for by slaying the sons of Pāṇḍu, you have brought about the destruction of your own family. Duryodhana says: "What is this? Have I slain the sons of Pāṇḍu? Gāndhārī says: "No, O King, you have not slain them; rather, they have themselves destroyed their own lineage through mutual slaughter. Duryodhana says: "How is that? Gāndhārī says: "O King, listen to the account of the lineage of the Kurus from its very beginning. Duryodhana says: "Tell it. Gāndhārī says: "In the lineage of the Moon, there was a king named Soma. From him was born Budha, and from him Purūravas. From Purūravas was born Āyu, from Āyu Nahuṣa, and from Nahuṣa Yayāti. From Yayāti were born Yadu and Turvasu. From Yadu came the lineages of the Yādavas and Bhojas. From Turvasu came the Turvaśas. From Nahuṣa was born Pūru, and from Pūru came the lineages of the Kuru-Pañcālas. In that lineage was born Śantanu, and from Śantanu was born Bhīṣma. From Śantanu was also born Vicitravīrya, and from Vicitravīrya were born Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu. From Dhṛtarāṣṭra were born the hundred sons, among whom you, O King, are the eldest. From Pāṇḍu were born Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva. Thus, O King, these are your kinsmen who have been slain by one another. Duryodhana says: "Alas! What a calamity! Alas! What a great misfortune! Gāndhārī says: "O King, do not grieve; this is the way of the world. Now, having heard this account of the lineage, you must act accordingly. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must now perform the funeral rites for your kinsmen. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also offer water-libations to your ancestors. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also perform the ancestral sacrifices (*śrāddha*) for your forefathers. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also bestow gifts upon the Brahmins. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also perform the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also perform the *Rājasūya* sacrifice. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also perform the *Vājapeya* sacrifice. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also perform the *Gomedha* sacrifice. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also perform the *Naramedha* sacrifice. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also perform the *Puruṣamedha* sacrifice. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says: "O King, you must also perform the *Sarvamedha* sacrifice. Duryodhana says: "I shall do so. Gāndhārī says:
(vi, ha) Regarding "alikulā"—this statement, beginning with "this is Prabhāvatī," was made by Bhrama regarding Cūtalatikā;
namely, "this here is Cūtalatikā.
Who indeed is Prabhāvatī, and of what nature is she?
She whose hair is as beautiful as a swarm of bees,
and she whose delicate hand is like a tender sprout; here,
the word *kokila* refers to its song.
And thus, the meaning is that they possess a variety of speech forms; it does not mean that they have the habit of speaking like cuckoos,
because since they speak with distinctions, the superimposition of non-distinction would be untenable.

And here, because there is no superimposition (āhāryāropa), it is not a metaphor (rūpaka); rather, due to a natural delusion (vāstavabhrama), it is precisely the figure of speech "bewildered" (bhrāntimad). The same applies to other instances of irrelevant answers (asambaddhottara).

In that regard, as in my own verse: "A twice-born bird (dvija) possessed of branches (śākhā)—a cuckoo who has feigned his identity upon you—should be told by you: 'O dull-witted one, how great is the sin in me, a victim of separation!'"
Thus, when questioned by the wind, the mango creeper—her hair standing on end like buds—surely kept her head bowed and did not answer as to how much she had been shaken.
For here, in the case of the mango creeper whose crest is shaken by the wind, there is an attribution of a sinful state through the bowing of the head by the gentle breeze;
the meaning of the first half-verse is the manner of the wind's questioning.
He says "O twice-born" (*dvija*) because it is appropriate for a single question to be addressed to a person who has already been established as having committed a sin.

The "bird" (*dvija*) situated on the branch-end (*viṭapa*) is the *kokila* (cuckoo) itself; he is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the *drupadā* mantra. He is a twice-born (*dvija*) who possesses the Vedic branch named *kokila*, and since he has made his abode in you, this must also be told to you, who are dull and devoid of the Vedas.
This is the question: how great is the sin in the killing of one separated from her husband?
This question arises because the gentle breeze, by kindling passion, acts as a slayer of those separated from their lovers;
it is spoken with horripilation born of joy when describing the established order.
An example of the third [type] is the beneficial speech of Gāndhārī to Duryodhana in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*.
Alternatively, this statement by Vibhīṣaṇa to Rāvaṇa—"Let Maithilī be given to the son of Daśaratha"—should also be understood here.
*Vyāhāra* is speech intended for another's sake that causes laughter or agitation;
as in the *Mālavikāgnimitra* (at the conclusion of the dance performance, when Mālavikā wishes to depart): [text follows].
Vidūṣaka: Do not, for heaven's sake, go astray from my instruction!
(With these words, he begins.
Gaṇadāsa: (To the Vidūṣaka)—Noble sir!
"Tell me then what sequence-break you have observed.
Vidūṣaka: "First there is the worship of the Brahmins;
that has been bypassed by her."
The utterance [of the hero] with words such as "Mālavikā is remembered," which cause laughter and longing, is prompted by his sight of the heroine in her pure state.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ka) He states the subsidiary element (*aṅga*) consisting of dialogue (*vyāhāra*): "Dialogue" [is used] at the conclusion of *lāsya*, that is, upon the completion of the dance.
"Mā dāva" [means]... [etc.]
"Do not go forth, being deluded by instruction" (in Sanskrit).
"Instruction" (*upadeśa*) refers to the teaching found in the scriptures;
the ellipsis is "having become one who acts while obstructed by logic, being utterly deluded by that."
"First" means that first there is the honoring of Brahmins; that has been transgressed by her. (Thus he reflected.)

In this context, he states the words of the jester, intended to provoke laughter for the sake of the gain of another king: "That wherein faults are virtues and virtues are faults is indeed intoxication (mṛdaṃ). (VisSd 6.263)
In sequence, for example:
"O beloved! Cruelty, lack of affection, and ingratitude—by the very sight of you, these have become virtues in me."
That beauty of form of hers, adorned with the splendor of youth and once the sole abode of happiness, has now become a source of nothing but suffering for me.

Although these constituent elements (aṅgas) may occur in dramas (*nāṭaka*) and the like, they must necessarily be employed in the *vīthī*. Even though they are clearly established in dramas and other forms, they are cited here [in this context]. This is called a *vīthī* because, like a street (*vīthī*), various sentiments (*rasas*) are arranged here in the form of a garland (*mālā*).
For example: *Mālavikā*.
Now, the *prahasana* (farce):

A *prahasana* is constructed like a *bhāṇa*, with junctures (*sandhi*), sections (*saṃdhy-aṅga*), and the limbs of *lāsya* (*lāsya-aṅga*), as well as acts (*aṅka*); its plot consists of characters who are objects of censure, as imagined by the poet. (Viśvavidyā-sāra 6.264)
In this [play], there is no *ārabhaṭī* style, nor are there *viṣkambhaka* or *praveśaka* interludes;
the predominant sentiment (*rasa*) therein is the comic (*hāsya*), and there is no presence of the constituent parts of the *vīthī*.
In that regard:
where there is a single hero among ascetics, gods, brahmins, and so forth,
and he is joyful therein, that is called pure *hāsya* (comic).
Just as in the *Kandarpakeli*, they know that [the state] is "mixed" (*saṃkīrṇa*) when it relies upon some particular person. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.266)

For example—the *Dhūrtacarita*. Some have stated that the *vṛtta* genre consists of the combined deeds of many audacious individuals; furthermore, it is composed of two acts or even one act. (VisSd 6.267)
For example—the *Laṭakamelaka* and so forth. But the Sage said:
"Where there may be courtesans, servants, eunuchs, parasites, rogues, and unchaste women..."
However, assuming a disguise, equipment, and behavior that are inconsistent with one's true nature is "confused" (saṅkīrṇa).
Thus it is said:

"But they know that [theatre] to be 'transformed' (vikṛta) where eunuchs, actors, and ascetics, as well as those assuming the dress and speech of rogues, performers, soldiers, and so forth, perform. (Viṣṇudharmottara 6.268)
However, since this [topic] has already been covered by the discussion on mixed forms (*saṅkīrṇa*), it was not mentioned separately by the Sage.
Now, the minor dramatic forms (*uparūpaka*):
among them, the *nāṭikā* shall have a contrived plot, consist mostly of female characters, and contain four acts.
In that case, the hero should be a renowned king, characterized by the *dhīralalita* (graceful and composed) temperament.
The heroine here is a maiden born of a royal lineage, who may be connected with the inner apartments, occupied with musical performances, or possessed of fresh passion. (VisSd 6.270)
The leader might act with apprehension out of fear of this queen;
however, the elder sister, born of a royal lineage, would become bold once again.
At every step, the union of the two should be under the influence of the proud woman;
the style should be Kauśikī, and the junctures should involve only slight deliberation.
Of two heroines and heroes—
for example, the *Ratnāvalī*, the *Viddhaśālabhañjikā*, and so forth. Now, the *troṭaka*:
They say that a work consisting of seven, eight, nine, or five acts, based on both divine and human characters, and containing a *vidūṣaka* in every act, is called a *troṭaka*.
In this case, because the *vidūṣaka* is present in every act, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is the primary element.
An example of a play with seven acts is *Stambhitarambha*;
an example of one with five acts is *Vikramorvaśī*.
Now, as for the *goṣṭhī*:
it is adorned by nine or ten ordinary men, its speech is not elevated, and it is characterized by the *kauśikī* style of dramatic representation. (Viśvāvasu-śāstra 6.274)
It is inferior due to its deliberation on the womb; it is accompanied by five or six women, joined with the erotic sentiment of love, and composed in a single act.
For example—*Raivatamadanikā*.
Now, as for the *saṭṭaka*:
a *saṭṭaka* consists entirely of Prakrit recitation and lacks an *apraveśaka* (interlude).
Moreover, even the heroic sentiment (*viṣkambhaka*) is not predominant here, nor is the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*).
The acts (aṅkas) are called *javanikās*; otherwise, it is similar to a *nāṭikā*, as for example the *Karpūramañjarī*.
Now, the *nāṭyarāsaka*:
The *nāṭyarāsaka* consists of a single act and is established upon many *tāla*s and *laya*s.
Likewise, that [play] has a noble hero and a *pīṭhamarda* as a secondary hero;
its dominant sentiment is the comic (*hāsya*), yet it contains the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), and features a woman adorned in her chamber (*vāsakasajjikā*). VisSd 6.278.
In the *mukhanirvahaṇa* (the conclusion of the opening), all ten *lāsyāṅga*s (elements of dance) are combined;
however, some do not desire the *pratimukha* (the development of the plot) at all here.
Locanā:
(lo, i) *Tāla* refers to the *cañcupuṭa* and other such [rhythmic patterns].
The *pīṭhamarda* here is of the type described in this very [work].
Gīta is well known from the works of Bharata and others.
Among these, that which possesses two *sandhi*s is exemplified by *Narmavatī*;
that which possesses four *sandhi*s is exemplified by *Vilāsavatī*.
Now, the *Prasthānaka*:
in the *Prasthāna*, there should be a lowly servant named [the hero], and a female servant as the heroine; the styles (*vṛtti*) are Kauśikī and likewise Bhāratī.
Through the practice of drinking liquor, there is the withdrawal of the intended object;
likewise, there are the two marks (aṅka), dissolution (laya), rhythm (tāla), and so forth, as well as abundant graceful movement (vilāsa).
For example—the *Śṛṅgāratilaka*.
Now, the *ullāpya*: it features a noble hero (*udāttanāyaka*), a divine plot (*divyavṛtta*), and is adorned with a single act (*ekāṅka*).
It is endowed with the components of the arts and the sentiments of humor, the erotic, and the pathetic.
Some maintain that this [drama] consists of four heroines and three acts; it is to be celebrated, featuring many battles and captivating songs of weaponry. (VisSd 6.283)
The components of the arts (śilpāṅgas) will be described hereafter—
for instance, the Devīmahādeva—
and now, the poetry (kāvyam).

The *kāvya* is devoid of the *ārabhaṭī* style, consists of a single act (*aṅka*), is filled with humor, and is adorned with *khaṇḍamātrā*, *dvipadikā*, and *bhagnatāla* meters. (Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa 6.284)
Locanā:
(lo, ī) The [syllables] beginning with *khaṇḍa* and *mātrā* should be understood from the source texts (*ākara*).
They occur at the beginning of the *mukha* and *pratimukha* sections.
The finale (nirvahaṇa) consists of speech characterized by erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), accompanied by the dropping of syllables and measures;
the hero and the heroine here are both noble (udātta), and the junctures (sandhi) are the first and the last.
For example: *Yādavodaya*.
Now, regarding *preṅkhaṇa*:
*Preṅkhaṇa* is devoid of the *garbha* and *avamarśa* junctures and lacks a principal hero.
It consists of a single act without a prologue, and lacks both interludes and entrances.
It is endowed with wrestling and combat and relies upon all dramatic styles (*vṛtti*).
Locanā:
(*lo*, *u*) Wrestling (*niyuddha*) is arm-to-arm combat.
*Saṃpheṭa* is speech uttered in anger;
the *nāndī* is sung in the wings (*nepathya*), and likewise, the *prarocanā* is performed there.
For example—the slaying of Vālin.
Now, as for the *rāsaka*:
the *rāsaka* consists of five characters and is endowed with the *mukha* (opening) and *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion) junctures.
It abounds in speech and exposition, and is endowed with the Bhārati and Kauśikī styles of dramatic delivery.
Locanā:
(lo, ū) Regarding "speech" (*bhāṣā*): as it is stated in the *Bhāṣāvibhāga*, for example, in the *Bhāṣārṇava*:
"Speech [is assigned] to middling characters, especially in dramas and the like."
The learned have stated that the languages are of two kinds: Mahārāṣṭrī and Saurasenī.
That which is spoken by the low-born is called Vibhāṣā, and it is traditionally held to be of seven types:
Prācyā, Āvantī, Māgadhī, Śākārī, and others.
They are distinguished as Cāṇḍālī, Śāvarī, and likewise Bhīrī.

It should lack a formal prologue (*sūtradhāra*), consist of a single act, possess the components of a *vīthī*, and be endowed with artistic skill; it should include a double entendre in its opening benediction (*nāndī*), feature a well-known heroine, and have a foolish hero.
Some also declare that the *pratimukha* juncture consists of the successive arrangement of exalted emotional states (*udāttabhāva*). (VisSd 6.290)
For example—the *menakāhita*.
Now, as for the *saṃlāpaka*:
in a *saṃlāpaka*, there are four or three acts, and the hero appears again.
In that [work] there may be a heretical sect, and the sentiment (rasa) therein shall be primarily the erotic and the pathetic.
In cases of siege of a city, feigned battles,
or routs, neither the Vṛtti nor the Kauśikī style is appropriate there.
For example— the *Māyākāpālika*.
Now, that which is called a *śrīgadita* is a one-act play (*ekāṅka*) featuring a well-known plot and a celebrated, noble hero.
It possesses a well-known heroine and is devoid of the *garbha* and *vimarśa* junctures.
That which abounds in the *bhāratī* style of delivery, is filled with the word "śrī," and is known as *śrīgadita*, is considered by the learned to be a type of *uparūpaka*.
For example: *Krīḍārasātala*.

Some declare that what is sung or even recited by Śrī when seated at the place described as "Śrī" is a one-act play (*ekāṅka*), consisting primarily of the Goddess of Speech (*bhāratī*). (Viśvavidyā 6.295)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) He describes the minor dramatic form (*uparūpaka*) called *Śrīgadita* with the words "Now" (*atha*).
By the word "joy" (*prīti*), he means a word that generates joy.
Regarding "Śrīrāsīnā": Śrī is Lakṣmī; āsīnā means she has entered.
The illustration is to be inferred.
Now, regarding the *śilpaka*: there should be four acts (*aṅka*) in a *śilpaka*, and likewise four meters (*vṛtti*).
The sentiments (rasas) are characterized by unquiet laughter, and the hero is considered to be a brahmin.
In this context, the description of the cremation ground and so forth serves as the *upanāyaka* (the lead character).
Its constituent parts (*aṅga*) are twenty-seven; they are as follows: Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 6.297.
Hopes, conjectures, doubts, distress, agitation, attachments, efforts, compositions, longings, dissimulation, and lack of comprehension; 6.298.
Amorous playfulness, languor, tears, exultation, breathlessness, bewilderment, as well as the attainment of exertion, pursuit, joy, and astonishment; VisDh 6.299.
Gain, forgetfulness, exhilaration, fearlessness, awakening,
and wonder— since these are so evident, their defining characteristics are not stated here.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ga) He speaks of the minor drama (*uparūpaka*) called *śilpaka* with the words "Now," etc.;
[and] "inferior," etc.
An inferior person is one who lacks assistance;

since the limbs of his aspiration and so forth have already been mentioned, their definitions and examples are omitted here for the sake of clarity. Furthermore, because the characteristics of *saṃphoṭa* and *grathana* have already been stated previously, their definitions are established.
For example—*Kanakāvatīmādhava*.
Now, as for the *vilāsikā*: it abounds in the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), consists of a single act (*ekāṅkā*), and is endowed with the ten limbs of the *lāsya* dance.
And she is adorned by the Vidūṣaka, the Viṭa, and the Pīṭhamarda.
Deficient in both the examination of the womb and the two joints, lacking a leading hero,
with very few verses and elegant costumes— that is known as the *vilāsikā*.
Some, however, read "Vināyikā" instead of "Vilāsikā" in that place;
others maintain that she is included within "Durmallikā.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, gha) He describes the minor drama (*uparūpaka*) called *vilāsikā*: "Now," etc.
Now, the *durmallikā*—the *durmallikā* should consist of four acts and be endowed with the *kauśikī* and *bhāratī* styles.
The city-dwellers are without children and are adorned by a leader who is deficient.
