The first act in this [play] should consist of three *nālikās* and be filled with the amorous sports of a *viṭa*;
the second act, possessing the dalliances of a *vidūṣaka*, should consist of five *nālikās*.
The third [type of] *pīṭhamarda* is one who possesses six *nālikās* of grace;
the fourth is the *aṅka*, a playful urbanite (*krīḍitanāgara*), who possesses ten *nālikās*. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 6.305)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṅa) He speaks of the minor drama (*uparūpaka*) called *Durmallikā*—beginning with "atha":
it is "without a core" (*agarbhā*), meaning it lacks the *garbhasandhi* juncture.
The city-dwellers are the citizens;
the leader is base;
three *nālis* is that which is accomplished by three *nālikās*.
The same applies hereafter:
the game of the courtesan, the game of the rogue;
as in the case of Bindumatī.
Now, the *prakaraṇikā*: it is indeed a *nāṭikā*, but with a merchant (*sārthavāha*) or similar person as its hero;
furthermore, the heroine in it must be born of the same lineage as the leader.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ca) He speaks of the minor drama (*uparūpaka*) called *prakaraṇikā*— beginning with "atha" [and ending with] "nāṭikaiva."
The meaning is that it does not conform to the characteristics of a *nāṭikā*.
"Merchants" refers to travelers; by the word "and so forth," those who are abroad are also included.
An example must be sought.
Now, as for the *hallīśa*: in a *hallīśa*, there is a single actor and seven, eight, or ten women.
The speech is in the *udātta* register with a single speaker; the *kauśikī* style is radiant;
likewise, the *mukha* and final *saṃdhi*s are employed, and there is a stable presence of many *tāla*s and *laya*s.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) He describes the minor drama (*uparūpaka*) called *hallīśa* with the words "Now" (*atha*).
It possesses the two junctures (*sandhi*) of the opening (*mukha*) and the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*).
For example—the *Kolīraivataka*.
Now, as for the *bhāṇikā*:
the *bhāṇikā* involves smooth costumes and is endowed with the *mukha* (opening) and *nirvahaṇa* (conclusion) junctures.
It is composed in a single act, employing both the Kauśikī and Bhāratī styles of dramatic performance.
The heroine of noble character and the gentle hero; here are the seven constituent parts:
introduction, arrangement, awakening, and likewise apprehension.
Dedication, cessation, and withdrawal constitute the seventh [chapter]. An introduction is the mention of a subject matter by way of a relevant context. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.310)
The mastery of words expressing world-weariness is known as *vinyāsa*;
the destruction of delusion is *vibodha*, while false proclamation is *sādhvasa*.
The offering here [of the self] with words of reproach and the affliction of anger, and the presentation of an illustrative example, is called "cessation" (nivṛtti). VisSd 6.312.
They call "conclusion" (saṃhāra) the completion of an action;
there are clear examples of this,
such as Kāmadattā.

Although all of these constitute the foundational elements (*prakṛti*) of a drama, they are to be adopted according to propriety and availability, following the specific requirements mentioned for each drama.
Furthermore, where there is a re-mention of what has already been stated for a drama, there it is a rule that those elements must be present.
— *Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ja) He describes the minor drama (*uparūpaka*) called *bhāṇikā* with the words "Now," etc.
"Manda" means base or inferior.
He states its constituent parts with the words "Introduction," and so forth.
He states their characteristics, beginning with "the presentation" (upanyāsa).
The arrangement (*vinyāsa*) is the systematic exposition (*vyutpatti*) of a discourse on world-weariness (*nirveda*);
that [exposition] is designated by the term *vinyāsa*.
The meaning is that the task called "offering words of reproach" is performed under the pressure of anger.
The meaning is the presentation of an illustration, that is, an example.
The meaning of "the completion of the task" is the completion of both the primary task and its subordinate tasks.
Because these functions are appropriate for all dramas (*nāṭaka*), he states that these functions belong to all dramas by saying "of these" (*eṣām*).
The analysis of the compound is: "the inclusion [of these] within the specific [requirements] stated for the *nāṭaka*.
Accordingly, it has been stated that the function described for the *bhāṇikā* should also be applied in other types of drama.
Regarding the phrase "and that which":
for in a drama, thirty-six characteristics, ornaments, and so forth have been described;
it should be understood that this refers to the further adoption of a subject matter already mentioned in another drama.
"Of its existence"—the meaning is that there is a necessary rule (niyama) regarding its existence therein.

Now, as for the poetic works intended to be heard (*śravyakāvya*): "That which is to be heard (*śravya*) is merely that which is to be listened to; it is of two kinds, consisting of verse (*padya*) and prose (*gadya*). (VisSd 6.313)
Vijñapriyā:
Regarding "poetic works intended for recitation" (*śravyakāvyāni*),
he states their two divisions as "verse and prose" (*padyagadya*).
Regarding that, he speaks of those consisting of verse: "Verse (*padya*) is that whose words are bound by meter; that which is free from such [binding] is the *muktaka* (isolated verse).
A pair (*yugmaka*) is formed by two [verses], while a *sandānitaka* is held to consist of three. (VisSd 6.314)
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) It should be understood that in the four [sections] beginning with "by two," there is mutual syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).
A *kalāpaka* consists of four [verses], and a *kulaka* is considered to consist of five.
Among these, an independent verse (*muktaka*) is as follows, by me:

"Those fortunate and sweet-smiling young women are truly blessed, who out of curiosity— [even though] that Brahman is the supreme, which yogis, intent on meditation, repeatedly worship in order to directly perceive for a moment that which is dense bliss, infinite, imperishable, and unborn."
They embrace, caress, pull at one another in a hundred ways, and kiss.”
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṭa) Regarding the phrase "thick with bliss" (*sāndrānanda*): that supreme, most excellent Brahman which yogis—intent solely on meditation and absorbed in meditation alone—worship at every moment even for a single instant; that very Brahman whom the young women of the city of Mathurā embrace out of curiosity, and so forth—they are truly blessed.
An example of a pair (yugmaka) is as follows from my own work: "What are you doing, O beloved, at the edge of your hand upon this cheek?"
O beloved, when one is inclined toward affection, outbursts of anger are not appropriate in private.
Even as we were thus desirous of speaking to the fawn-eyed one, the sweet humming of bees suddenly arose from the mango tree.
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ṭha) Speaking to her two friends about the manner in which the prideful woman’s pride was broken, [the poet] says: "What are you doing? and so forth.
O beloved, why do you rub this cheek with the edge of your hand?
The passage beginning with "tataḥ praṇayapravaṇa" (then, inclined by affection) is clear.
While we were still striving to address her as "the deer-eyed one" (*kuraṅgākṣīm*), the sweet sound of bees manifested upon the mango tree (*cūta*).
Here, the meaning of the first verse is stated as the object of the desire (*utka*) in the second verse; thus, there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*).
The same applies to other [verses] as well.
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍa):
"In this way" means that it should be understood in the same manner even in the case of *sandānitaka* and other such forms.
A Mahākāvya is a composition consisting of cantos; in it, there is a single hero who is a deity.
Whether he be a Kṣatriya of noble lineage, endowed with the qualities of a hero of the *dhīrodātta* type, or kings born of a single dynasty, or even many born of a noble family; VisSd_6.316 //
Among the erotic, the heroic, and the peaceful sentiments, one is intended to be the predominant sentiment;
all other sentiments are its subordinate members, as are all the junctures of the drama.
An event derived from history or another [event] based on virtuous people—this is the definition of a *mahākāvya*, as stated in the verse beginning with "composed in cantos" (*sargabandha*).
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ḍha) He states the characteristics of a *mahākāvya* with the words "composed in cantos" (*sargabandha*), etc.
*Sargabandha* is a composition consisting of distinct sections (*pariccheda*) in which a creation (*sarga*) is bound;
*sura* means a god;
and *sarve nāṭakasandhayaḥ* refers to all the dramatic junctures (*sandhi*), such as the *mukha*, *pratimukha*, and so forth, numbering five.
"Sajjanāśrayam" means the conduct of the excellent person who is to be described.
It has four sections, and there shall be one fruit among them. (Viṣṇusmṛti 6.318)
At the beginning, there may be a salutation, a benediction, or simply the statement of the subject matter;
in some cases, there is the censure of the wicked and the like, as well as the praise of the virtues of the virtuous. (VisSd 6.319)
In this work, there are more than eight cantos, composed in verses of a single meter with other meters appearing at the conclusion, neither too short nor too long.
A certain creation consisting of various meters is seen somewhere;
at the end of a creation, there is an indication of the narrative of a future creation. (VisSd 6.321)
The twilights, the sun, the moon, night, the onset of darkness, and day;
morning, midday, the hunt, mountains, seasons, forests, and oceans.
The sharing of wealth, separation, the Sage, heaven, the purifier,
the sacrifice, battle, departure, marriage, mantras, the afterlife, prosperity, and so forth.

These [elements], along with their primary and secondary components, should be described here as appropriate, either by the name of the poet, the meter, the hero, or another [character]. (VisSd 6.324)
Its name is "Sarga" (Creation) because it tells of what is to be adopted for the sake of creation; however, [it is called] "Sarga" [because]—Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa)—the four, namely dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, which are the four categories (*varga*), even one among them is its fruit—this is the meaning.
"Consisting of single meters" means pervaded by a single meter.
"At the conclusion" means at the end of the canto.

"With all its limbs and sub-limbs" means that these topics, beginning with the twilight [scenes] of the sun and moon and ending with the birth of the son, should be described in this poem according to their respective requirements and possibilities, including all their constituent parts and sub-parts.
In that regard, the components of the twilight are the separation of the cakravāka birds;
the components of the day are the water-sport and so forth;
and the components of the night are the drinking of wine and so forth.
The subsidiary limb (*upāṅga*) consists of jesting and so forth in that very context;
the sage (*muni*) refers to Nārada and others;
and the departure (*prayāṇa*) refers to the journey.
*Upayama* is marriage;
*mantra* is counsel;
*putrodaya* is the birth of a son.

"Of the other," meaning of the rival protagonist; "by his name" means that this [work] takes its name from him. "To be adopted in the creation" (sargopādeyā) means that the narrative described therein is to be adopted in the creation [of the plot]; thus, it has the name "Sarga" (Creation).
The *sandhyaṅgas* (intermediate episodes) should be employed here as far as possible; in the rule "at the conclusion with other *vṛttakas*," the plural number is not intended to be restrictive.

"With all their limbs and sub-limbs" refers to [episodes] such as water-sports, wrestling, and drinking bouts—as seen, for example, in the *Raghuvaṃśa*, the *Śiśupālavadha*, the *Naiṣadha*, and so forth.
Or as in my own work, such as the *Rāghavavilāsa* and others.

[The author of] the *Vijñapriyā* [comments]: "The plural number is not intended to be significant," because it is observed that even at the conclusion, there is a single [verse] belonging to another meter.
For example, as in the case of the *Raghuvaṃśa*.
Therein, the name of the composition is *Raghuvaṃśa*;
it refers to many kings born of a single lineage.
It is titled *Śiśupālavadha* after the name of the antagonist;
however, in works such as the *Naiṣadha*, it is named after the hero.
The hero, moreover, is a Kṣatriya of noble lineage.
Furthermore, in this Vedic tradition (ārṣa), there are creations known as "narratives" (ākhyāna).
In this great poem,
just as in the Mahābhārata.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, tha) Regarding the phrase "in this *ārṣa*": the meaning is "in this great epic (*mahākāvya*) composed by a seer (*ṛṣi*).
Regarding the phrase "designated as *ākhyānas*":
the meaning is that they bear such designations as chapters (*adhyāya*), which are the names given by teachers when explaining the *ākhyāna* treatises to their disciples.
In that which was composed in the Prākṛta language, the chapters are designated as "resting places" (āśvāsas);
it is written in the Skandhaka meter, and in some places also in Ralita meters.
For example—the *Setubandha*;
or, for example, my own *Kuvalayāśvacarita*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
In the *Skandhakagalitaka*, there are two specific types of meter;
in this work composed in Apabhraṃśa, the cantos are called *kuḍavakas*, and it likewise contains various meters suitable for the Apabhraṃśa language. (ViSd 6.327)
For example—Karṇaparākrama.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, dha) Those called *kaḍavakas*—that is, those named *kaḍavakas*.
Due to the absence of rules regarding language and its dialects, such poetry is devoid of formal cantos;
it consists of verses directed toward a single theme and is free from the requirements of formal junctures.
For example: *Bhikṣāṭana* and *Āryāvilāsa*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, na) Regarding "distinction of language": there is no restriction as to whether such a sentence is in Sanskrit or Prakrit.
A *khaṇḍakāvya* (minor poem) follows a single portion of a [larger] *kāvya*.
For example—the *Meghadūta* and others.
A *kośa*, however, is a collection of verses that are independent of one another.
That very same [work], composed according to the sequence of journeys, is exceedingly charming.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"(vi, pa) Independent of one another"—that is, mutually independent.
Arrangement of similar things in one place is *vrajyā*,
such as a string of pearls and so forth;
now, [we shall discuss] poetic compositions (*gadyakāvya*).
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, pha) He states the meaning of the term *vrajyā*: "of those belonging to the same class" (*sajātīyānām*).
Their commonality of class (*sājātya*) consists in the unity of the subject being described (*varṇanīya*).

Regarding that, prose (*gadya*) is of two kinds: that which is devoid of the scent of meter (*vṛttagandha*), known as *muktaka*, and that which possesses the scent of meter (*vṛttagandhin*). (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 6.330)
There are four types of *cūrṇaka*: primarily *utkalikā* and [the others];
the first is devoid of compounds, while the latter is endowed with metrical sections (*vṛttabhāga*).
Another [type] is rich in long compounds, while the fourth has few compounds;
it is devoid of the scent of meter, as stated in the *Vijñapriyā* (vi, ba).
The general definition of prose (*gadya*).
He states its fourfold classification, beginning with "the detached" (*muktaka*); the first is the detached.
"Paraṃ vṛttagandhiḥ": *vṛtta* means a meter measured by the number of syllables; the meaning is that it possesses one part of such a meter. *Turyaṃ* means the fourth, namely the *cūrṇaka*.
An example of the *muktaka* (detached) type is: “The teacher in speech, the great one in chest,” and so forth.

An example of the *vṛttagandhi* (resembling a verse) type is my own: “The city of his enemies awakened by the twang of the bowstring as the bow was drawn into a circle by his thick, battle-itching staff-like arms,” and so forth.

Here, the line "kuṇḍalīkṛtakodaṇḍa" is a quarter-verse (pāda) of the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and the line "samarakaṇḍūla," with its first two syllables removed, is likewise a quarter-verse of that same meter. An example of the *utkalikāprāya* [meter] is as follows from my own work: "aṇisavisumaraṇisidasaravisaravidalidasamaraparigadapavaraparavala—" and so forth.
An example of *cūrṇaka* (the powdered style) is as follows: "O ocean of the jewels of virtues! O sole connoisseur of the world!
O you who madden women!"
"Delighting the people," and so forth.

*Vijñapriyā* explains: "In the arms, which are thick, firm, and bristling with the vigor for battle (*samarotsāha-kaṇḍula*), the enemy city was swallowed up by the roar of the string of the curved bow."
"By which" means "by such [a person]. Here, he demonstrates that it is endowed with a metrical portion, saying: "In this."

"Devoid of the first three syllables"— this refers to the subsequent quarter-verse of this very *anuṣṭubh* verse [beginning with] "samara," where the three syllables are replaced by "kaṇḍūlanibiḍabhūjaḥ."
It is of such a nature.
Regarding "aṇiśe": the Sanskrit equivalent is *aniśaviṣamaniśitaśaravisaravidalitaparighagadapara-bala*.

This means: because he possesses a hostile army (*parabala*) in which the iron clubs (*parighas*), mallets (*mudgaras*), and maces (*gadās*) have been shattered by the discharge—that is, the falling—of incessant (*aniśam*), uneven (*viṣama*), and sharpened (*niśita*) arrows (*śaras*).
"He" means "of such a kind.

Regarding the passage beginning with "ocean of the jewels of virtues" (*guṇaratnasāgara*) and so forth: here, there are two names ending in *ra* and two vocatives ending in *n*, both with short compounds.
In this narrative (*kathā*), the charming subject matter is composed entirely in prose (*gadya*). (VisSd 6.332)
In some places here there may be Āryās, and in others Vaktras or Apavaktras;
at the beginning, there is a salutation in verses, followed by the description of the conduct of wicked people and the like.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) Regarding the phrase "possessing the excellence of narrative poetry" (*kathārūpakāvyadharamānaha*): in the word *kathā*, the meter is composed of *āryā* measures.
*Vaktra* and *apavaktraka* are specific types of meter.
He states its other characteristics, beginning with the word "at the beginning":
for example, the *Kādambarī* and similar works.
An *ākhyāyikā* is like a *kathā*, consisting of the poet's own lineage;
in it, the deeds of other poets are also recounted, with verse interspersed here and there.
The division of narrative sections is called an *āśvāsa*, composed in any meter whatsoever, such as *āryā*, *vaktra*, or *apavaktra*. (VisSd 6.335)
The indication of future events at the beginning of a narrative under a pretext is [the definition].
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ya) states the characteristics of poetry in the form of an *ākhyāyikā*: "It is called an *ākhyāyikā*... [and so forth].
Regarding the term *kathāvat*—it means that the story possesses qualities similar to those qualities already mentioned.
He states the distinction from *kathā* with the words "of the poet" (*kaveḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "in this"—the meaning is that in this *ākhyāyikā*, there is the mention of the lineage and so forth of other poets.
"Thus" means that in some instances, the meter is defined by the number of syllables in the verse.
"Āśvāsa" means a section consisting merely of a consolation.

"Āryā" means that among the various meters such as the Āryā and others, by whichever meter the opening of the *āśvāsa* begins, there is an indication of the future meaning—the subject matter to be discussed—by way of another pretext, that is, under a different guise.

For example, the *Harṣacarita* and others. However, because of the statement of the teacher Daṇḍin, "But an absence of restriction is observed there as well, since it is composed by others," some say that an *ākhyāyikā* must be composed by the hero himself.
That is incorrect;
for narrative accounts (*ākhyāna*) and the like are not mentioned separately because they are included within the categories of *kathā* (tale) and *ākhyāyikā* (romance).
As Daṇḍin himself has stated: "The remaining varieties of narrative accounts will be included herein."
Thus.
An example of these is the *Pañcatantra* and similar works.
*Vijñapriyā*:

Regarding what was said by someone that "the *ākhyāyikā* must be composed by the hero himself," the meaning is that this is incorrect because of the statement of the teacher Daṇḍin beginning with "āpitu" [and so forth].
He states the separate logical basis for other types of poetry such as the *ākhyāna* and others: "The *ākhyāna*s, etc."—that is, because it was stated by Daṇḍin himself.
"In this very [context]"—the meaning is "and so forth.
Now, those consisting of both prose and verse:
"A poem (*kāvyam*) consisting of both prose and verse is designated as *campū*. (VisSd 6.336)
Vijñapriyā: (vi, la) He mentions another type of poetry called *campū*, characterized by being composed of both prose and verse— as,
for example, the *Deśarājacarita*.
A panegyric of a king composed in both prose and verse is called a *viruda*;
for example—the *Virudamaṇimālā*.
*Vijñapriyā*:
The *virudamaṇimālā* is a specific type of literary composition; the *karambhaka*, however, is composed in various languages. (VisSd 6.337)
Just as my *Praśastiratnāvalī* consists of sixteen languages,
so too other varieties have not been defined separately, because they are well-known merely by their enumeration and do not transcend the varieties already mentioned.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, śa) "In the same way, there are other divisions as well;
they are not defined separately"—this is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*).
He states the reason for their being defined separately: "because they are established by mere enumeration.
This means they are established simply by the mention of each one individually, rather than by having a formal definition composed;
he says this because they are already encompassed by the definitions of the aforementioned divisions.
Thus ends the exposition of the sixth chapter in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa-ṭīkā* composed by Śrī Maheśvara Nyāyālaṅkāra;
this concludes the sixth chapter of the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*, titled "The Definition of Dramatic and Recited Poetry."
